title: Data Warehousing and Data Mining
text:
Preface
These lecture notes cover the full end-to-end data value cycle: analytical warehouse design, pattern mining, preprocessing, supervised classification, and probabilistic modeling. Each topic combines rigorous theoretical foundations with executable Python code.

title: Data Warehousing and Data Mining
text:
Part I
    Data Warehouses & ETL
    DW architecture, multidimensional modeling, ETL/ELT pipelines with PySpark on Databricks, heterogeneous sources, and OLAP cubes.
  
  
    Part II
    Data Mining Process
    CRISP-DM methodology, univariate and multivariate EDA, preprocessing with sklearn Pipelines, missing data imputation, PCA, and feature selection.
  
  
    Part III
    Pattern Mining
    Association rules: Apriori and FP-Growth. Support, confidence, lift, conviction, leverage, and Zhang metrics.
  
  
    Part IV
    Supervised Classification
    CART decision trees, Random Forests, XGBoost, SVMs, logistic regression, Naive Bayes, GMMs, neural networks, and ROC-AUC evaluation.
  
  
    Part V
    Unsupervised Learning
    K-Means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, t-SNE, UMAP, and autoencoders for uncovering latent structure without labels.
  
  
    Cross-Cutting
    Python & Modern Tooling
    PySpark, Databricks, Delta Lake, dbt, scikit-learn, PyTorch, and JAX with interactive visualizations in every chapter.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
text:
1.1 Identification of Stakeholders
In most data mining and data warehousing courses, the starting point is usually a clean database or a supervised learning algorithm such as decision trees or logistic regression. However, in the real world, analytical projects do not begin with data ready to be processed. They begin with a business need, a vague question, or an operational problem expressed by people who do not necessarily understand algorithms or dimensional modeling.
The success of a data project is not measured by the accuracy of the model (for example, an AUC of 0.95), but by the economic or strategic impact it generates for the organization. Therefore, the initial phase of any successful data project, Business Understanding (the initial phase of the CRISP-DM methodology that we will study later in the course (Chapman et al. 2000)), is the most critical. Before writing the first line of code or importing modeling libraries, we must deeply understand what the organization seeks to solve. To execute this successfully, it is essential to master communication with stakeholders (interested parties) and translate their qualitative needs into structured quantitative technical problems.
In analytics and data mining projects, identifying stakeholders makes it possible to understand who will use the results, who might be affected, and who has the capacity to guide or decide the project’s direction. Following the identification and analysis techniques described by Bryson (2004), stakeholders can be studied using two complementary criteria: their relationship with the organization and their role within the project.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
text:
Definition (stakeholder or interested party). According to the Community Tool Box framework from the University of Kansas (Center for Community Health and Development, University of Kansas 2023), a stakeholder is any person, group, or organization that can be affected by a project, or that can directly or indirectly influence its development and success. This definition builds upon the classic stakeholder theory proposed by Freeman (1984) and widely adopted in modern project management.





1.1.1 Classification by Relationship with the Organization
One way to classify stakeholders is based on their relationship with the organization responsible for the project.




  
    Stakeholders by Relationship with the Organization
  

  
    Organization
  

  

    
      Internal Stakeholders

      
        Part of the organization and directly participate in its decisions, processes, or activities.
      

      
        Owners
        Shareholders
        Executives
        Employees
      
    

    
      External Stakeholders

      
        Not part of the organization, but may be affected by or influence its activities.
      

      
        Customers
        Community
        Suppliers
        Government
        Banks
        Authorities
      
    

  



1.1.2 Classification by Role in the Project
This second classification does not replace the previous one. The same stakeholder can be internal or external while simultaneously being primary, secondary, or key.




  
    Stakeholders by Role in the Project
  

  
    Analytical Project
  

  

    
      Primary

      
        Directly receive the benefits or consequences of the project results.
      

      
        Examples:
        end users, customers, and operators.
      
    

    
      Secondary

      
        Indirectly affected because the project modifies their processes, responsibilities, or environment.
      

      
        Examples:
        IT teams, DBAs, and legal department.
      
    

    
      Key

      
        Have authority, influence, specialized knowledge, or funding capacity over the project.
      

      
        Examples:
        sponsors, executives, and regulators.
      
    

  

  
    Important: categories can overlap. A key stakeholder can also be primary or secondary, depending on how they participate in the project.
  



1.1.3 Example: An International Airport

In the operations of an international airport, internal stakeholders can be identified, such as the airport authority, security personnel, and operational managers; and external stakeholders, such as passengers, airlines, suppliers, ground transportation companies, government agencies, and investors.
If an analytical system is developed to predict delays, passengers, pilots, and operators could be considered primary stakeholders; service providers and ground transportation companies, secondary stakeholders; and the airport authority, regulatory bodies, and project sponsors, key stakeholders.
The classification depends on the scope of the project and how each actor is affected or can influence decisions.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
section: 1.2 Stakeholder Analysis: The Power vs. Interest Grid
text:
1.2 Stakeholder Analysis: The Power vs. Interest Grid
To manage expectations efficiently and prevent a lack of alignment from derailing a data project, the Power vs. Interest Grid (also known as the Influence/Interest Matrix) is used. Originally proposed by Mendelow (1981) and adopted as a standard stakeholder management practice by the PMBOK Guide (Project Management Institute 2017), this tool classifies stakeholders on a grid based on two key dimensions:

Power (Influence): The ability to change the project direction, allocate resources, approve deliverables, or cancel it entirely.
Interest: The level of attention and concern the stakeholder has regarding the impact of the project on their area.

Below is the strategic alignment matrix diagram for data analytics projects:

  
    
    
      High Power
      Low Power
    
    
    
    
      
      
        
          
          Keep Satisfied
        
        High Power, Low Interest. Engage at key security, legal, and IT touchpoints to avoid late blockages.
      

      
      
        
          
          Manage Closely
        
        High Power, High Interest. Sponsors and key business leaders. Strategic project partners.
      

      
      
        
          
          Monitor
        
        Low Power, Low Interest. Minimal communication effort. Passive progress tracking.
      

      
      
        
          
          Keep Informed
        
        Low Power, High Interest. Operational model users. Provide valuable feedback.
      
    
  
  
  
  
    Low Interest
    High Interest
  


1.2.1 Quadrant Management Strategies

High Power, High Interest (Manage Closely): Must actively participate in project planning phases, validate intermediate deliverables, and receive regular progress reports.
High Power, Low Interest (Keep Satisfied): Engage at critical checkpoints. It is essential to ensure that the project complies with security, governance, and cloud governance regulations.
Low Power, High Interest (Keep Informed): Keep them enthusiastic and informed about how the model will ease their work. Requesting early feedback is vital.
Low Power, Low Interest (Monitor): Passively monitor with general communication.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
section: 1.3 Scope Definition and Translation of Business Questions
text:
1.3 Scope Definition and Translation of Business Questions
One of the most frequent errors in analytics projects is accepting a business question as originally phrased and immediately starting to work with the data. Expressions such as “we want to prevent customers from leaving” or “we need to increase sales” convey a legitimate concern, but they do not yet constitute an analytical objective.
The analyst’s role is not solely to extract data or build models. They must also act as a translator between business needs and the organization’s analytical capabilities. This involves transforming a general concern into a concrete, measurable question tied to a decision.
Scope definition—or scoping—is the process by which the following are clarified:

the problem to be solved;
the decision to be taken based on the result;
the population or unit of analysis;
the relevant time frame;
the success metrics;
operational constraints;
and the expected delivery format.

Only after establishing these elements does it make sense to evaluate what data is available and what methodology could be used.
This translation is the starting point for any analytical project. Once the business need is understood, the team can study the available data, prepare it, perform the analysis, evaluate whether the results answer the original question, and, when necessary, deploy a solution into production. Therefore, scope definition is not a formality prior to analysis: it is the stage that guides all subsequent decisions.

1.3.1 From Business Problem to Analytical Objective
A qualitative question must pass through several layers of definition before becoming a technical objective. The goal is not to replace stakeholder language with statistical jargon, but to build a shared specification that connects analysis with concrete action.


  
    1. Need
    Business question
    “We want to prevent customers from leaving.”
  

  →

  
    2. Refinement
    Analytical translation
    Define churn, population, time horizon, variables, and expected action.
  

  →

  
    3. Specification
    Quantitative objective
    Estimate which customers have the highest probability of cancelling their subscription in the next 30 days.
  


In this example, the outcome of the process is not yet the selection of an algorithm. Deciding in advance that XGBoost, Random Forest, or any other technique will be used can restrict the analysis before understanding the problem. The methodology should be chosen after confirming the objective, reviewing the data, and establishing how the solution’s utility will be evaluated.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
text:
1.4 Iterative Refinement Through Questioning
A stakeholder’s initial question rarely contains all the necessary context. Therefore, scope definition should be treated as an iterative conversation rather than a single-pass questionnaire.
A useful strategy is to move forward layer by layer. Each response allows for formulating a more precise question, detecting assumptions, and returning to the stakeholder to validate understanding. The cycle ends when both parties can clearly articulate what will be analyzed, what it will be used for, and how a useful outcome will be recognized.


  
    Objective Refinement Cycle
    Each response generates a more specific question and a new validation opportunity.
  

  

    
      LAYER 1
      Context
      What situation prompted the request?
    

    →

    
      LAYER 2
      Decision
      What decision will change with the analysis?
    

    →

    
      LAYER 3
      Measurement
      What metric represents the expected outcome?
    

    →

    
      LAYER 4
      Scope
      To whom, when, and under what constraints does it apply?
    

    →

    
      LAYER 5
      Validation
      Does this formulation represent the true need?
    

  

  
    ↺ If ambiguities, unconfirmed assumptions, or new constraints appear, return to the corresponding layer and reformulate the objective.
  



1.4.1 Strategies for Asking Better Questions
Several inquiry strategies can be combined during this cycle:

Ask about context before asking about the solution.
Instead of starting with “what dashboard do you need?”, it is better to ask “what situation motivated this request?”. This avoids confusing delivery format with the problem to be solved.
Connect analysis with a decision.
Questions such as “what would you do differently if you had this information?” help determine if the analysis will have a concrete application. If no decision is attached, the request may still be too broad.
Turn ambiguous concepts into operational definitions.
Terms like active customer, churn, success, profitability, or underperformance can mean different things across departments. The analyst must ask how they are practically observed and calculated.
Define population, timeframe, and level of detail.
It is necessary to specify whether analysis will be conducted by customer, transaction, product, store branch, or region, as well as establishing the relevant historical window and future horizon.
Explore constraints and actionability.
Detecting a pattern is not enough if the organization cannot act upon it. Ask what interventions are available, their cost, and how many cases the team can handle.
Reformulate and validate.
After listening to responses, the analyst should summarize the shared understanding: “So, what we need is…”. This reformulation allows the stakeholder to correct misinterpretations before investing time in analysis.



1.4.2 Example of a Refinement Conversation
Suppose a stakeholder presents the following need:

“We want to prevent customers from leaving.”

The conversation might progress as follows:

Context: What recent behavior indicates that a churn problem exists?
Definition: What exactly does it mean for a customer to “leave”: cancel, stop purchasing, or remain inactive?
Population: Does the issue affect all customers or a specific segment?
Horizon: How far in advance do we need to identify the risk?
Decision: What action will be taken when a customer is flagged as high-risk?
Capacity: How many customers can the retention team contact each week?
Success: How will success be measured: churns prevented, revenue retained, or campaign ROI?
Validation: Is the priority to identify as many potential churners as possible, even if it leads to some false positives?

After this iteration, the original question might be reformulated as follows:

Analytical Objective: Identify weekly monthly-subscription customers with the highest probability of cancelling over the next 30 days, using their activity over the last 90 days, to prioritize up to 2,000 contacts for the retention team. The solution will be evaluated on its ability to identify actual cancellations and on revenue retained through intervention.

This formulation establishes a target population, observation window, prediction horizon, operational capacity, and metric of business value. From here, the team can evaluate data availability and compare candidate methodologies.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
text:
1.5 Examples of Business Question Translation








Stakeholder Question
Analytical Translation
Possible Methodology




How can we increase average order value in the online store?
Identify products that tend to be purchased together and evaluate which combinations could be used in recommendation systems during checkout.
Association rules—Apriori or FP-Growth—evaluated via support, confidence, and lift.


How do we prevent customer churn in monthly subscriptions?
Estimate cancellation probability during the next 30 days based on recent activity, aiming to prioritize retention interventions.
Supervised classification models evaluated with metrics aligned with operational capacity and intervention costs.


We want personalized campaigns, but don’t know how to group customers.
Identify customer clusters displaying similar recency, frequency, monetary value, and purchasing patterns.
RFM segmentation and clustering techniques like K-Means or DBSCAN, paired with profile interpretation.


We need to know if end-of-year discounts worked.
Estimate the net margin effect of discounts and isolate it from seasonal shifts or concurrent factors.
Causal inference or quasi-experimental analysis, depending on control group availability and historical data.



These methodologies are starting points, not automated decisions. The final choice depends on data quality, underlying assumptions, and how the results will be operationalized.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
text:
1.6 The Data Request Process
Once the objective is validated, the agreement should be recorded. The Data Request is the formal mechanism through which business units communicate a need to the analytics team and document context, scope, and success criteria.

Definition — Data Request: A formal process, typically represented via an intake form or ticket, that captures business needs and key details to evaluate, prioritize, and execute an analytical project.

The request ticket does not replace conversation with the stakeholder. Its function is to preserve agreements reached during refinement and minimize subsequent ambiguity.

1.6.1 Key Elements of a Data Request Ticket

Main Problem or Question
What situation needs to be understood, solved, or improved?
Business Context
Why did this need arise, and why is it relevant now?
Expected Action or Decision
What will be done differently based on the result?
Population and Scope
Which customers, products, transactions, regions, or time periods are included?
Success Metrics
How will the business determine if the analysis was useful?
Known or Suggested Data Sources
Are there existing tables, files, systems, or third-party providers with relevant data?
Delivery Format
Is an exploratory analysis, report, dashboard, prioritized list, experiment, or embedded model required?
Validation Lead
Who will sign off on definitions, results, and downstream decisions?
Constraints and Risks
Are there timelines, privacy concerns, budget limits, operational capacities, or data quality risks?
Target Decision Date
By when must the results be delivered to remain actionable?

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
text:
1.7 Conclusion
The quality of an analytical project depends heavily on the quality of the originating question. An ambiguous goal can produce technically sound but useless analysis; a well-defined goal enables coherent selection of data, metrics, and methods.
Defining scope means building a shared understanding between the stakeholder and data team. To achieve this, analysts must ask, listen, reformulate, and validate iteratively. The result is not merely a technical question, but an explicit bridge between data, decisions, and business value.

title: 1  Requirements and Stakeholder Management
section: 1.8 Practical Case Study: Alignment at TheLook eCommerce
text:
1.8 Practical Case Study: Alignment at TheLook eCommerce
Imagine you are hired as the Lead Data Analyst at TheLook eCommerce (the recurring case study used throughout this course). The Marketing Director approaches you with the following request:

“I need a report with all customers and everything they buy because women’s clothing sales fell this month and we want to launch a discount.”

If you act reactively, you will write a heavy SQL query, export a multi-gigabyte CSV with millions of rows, and email it. This is a direct path to project failure: the stakeholder will fail to open the file due to size limits, or spend hours filtering Excel without extracting clear conclusions.

1.8.1 The Strategic Alignment Conversation

You (Analyst): “To refine the data extraction, what is the target of the discount campaign? Are we looking to win back inactive customers, or encourage active buyers to try higher-margin categories?”
Director (Stakeholder): “We want to encourage customers who regularly buy designer dresses to explore our new high-margin luxury accessories line.”
You (Analyst): “Great. Instead of exporting all customers, I will pull a focused report on high-frequency buyers in the women’s/dresses category. I will also run an association rule model to identify which accessories are most commonly bought alongside dresses to suggest targeted bundles.”

Outcome: You saved technical effort from extracting entire databases, delivered a high-impact analysis targeting high-margin conversions, and aligned business expectations from day one.

title: 2  Data Team Roles and the Data Lifecycle
text:
2.0.1 Comparison of Data Engineering and Data Science Roles
In modern organizations, analytics projects are rarely developed by a single individual. As data volume grows and technologies specialize, the need for multidisciplinary teams arises. According to the DAMA-DMBOK data governance framework (DAMA International 2017) and the characterization of the data scientist role by Davenport and Patil (2012), there are four main profiles, each with specific responsibilities, tools, and deliverables.
The dimensional modeling practices employed by the Data Architect, which we will revisit in Part I of the course, follow the classic methodology of Kimball and Ross (2013).

title: 2  Data Team Roles and the Data Lifecycle
text:
2.1 The Data Lifecycle






Definition (Data Lifecycle). The sequence of phases through which information passes within an organization, from initial planning to eventual secure disposal, passing through ingestion, storage, and analysis (DAMA International 2017).



The data lifecycle describes the sequence of phases through which information passes within an organization. This cycle is fundamental for structuring the development of this course: Part I (Data Warehouses) mainly covers the capture and storage phases, while Part II (Data Mining) focuses on strategic and predictive analysis.
Neither infrastructure management (storage phase) nor applied analytics (exploration and modeling phase) occurs in isolation. They are integrated within a sequential and iterative process for data projects. Before building any model or database, we must go through stages that help us evaluate project viability: business understanding, data collection and inspection, preprocessing, and subsequent evaluation of results to ensure successful production deployment. This structured approach is what sets professional analytical projects apart from academic proofs-of-concept.
The lifecycle consists of six key stages (Google 2022):

  
  1. Plan
  ➔
  2. Capture
  ➔
  3. Manage
  ➔
  4. Analyze
  ➔
  5. Archive
  ➔
  6. Destroy



Plan: Determine data requirements to solve the business problem, define necessary sources, and identify the required team.
Capture: Collect data from internal and external sources (transactional databases, web logs, APIs). In this phase, data is extracted and prepared.
Manage: Store data in a structured manner within relational databases or analytical data warehouses. Here, security policies, initial cleaning, and data lineage are enforced.
Analyze: Explore data using statistics and data mining (EDA), and train analytical models to answer key questions or automate processes.
Archive: Move historical data that is no longer queried frequently to low-cost passive storage systems (e.g., Glacier or Google Cloud Coldline Storage), safeguarding it against accidental modifications.
Destroy: Permanently delete data once the required retention period has expired, ensuring that no residual or unsecure copies of personally identifiable information (PII) remain under secure erasure policies.

title: 2  Data Team Roles and the Data Lifecycle
text:
2.2 Critical Phases of Data Management
Regardless of the stage of the lifecycle, two questions cross the entire process: how sensitive is the data being handled and who is permitted to access it. Neither is resolved informally; both are governed through explicit policies that the data team must know before touching a single table.

2.2.1 Data Requiring Special Handling
Not all data presents the same risk level if exposed or misused. Certain categories—known as sensitive data or special categories—require additional collection, storage, and access controls:

Personally Identifiable Information (PII): Name, address, official ID number, email, or any data allowing a person to be directly or indirectly identified.
Health Data: Clinical records, diagnoses, or lab results; explicitly protected in Mexico as sensitive personal data under the Federal Law on Protection of Personal Data Held by Private Parties (Congreso de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos 2010).
Financial and Biometric Data: Credit card numbers, credit history, fingerprints, or facial recognition.

Thus, before capturing any of these data types, the minimization principle is applied: collect only what is strictly necessary to answer the business question, rather than hoarding sensitive information “just in case”, which increases risk without contributing analytical value.


2.2.2 Governance, Usage Policy, and Access Control
The most common way to mitigate these risks is working with a data usage policy: a formal document defining what data exists, who can query it, under what conditions, and for what purpose. In modern enterprises, this policy is typically designed by the Data Architect alongside legal and security teams, and translates operationally into:

Least Privilege Access Control: Each user or role receives specific access capabilities limited strictly to data essential for their function—a Data Analyst can query aggregated sales by region, but not necessarily individual credit card numbers—implemented via Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
Encryption: Of data at rest and in transit.
Data Catalog: An updated inventory documenting sensitive fields, data owners (data owners), and applicable retention rules, preventing misinterpretations between teams.



  
  
    
      Operational Data Governance Framework
    
    
      The usage policy connects data owners with technical controls and stakeholders who need to utilize the information.
    
  

  
  
    1. Responsibility and Oversight
  

  

    
      
      Data Owner
      
        Defines purpose, sensitivity, and usage rules for the data.
      
    

    
      
      Data Architect / Steward
      
        Translates policies into standards, metadata, and processes.
      
    

    
      
      Legal & Security
      
        Validate privacy, regulatory compliance, and risk management.
      
    

  

  
  
    ↓
  

  
  
    
      Central Framework
    
    
      Data Usage and Governance Policy
    
    
      Establishes what data exists, who can use it,
      for what purpose, under what conditions, and
      for how long.
    
  

  
  
    ↓
  

  
  
    2. Operational Controls
  

  

    
      
      Least Privilege
      
        IAM, RBAC, and permissions restricted to function needs.
      
    

    
      
      Protection
      
        Encryption at rest and in transit, anonymization, and masking.
      
    

    
      
      Data Catalog
      
        Classification, definitions, owners, lineage, and retention rules.
      
    

    
      
      Monitoring & Auditing
      
        Query logging, periodic reviews, and misuse alerts.
      
    

  

  
  
    3. Governed Access Flow
  

  

    
      Request
      Need & Purpose
    

    →

    
      Evaluation
      Role, Risk & Sensitivity
    

    →

    
      Authorization
      Owner Approval
    

    →

    
      Access
      Minimal & Temporary Permission
    

    →

    
      Review
      Audit, Renew, or Revoke
    

  

  
  
    Outcome:
    discoverable, understandable, protected data used solely by authorized individuals.
  


This principle of least privilege—granting each user only essential access, and no more—is now the de facto standard across the industry: it is as relevant for the Data Engineer configuring permissions in Snowflake or BigQuery as it is for the Data Analyst requesting access to a Data Warehouse table.

2.3 Guided Activity: Designing a Lifecycle Plan for TheLook eCommerce
As an introductory practical activity for this course, you will design the initial data plan for the fictitious company TheLook eCommerce, based on requirement requests from the executive board of the Marketing and Sales departments.

2.3.1 Business Scenario
TheLook eCommerce has grown rapidly thanks to its omnichannel offering. However, its current data infrastructure is chaotic. The Marketing team has identified four main business questions they need answered to launch effective campaigns next quarter.


2.3.2 Goal Alignment and Data Planning Exercise
For each business question, we will associate its analytical objective and identify the necessary data that must be captured and managed in our future Data Warehouse.









#
Business Question (Stakeholder)
Analytical Objective
Data Required to Capture




1
“Which products should we promote together on our homepage?”
Discover association rules between product categories co-purchased by users.
• Order history (orders and order_items).• Product ID and clickstream history from browsing sessions.


2
“How can we optimize inventory levels of women’s dresses across regional warehouses?”
Predict weekly future demand for specific products by geographical location.
• Daily warehouse inventory logs (inventory_items).• Shipping addresses and postal codes of historical purchases.


3
“What is the long-term cumulative value of customers acquired through paid Google ads?”
Calculate Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) grouped by acquisition channel.
• User tables (users) with registration date and referral channel.• Total historical transaction value linked to each unique user ID.


4
“How do we detect and prevent fraudulent returns of high-cost merchandise?”
Develop a suspicious transaction classifier prior to return processing.
• Return history by user.• Payment methods and elapsed time between delivery and return request.

title: 3  Real Project Planning: The Business Understanding Canvas
text:
3.1 Step 1: The Stakeholder Meeting Log
In the previous chapter, you learned to identify stakeholders, map them onto the power vs. interest grid, and translate qualitative questions into analytical objectives. However, in a real-world project, that translation does not happen spontaneously inside your head: it is documented. A professional data team leaves a written audit trail of every business conversation and condenses that evidence into a single-page artifact that any team member—or any new stakeholder—can read in five minutes and understand exactly what will be done, why, and how success will be measured.
That artifact is the Business Understanding Canvas. It serves as the tangible output of the first phase of any structured data mining methodology (you will formalize this later as the Business Understanding phase of CRISP-DM (Chapman et al. 2000; Shearer 2000; Wirth and Hipp 2000)). Here, we will build it practically around a real case study so that when you reach the full methodological framework, you already have an intuitive grasp of the problem each component solves.
In this chapter, you will construct the five core pieces that comprise a project’s business understanding documentation:
We will do this by continuing the TheLook eCommerce case study introduced in the previous chapter, where the Marketing Director requested a drive to promote the new luxury accessories line among frequent buyers of designer dresses.
Before synthesizing anything, the conversation is documented exactly as it occurred. A meeting log is not an embellished summary: it is an accurate record of who said what, what was agreed upon, and what remains pending. It serves as a single source of truth if scope disagreements arise later.

3.1.1 Essential Components of a Meeting Log

Metadata: Date, time, duration, modality, and location.
Participants: Name, role, and quadrant on the power/interest grid.
Context: What triggered the meeting.

Decisions and Agreements: What was explicitly accepted by both parties.
Action Items and Next Steps: With assigned owners and deadlines.



3.1.2 Applied Example: “Luxury Accessories” Project Kickoff

title: 3  Real Project Planning: The Business Understanding Canvas
section: 3.2 Step 2: The Business Understanding Canvas (Single Page)
text:
3.2 Step 2: The Business Understanding Canvas (Single Page)
The canvas condenses the meeting log into six blocks that anyone from business or technical teams can review in minutes. These six blocks correspond directly to tasks defined in the CRISP-DM guide (Chapman et al. 2000) for the Business Understanding phase—determining business objectives, assessing the situation, determining data mining goals, and producing a project plan—unfolded here into business and technical success criteria. Unlike the meeting log (which is chronological and detailed), the canvas is timeless and synthetic: it is the document archived and referenced throughout the project.


  
    1. Business Objectives
    Increase the gross margin of frequent designer dress buyers through cross-selling luxury accessories before the end-of-year campaign.
  

  
    2. Business Success Criteria
    +8% incremental margin in the pilot segment during the 6 weeks post-launch, measured against a control group.
  

  
    3. Situation Assessment
    
      Resources: Access to TheLook DW (tables orders, order_items, users, inventory_items); one data analyst; Inventory Manager as stock availability source.
      Requirements: Actionable results within 6 weeks; recommendations adhering to regional stock availability.
      Assumptions: Historical co-purchase behavior (dress + accessory) is representative of future customer behavior.
      Risks: See risk table in the following section.
    
  

  
    4. Data Mining Objectives
    Discover association rules between designer dresses and accessories, and generate a recommendation ranking per customer, filtered by regional inventory availability.
  

  
    5. Technical Success
    Lift > 1.2 and confidence > 30% on association rules selected for the campaign.
  

  
    6. Project Plan
    Week 1: extraction and EDA of segment. Weeks 2-3: association rules and inventory validation. Week 4: review with Marketing Director. Weeks 5-6: controlled pilot and incremental margin measurement.
  


Note that Block 5 (Technical Success) uses a model metric (lift, confidence), whereas Block 2 (Business Success Criteria) uses a financial metric (incremental margin). This distinction is intentional and explored further in the next step.

section: 3.4 Step 4: Success Criteria in Business Terms
text:
3.4 Step 4: Success Criteria in Business Terms
A common mistake among junior analysts is defining success exclusively through model metrics (accuracy, recall, AUC, lift). Those metrics are necessary but are not the project success criteria: they are the model success criteria. Stakeholders cannot evaluate whether an AUC of 0.83 represents a good investment; they can evaluate whether gross margin increased. This distinction between business objectives and data mining goals is, according to Provost and Fawcett (2013), the most frequent source of analytical projects that produce technically correct but commercially irrelevant models.








Criteria Type
Project Example
Evaluated By




Business (the one that matters to approve or cancel the project)
+8% incremental margin in pilot segment vs. control group over 6 weeks
Marketing Director


Technical (the one used by data team to iterate model)
Lift > 1.2 and confidence > 30% on association rules
Data Analyst









Rule of Thumb. Every project should summarize its success in a single sentence that a non-technical executive can repeat from memory. If that sentence contains a statistical term (AUC, lift, silhouette), you are likely describing technical success, not business success.

title: 3  Real Project Planning: The Business Understanding Canvas
text:
3.5 Step 5: Assumptions and Risks
Every canvas simplifies project complexity. Therefore, it must be complemented with a list of assumptions and a risk log.
An assumption is a condition accepted as true even if unverified. A risk is an uncertain event that could impact project development or results. Assumptions must be validated; risks must be evaluated and mitigated.

3.5.1 Assumptions
For the pilot project, the following assumptions are established:

Historical co-purchase behavior (e.g., dress + accessory) reasonably represents future customer behavior during the campaign.
Inventory files will be updated weekly during the six weeks of the pilot.
The frequent customer segment contains sufficient transaction volume to generate reliable association rules.
The Marketing team can incorporate recommendations into their campaign schedule.

Key assumptions should be tested in early stages. If any prove false, adjustments to data, methods, or scope may be required.


3.5.2 Risk Classification
Classifying risks ensures ownership allocation and prevents narrowing analysis strictly to technical issues. In analytics projects, five main categories are recognized:

Data: Quality, availability, recency, or representativeness issues.
Analytical: Bias, seasonality, overfitting, spurious associations, or performance decay.
Operational: Stock outages, insufficient operational capacity, or downstream processes unable to consume results.
Technological & Security: Integration failures, excessive permissions, unauthorized access, or system outages.
Legal, Ethical & Reputational: Misuse of personal data, algorithmic bias, or invasive personalization perception.

Adoption risks may also exist if end users do not understand, trust, or adopt the solution.


3.5.3 Risk Evaluation
Each risk must be evaluated based on its probability and impact. This scoring allows prioritizing risks requiring immediate attention.
Alongside mitigation plans, it is best practice to record:

Assigned owner;
Warning signal indicating risk occurrence;
Preventive control;
Contingency plan.

3.5.5 Risk Treatment and Follow-Up
After evaluating risks, the team can choose to:

Transfer: Share management with a vendor or specialized department.

The risk log should be reviewed during the pilot and updated as data, models, or operational conditions evolve.






A model can be technically correct and yet prove unusable if it relies on unauthorized data, recommends out-of-stock items, or produces outputs that operational teams cannot execute. Therefore, risks must be identified during business understanding and monitored throughout project execution.

title: 4  Introduction
text:
4.1 Architecture in Computer Science
In Computer Science (CS) and Software Engineering, the term architecture does not refer to the aesthetic design of a physical building, but to the definition and structure of complex digital systems.
A solid data architecture ensures that information is available to those who need it, in the proper format, securely, and with predictable performance. Yet that definition conceals a more fundamental question: why is it not enough to simply “save data to disk and call it a day”? Why has the industry spent four decades designing and redesigning how analytical data is persisted?
The answer has little to do with aesthetics or technological trends, and much to do with three very concrete physical constraints:
Every storage architecture—Data Warehouse, Data Lake, or Data Lakehouse, which we will study in subsequent chapters—is ultimately a distinct design choice along these three axes. Before defining them by name, it is worth understanding why they exist: their fundamental purpose from a technical perspective.

title: 4  Introduction
text:
Definition (Data Systems Architecture). The structural organization of hardware, software, and storage systems that enable capturing, transforming, organizing, and querying data at scale, defining information flows and operational boundaries between system components.






How information is laid out on disk/memory determines how fast (and how expensive) it is to answer a query.
How rigid or flexible the persistence system is determines which data types it can store efficiently, and how far it can scale.
How strict the consistency guarantees offered by the system are determines how costly it is to coordinate concurrent writes.

title: 4  Introduction
section: 4.2 Axis 1: The Cost of Reading Data — Rows vs. Columns
text:
4.2 Axis 1: The Cost of Reading Data — Rows vs. Columns
When a database engine executes a query, the bottleneck is rarely CPU performance; it is the volume of data that must be read from disk to answer it. How records are physically organized on storage—row by row or column by column—radically alters how much data must be fetched.






Definition (Row-oriented Storage). A persistence model where all values belonging to a single record (row) are stored contiguously on disk. This is the classic model for transactional systems (OLTP).









Definition (Column-oriented Storage). A persistence model where all values of a single attribute (column) are stored contiguously on disk, separating each table column into its own physical block. This is the dominant model for analytical systems (OLAP).




4.2.1 Visualization: Same Data, Two Distinct Physical Layouts


  
  
    Row-oriented (OLTP)
    Ideal for: INSERT, UPDATE, and fetching full records.
    
      [ 1, Ana, Sales, 3200 ]
      [ 2, Luis, IT, 4100 ]
      [ 3, Eva, Sales, 2900 ]
      [ 4, Iván, IT, 4600 ]
    
    To compute average salary, the engine must read all blocks, even though it only needs a single column.
  

  
  
    Column-oriented (OLAP)
    Ideal for: aggregations (AVG, SUM) across few columns and many rows.
    
      id: [1, 2, 3, 4]
      name: [Ana, Luis, Eva, Iván]
      department: [Sales, IT, Sales, IT]
      salary: [3200, 4100, 2900, 4600]
    
    For AVG(salary), the engine reads only the salary column block, skipping everything else.
  


This structural distinction, which might seem like an implementation detail, has massive implications at scale:

Reduced I/O: If a table has 50 columns and an analytical query only requires 3, a columnar engine reads, in theory, only 6% of the data a row-oriented engine would fetch.
Superior Compression: A single column holds homogenous data types with lower cardinality (for example, repeating department names), allowing far more aggressive compression algorithms than heterogeneous rows permit.
Vectorized Execution: Because values for a column sit contiguously in memory, CPUs can apply SIMD operations (summing, filtering, comparing) across entire vectors rather than evaluating record by record.

Consequently, transactional systems (operational databases for e-commerce, banking, or logistics) are row-oriented—they require fast writes and single-record lookups—while analytical systems (Data Warehouses, Data Lakehouses) are column-oriented, or use columnar file formats like Parquet or ORC, because their dominant workload involves aggregations over massive row counts.


4.2.2 OLTP vs. OLAP: Two Distinct Workloads
The choice between row-oriented and column-oriented storage is not arbitrary: it stems from the recognition, since the 1990s, that computing workloads fall into two fundamentally opposing paradigms.






Definition (OLTP / Online Transaction Processing). Workload dominated by high-concurrency write and read operations on individual records, demanding low latency per operation. This is the characteristic pattern of operational applications.









Definition (OLAP / Online Analytical Processing). Workload dominated by complex aggregation and exploratory queries over massive volumes of records, typically scanning a subset of columns with lower concurrency and tolerance for higher per-query latency.











Criterion
OLTP
OLAP




Objective
Record daily business operations
Analyze historical business performance


Typical Operation
INSERT / UPDATE of single records
SELECT ... GROUP BY across millions of rows


Operation Volume
Few rows, all columns fetched
Many rows, few columns fetched


Storage Pattern
Row-oriented

Users

Example
Processing a sale at a Point of Sale
Computing average regional sales over the past year



This comparison highlights why a Data Warehouse is never queried directly off an operational production database: they represent competing workloads vying for shared resources while requiring opposing physical storage layouts.

title: 4  Introduction
section: 4.3 Axis 2: The Cost of Rigidity — Homogeneous vs. Heterogeneous Data
text:
4.3 Axis 2: The Cost of Rigidity — Homogeneous vs. Heterogeneous Data
The second axis does not concern how data is laid out inside a table, but rather how willing the persistence system is to accept data that does not fit into a predefined tabular schema.
A traditional relational database requires data to match a rigid schema (defined columns, data types, and constraints) before ingestion. While exceptional for enforcing integrity, this creates a major barrier for non-tabular data: server logs, product images, nested JSON payloads with evolving structures, or audio transcripts.
For decades, organizations either discarded such unstructured data, forcibly transformed it into relational tables (losing context along the way), or stored it in isolated file servers detached from analytics pipelines.
Modern persistence systems solved this dilemma by combining two key concepts:

Object Storage (such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage): Storage systems that accept files without imposing schema constraints, offer low storage costs per byte, and scale near-infinitely.
Self-Describing Open File Formats (Parquet, Avro, JSON, ORC): Files that embed their own schema metadata, allowing structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data to coexist within the same repository without sacrificing query readability.

This pairing enables a Data Lake—and, subsequently, a Data Lakehouse—to house transactional tables, raw product images, and streaming web clickstreams side by side without requiring upfront schema enforcement. Schema resolution, when needed, occurs on read rather than on write.

4.3.1 Scaling Up vs. Scaling Out
The flexibility of a persistence system is also bound to its scaling strategy when data volumes surpass the limits of a single machine. Two primary strategies exist:






Definition (Scale-Up / Vertical Scaling). Strategy that increases system capacity by adding resources (CPU, RAM, disk) to a single machine. This is the traditional scaling model of monolithic relational databases.









Definition (Scale-Out / Horizontal Scaling). Strategy that increases system capacity by adding more nodes (servers), distributing data and processing tasks across a cluster. This is the native pattern of object storage and distributed computing.



Vertical scaling hits a physical and economic ceiling: single servers have hard limits on CPU and RAM, and high-end enterprise servers scale exponentially in cost as they approach those limits. Traditional Data Warehouse relational engines inherited this constraint.
Horizontal scaling, conversely, expands by appending nodes built from commodity hardware. This makes it cost-effective to persist petabytes of heterogeneous data in a Data Lake: capacity scales by adding distributed storage across commodity disks rather than upgrading expensive single-node hardware.

title: 4  Introduction
section: 4.4 Axis 3: The Cost of Consistency — ACID vs. BASE
text:
4.4 Axis 3: The Cost of Consistency — ACID vs. BASE
The third axis focuses not on read speed or data flexibility, but on how strictly the system guarantees that stored data remains in a consistent state, even amidst concurrent write operations or system failures.






Definition (ACID). Set of guarantees—Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability—ensuring that every transaction executes fully or not at all, preventing partial writes or corrupt states.









Definition (BASE). Set of relaxed guarantees—Basically Available, Soft state, and Eventual consistency—prioritizing availability and fault tolerance in distributed environments, accepting that different readers may temporarily observe slightly different versions of the data.



Enforcing ACID compliance incurs computational overhead: it demands synchronization primitives (locks, transaction logs, constraints) that become increasingly expensive across distributed nodes. Traditional relational databases (designed to scale vertically on single nodes or tightly coupled clusters) enforce ACID efficiently, whereas massively distributed object storage systems (designed to scale out across thousands of nodes) historically adopted BASE guarantees, accepting short consistency delays in exchange for infinite scale and high availability.
This challenge gave rise to the Data Lakehouse: introducing a transactional metadata layer that restores ACID guarantees on top of scalable, BASE-oriented object storage.

title: 4  Introduction
section: 4.5 The Purpose of Data Storage Architectures
text:
4.5 The Purpose of Data Storage Architectures
No single system simultaneously maximizes all three axes: query speed (rows vs. columns), schema flexibility (scale-up vs. scale-out), and consistency guarantees (ACID vs. BASE) exist in trade-off states, as each guarantee carries computational or architectural overhead.
This three-way trade-off defines the design choices behind modern data storage architectures:

A system may prioritize Axis 1 and Axis 3 (columnar storage and strict ACID), restricting inputs to structured data in exchange for exceptional query performance and absolute consistency.
A system may prioritize Axis 2 (horizontal scaling and BASE), ingesting any data format with near-unlimited scale, while relinquishing immediate transactional consistency.
A system may combine all three, overlaying a transactional metadata layer (ACID) on top of scalable, flexible object storage.

In subsequent chapters, we will examine the Data Warehouse, Data Lake, and Data Lakehouse—concrete implementations of these architectural trade-offs. The key insight is that none of these patterns are mere trends; each exists to solve, through deliberate design trade-offs, the fundamental physical constraints of data engineering.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
5.1 Data for Decision Making
Modern organizations generate vast volumes of data daily: sales, financial transactions, academic records, medical consultations, and digital interactions.
However, operating a business is fundamentally different from analyzing it. Operational systems are engineered to log transactions efficiently, not to answer strategic questions.
For instance:
requires a distinct structure optimized for historical analysis, aggregation, and temporal comparisons.
The difference represents a shift in perspective: operational systems observe each event as it occurs, while a Data Warehouse gathers those events to explain how the business changes over time. The former answers “what just happened?”; the latter helps answer “what pattern is emerging, and what decision should be taken?”.
In this context, data analysis does not begin with technology, but with a clear definition of the business problem. One of the most widely used frameworks to structure this process is CRISP-DM (Cross Industry Standard Process for Data Mining).
CRISP-DM proposes a systematic framework consisting of six phases:
Figure 1. CRISP-DM Process Diagram. Source: Wikimedia Commons, “CRISP-DM Process Diagram”, public domain.
CRISP-DM is not a linear process, but an iterative one. In practice, phases continuously feed back into one another. During modeling, data quality issues may be discovered, forcing a return to the preparation phase. During evaluation, it may emerge that the business problem was incompletely specified, requiring a return to the first phase. Even after deployment, outcomes generate new strategic questions, restarting the cycle.
This iterative nature matches organizational realities: decision-making is a continuous process of refinement and learning. Thus, before creating tables, defining dimensions, or selecting tech stacks, teams must address questions such as:
The data architecture must be flexible and scalable, allowing new sources, metrics, and dimensions to be added as business needs evolve. Data architecture is not an end in itself; it is the technical foundation enabling operational data to become actionable knowledge within a continuous improvement loop.
CRISP-DM defines the analytical workflow, while the Data Warehouse provides a reliable organizational memory to support it. Not every CRISP-DM project requires a Data Warehouse, but when questions require combining multiple sources, comparing periods, and reusing consistent metrics, the data warehouse becomes a core element.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
A sales system records individual purchases.
But answering questions like:

Which product sold the most over the past year?
How have sales evolved over the last five years?
Which store branch exhibits top performance?





  
    
      Daily Operations
      Sales, enrollments, payments, consultations, and individual events.
      Question: What just happened?
    
    →
    
      Data Warehouse
      Integrates sources, standardizes definitions, and preserves a queryable historical memory.
      Function: Convert disparate events into context.
    
    →
    
      Informed Decision
      Trends, comparisons, KPIs, alerts, and shared domain insights.
      Question: What should we do?
    
  
  Conceptual Diagram: The Data Warehouse acts as a bridge between daily operations and decision-making.




Business Understanding: Identify strategic goals and translate them into analytical questions.

Data Understanding: Explore available data sources, evaluate quality, and detect inconsistencies.

Data Preparation: Clean, transform, and integrate information.

Modeling: Apply analytical techniques or statistical models.

Evaluation: Verify whether results meet the original business objectives.

Deployment: Implement findings into operations or decision support systems.




Figure 1. CRISP-DM Process






Which decisions does the organization wish to improve?

Which metrics are critical?

What time horizon needs to be analyzed?

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
5.2 Data Warehouse
William H. Inmon (1996) defines a Data Warehouse as:

“A data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, and non-volatile collection of data in support of management’s decision-making process.”

The four properties in this definition are interconnected. Together, they explain why a Data Warehouse offers a coherent, long-lasting view of the business:

  
    
      ◎
      Subject-Oriented
      Organizes data around business entities, such as customers, products, or students.
    
    
      ⇄
      Integrated
      Unifies codes, formats, business rules, and definitions across disparate systems.
    
    
      ◷
      Time-Variant
      Preserves historical states to compare time frames and track long-term trends.
    
    
      ◇
      Non-Volatile
      Prioritizes controlled loads and reads; history remains stable over time.
    
  
  Conceptual Diagram: Inmon's classic properties convert fragmented operational data into a shared analytical memory.

A Data Warehouse is subject-oriented, meaning it is structured around core business entities rather than operational applications. For example, in an insurance company, the warehouse is organized around concepts like customer, policy, or claim, rather than separate software modules like auto insurance or life insurance. The focus is analyzing business entities rather than technical modules.
It is time-variant because it preserves historical data. Records are not overwritten as in transactional databases; new records are appended over time. This enables trend analysis across five, ten, or more years, answering questions regarding diagnosis trends or long-term sales growth patterns.
It is integrated because it consolidates data from multiple systems. If one system records gender as “M”/“F” and another as 0/1, they must be transformed into a unified format prior to storage. The same applies to differing date formats, currencies, or product codes. Integration involves data cleaning, transformation, and standardization.
Finally, it is non-volatile, meaning it is physically separate from operational systems. It primarily supports loading and querying operations, without frequent updates or operational transactions. Its purpose is analytical rather than operational.
Together, these properties ensure metrics retain consistent meaning across departments and time frames. For example, comparing student retention rates across cohorts is valid only if student identity, retention definitions, and academic calendars share unified rules, and historical records are preserved.
Reference:
Inmon, W. H. Building the Data Warehouse, 2nd ed., 1996.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
6.1 3-Tier Architecture
The classic Data Warehouse architecture is represented as a three-tier logical model. These tiers correspond to functional layers within the data ecosystem rather than separate physical servers.



Data Warehouse Three-Tier Architecture



  
    
      LAYER 1
      Operational Sources
      ERP · CRM · APIs · CSV · Logs
      
      Priority: Accurately record every event.
    
    
      LAYER 2
      Integration
      Extract → Validate → Standardize → Load
      
      Priority: Quality, traceability, and shared rules.
    
    
      LAYER 3
      Analytical Consumption
      Data Marts · Models · BI · Analytics
      
      Priority: Answer questions quickly and consistently.
    
  
  Architectural Diagram: Each tier addresses a specific gap: data access, data consistency, and business utility.


Operational Layer.
This level houses systems supporting daily organization activities. In an enterprise, these include ERP systems logging sales and billing, CRMs managing customers, academic portals storing grades, or hospital EHR systems documenting medical visits. Flat files (CSV, Excel), external public APIs, and application log streams also sit in this layer.
The goal here is transactional: recording events quickly, consistently, and securely. It is not designed for deep historical analysis or complex aggregations. A hospital system can track today’s patient visits, but is not optimized to analyze a decade of diagnostic trends.
Integration Layer (ETL / Data Integration Layer).
This layer forms the technical core of the Data Warehouse, executing extraction, cleaning, transformation, and loading processes. Inconsistencies are resolved here: gender codes (“M/F” vs 0/1) are normalized, date formats standardized, and currencies converted.
Additionally, duplicates are removed, surrogate keys generated, and business rules applied to consolidate data. Depending on architectural choices, this layer can manifest as a centralized Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW) where data is unified before presentation, or as pipelines feeding domain-specific dimensional models directly. In both cases, its role is guaranteeing enterprise-wide consistency and quality.
Presentation / Analytics Layer.
Data in this tier has been integrated and structured for analysis. Data marts, dimensional models (star schemas), BI dashboards, and visualization tools operate here. Analysts, executives, and business leads interact with this layer to answer strategic questions.
For example, a healthcare network can analyze annual patient volumes by clinic, wait times by specialty, or regional diagnostic distributions. Crucially, data is optimized for querying, aggregation, and time-series comparisons rather than transaction processing.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
6.2 Data Mart
A Data Mart is a specialized subset of a Data Warehouse focused on a specific business domain. While a Data Warehouse integrates enterprise-wide data, a Data Mart focuses on a domain like sales, finance, human resources, or academic tracking.






Figure 6.1: Data Marts within a Data Warehouse Architecture



For instance, a university might deploy an academic Data Mart containing enrollment, grade, and credit fact tables linked to student, course, and time dimensions. A commercial enterprise might build a sales Data Mart with transaction facts and product, customer, and regional dimensions.
The main purpose of a Data Mart is facilitating focused analysis and improving query performance for a business unit. They are commonly implemented using dimensional modeling (star schemas), which is optimized for reporting and aggregations.
Depending on the architectural strategy, Data Marts can be derived from a central Data Warehouse (top-down approach) or built iteratively per business process and linked via conformed dimensions (bottom-up approach).
A Data Mart is not merely a small warehouse. Its value depends on keeping metrics and dimensions consistent with the rest of the organization. A sales Data Mart and an inventory Data Mart can be analyzed together only if both define “product”, “store”, and “time” identically.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
6.3 Data Warehouse vs. Data Lake
In modern data architecture, a Data Lake is often discussed alongside a Data Warehouse, though their roles differ.
A Data Lake is a centralized repository that stores data in its raw format—structured, semi-structured, or unstructured. Unlike a Data Warehouse, which requires cleaning and transformation before loading, a Data Lake follows a flexible approach: store data first, transform later when needed for analysis.
For example, a Data Warehouse holds cleaned, normalized sales tables ready for reporting. A Data Lake can store raw sensor telemetry, medical images, JSON logs, app event streams, or unparsed text.
The primary distinction lies in purpose:

The Data Warehouse is built for structured analysis and business decision-making.
The Data Lake is built for flexible, massive-scale storage, particularly supporting Big Data workloads and Data Science exploration.

In modern platforms, both often coexist: the Data Lake acts as a raw landing zone, while the Data Warehouse provides curated structures optimized for business intelligence.

  
    
      Data Lake
      Stores structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, often in raw form.
      
        Schema: Defined on read
        Users: Data Engineers and Data Scientists
        Strength: Flexibility and scale
      
    
    
      Data Warehouse
      Publishes integrated, historical, structured data with controlled business definitions.
      
        Schema: Defined before consumption
        Users: Analysts and Business Leads
        Strength: Consistency and analytical performance
      
    
  
  Modern Architecture: They complement each other; choosing only one is not mandatory.
  Comparative Diagram: The main difference is not data volume, but data preparation level and consumption patterns.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
7.1 Kimball Approach (Bottom-up, Bus Architecture)
The Kimball approach prioritizes rapid value delivery via dimensional data marts (usually star schemas) built per business process. The core idea is integrating separate data marts through conformed dimensions—shared, standardized dimensions (for example, identical definitions of “Time” and “Product” across Sales and Returns).






Figure 7.1: Kimball Data Warehouse Methodology



Key characteristics:

Incremental implementation: Build one data mart (e.g., Sales) and expand iteratively (e.g., Inventory, Marketing).
Target model: Dimensional, query-oriented.
Focus on semantic layer: Consistent metric definitions (e.g., exact definition of “Net Sales”).
High utility for BI/analytics from early stages.

Advantages:

Fast delivery of tangible results to business users.
Simple, high-performance query patterns.
Natural alignment with business questions (the recommended starting point in this course).

Risks & Challenges:

Requires strict discipline to enforce conformed dimensions; otherwise, isolated data silos emerge.
Governance and integration can become complex if scaling without standards.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
7.2 Inmon Approach (Top-down, EDW First)
The Inmon approach proposes constructing a centralized, integrated Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW) first (typically using normalized models), then deriving domain data marts or dimensional views for analytical consumption.






Figure 7.2: Inmon Data Warehouse Methodology



Key characteristics:

Enterprise integration takes top priority: Unified corporate definitions from day one.
Centralized repository harmonizing core entities and business rules (customer, product, organization).
Data marts or dimensional models are downstream views derived from the EDW.

Advantages:

High enterprise consistency and centralized metric control.
Strong alignment with data governance, auditing, lineage, and compliance.

Risks & Challenges:

Longer time-to-value as the EDW development cycle can be lengthy.
Vulnerable to shifting business requirements because total integration is required before enabling use cases.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
7.3 Selecting Between Kimball and Inmon
Choosing an approach should not be framed as “which is better”, but “which fits the organizational context, timeline, and data governance maturity”. Practical criteria:

Analytics urgency and available resources

If functional dashboards are needed quickly by a small or mid-sized team, Kimball is often more practical: build a first data mart and iterate.
If an organization can sustain a large upfront investment and prioritizes unified corporate definitions from the start, Inmon may be preferable.

Source data fragmentation and heterogeneity

When dealing with disparate sources and conflicting definitions (e.g., “active customer” means different things across business units), an Inmon approach enforces central integration.
If source systems are manageable and the goal is accelerating domain analytics (sales, academics, healthcare), Kimball performs well.

Data governance, auditing, and lineage

Strict regulatory or compliance auditing requirements favor the top-down, centralized framework.
If data governance is maturing, an incremental approach is more realistic, provided conformed dimensions and metric glossaries are maintained.

Nature of use cases

Aggregated metrics and multidimensional navigation (trends, regional comparisons, cohorts) benefit from upfront dimensional modeling (Kimball).
Enterprise master data management and complex cross-domain reconciliation favor Inmon or a strong core integration layer.


Modern data platforms frequently use a hybrid strategy: building an integrated core layer (EDW or core data layer) while exposing dimensional models for BI consumption. The critical goal is consistency: establishing a clear single source of truth for metrics and dimensions.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
8.1 Data Sources
In a Faculty of Science, relevant institutional data is typically spread across independent systems:

Student Information Systems (SIS) recording enrollments, grades, and credits.
Admissions Systems holding applicant data, admission scores, and educational background.
Financial Systems managing tuition payments, scholarships, and financial aid.
Human Resources Systems managing faculty records and teaching loads.
External Files such as institutional surveys or academic evaluations.

Each system fulfills an operational need, but none offers a unified, longitudinal view of academic performance. Source fragmentation creates analytical barriers and metric inconsistencies.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
8.2 Integration Processes (ETL)
Transforming operational data into strategic insight requires systematic integration.
Data is extracted periodically from source systems, cleaned, validated, standardized, and merged. For example, if a student’s name varies slightly across systems, the integration process identifies the individual and unifies their profile.
Institutional concepts—degree programs, course codes, academic terms, and department categories—are standardized across the repository.
The output is not a raw copy of operational databases, but a consolidated, clean dataset ready for historical analysis.

title: 5  Data Warehouse
text:
8.3 Data Warehouse Consolidation
Once integrated, data is stored in a central repository that preserves history and ensures consistency. This repository is not designed for transactional updates, but for analytical queries and longitudinal studies.
Architecturally, the academic Data Warehouse becomes the foundation for specialized analytical models—such as an academic data mart—from which institutional reports, dashboards, and research are generated.
Through consolidation, the Faculty can:

Track student cohorts from admission to graduation.
Measure failure and attrition rates by generation.
Identify bottleneck courses with high fail rates.
Evaluate performance trends over time.
Combine academic KPIs with financial or administrative metrics.

The academic Data Warehouse transforms operational entries into strategic insight.

title: 6  Data Lakehouse
text:
6.1 Introduction to the Lakehouse Architecture
As discussed in the previous chapter, both the Data Warehouse (consistent but rigid and expensive) and the Data Lake (flexible but prone to disorganization and lacking transactional support) pose major challenges for modern data teams. To combine the SQL performance and governance of a Data Warehouse with the low cost and scalability of a Data Lake, the Data Lakehouse architecture emerged.
This characterization describes historical trends rather than absolute rules: elastic Data Warehouses and well-governed Data Lakes exist. The challenge arises when an organization maintains both as disconnected platforms. Data is copied from the lake to the warehouse for reporting, then prepared again for data science. Every copy adds latency, cost, and the risk of different teams operating on conflicting versions of truth.
The Lakehouse represents a natural evolution of the Data Lake. It retains object storage, multi-format ingestion, and the decoupling of storage from compute, while incorporating a table, metadata, and governance layer capable of enforcing ACID transactions, schema controls, access policies, and reliable SQL performance. It does not mean placing a Data Warehouse next to a Data Lake, but turning lake files into managed tables without relinquishing openness and flexibility.

title: 6  Data Lakehouse
text:
🌊
      Data Lake
      Data of any type, cost-effective storage, and flexible access for data engineering and data science.
    
    ＋
    
      🗂️
      Management Layer
      Catalog, table format, ACID transactions, schema evolution, lineage, security, and query optimization.
    
    ＝
    
      🏡
      Data Lakehouse
      A unified data foundation for BI, advanced analytics, real-time streaming, and machine learning.
    
  
  Conceptual Evolution: The Lakehouse adds semantics and reliability to scalable Data Lake storage.

title: 6  Data Lakehouse
text:
6.2 The Best of Both Traditions
The term Lakehouse signifies convergence. From the Data Lake, it inherits scale, low-cost object storage, multi-format compatibility, and multi-engine accessibility. From the Data Warehouse, it restores necessary enterprise-grade guarantees: verifiable quality, understandable domain models, concurrent queries, and centralized governance.

  
    
      🌊
      From the Data Lake
      Massive scale · low-cost object storage · structured and unstructured data · open formats · multi-engine compatibility.
    
    
      🏡
      In the Lakehouse
      A shared foundation for SQL, BI, streaming, data science, and AI, minimizing cross-platform duplication.
    
    
      🏢
      From the Data Warehouse
      Transactions · schema enforcement · governance · SQL performance · auditability · business-ready data.
    
  
  Convergence: The goal is not blurring workload differences, but serving them off coherent, governed data.

This unification does not mean all data must undergo identical transformations. A newly ingested log file can coexist with an executive-certified reporting table, provided the architecture distinguishes quality tiers, enforces access control, and tracks lineage.
To understand how this technology operates in practice, we examine the five logical layers composing a robust Data Lakehouse architecture.
