    title="Marginal Probabilities — Baseline Under Independence",
    yaxis_title="Probability",
    yaxis_range=[0, 0.85]
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            


Under independence:
\[
P(\text{Male}, \text{Coffee}) = P(\text{Male}) \times P(\text{Coffee}) = 0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.30
\]
Expected count \(e_{11}\):
\[
e_{11} = 0.30 \times 100 = 30
\]
Full expected frequency table:


Code
labels_x = ["Coffee", "Tea"]
labels_y = ["Male", "Female"]
esp = np.array([[30, 20], [30, 20]])

fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(
    z=esp, x=labels_x, y=labels_y,
    colorscale="Blues", showscale=False,
    text=esp, texttemplate="%{text}",
    zmin=0, zmax=40
))

for i, (row, rtot) in enumerate(zip(esp, [50, 50])):
    fig.add_annotation(x=1.6, y=labels_y[i], text=f"<b>{rtot}</b>",
                       showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13, color="#457b9d"),
                       xref="x", yref="y")
for j, (col, ctot) in enumerate(zip(labels_x, [60, 40])):
    fig.add_annotation(x=labels_x[j], y=-0.65, text=f"<b>{ctot}</b>",
                       showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13, color="#457b9d"),
                       xref="x", yref="y")

fig.update_layout(
    title="Expected Frequency Table Under Independence",
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            


The \(\chi^2\) test statistic quantifies overall deviation between observed (\(o_{ij}\)) and expected (\(e_{ij}\)) frequencies:
\[
\chi^2 = \sum_{i,j} \frac{(o_{ij} - e_{ij})^2}{e_{ij}}
\]


Code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

k_vals = np.arange(30, 56, 1)
chi2_vals = []

for k in k_vals:
    tabla = np.array([[k, 50 - k], [60 - k, 50 - (60 - k)]])
    if tabla.min() >= 0:
        chi2_v, *_ = chi2_contingency(tabla)
        chi2_vals.append(chi2_v)
    else:
        chi2_vals.append(np.nan)

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=k_vals, y=chi2_vals,
    mode="lines+markers",
    line=dict(color="#457b9d", width=2.5),
    marker=dict(size=5),
    name="χ²"
))

fig.add_vline(x=30, line_dash="dash", line_color="#2a9d8f",
              annotation_text="k=30: Exact Independence (χ²=0)",
              annotation_position="top right",
              annotation_font_color="#2a9d8f")

fig.add_hline(y=3.841, line_dash="dot", line_color="#e63946",
              annotation_text="Critical Value α=0.05 (df=1)",
              annotation_position="bottom right",
              annotation_font_color="#e63946")

fig.update_layout(
    title="χ² Statistic Increases with Deviation from Independence",
    xaxis_title="Coffee-drinking males (k) — Fixed Marginals (50/50 & 60/40)",
    yaxis_title="χ² Statistic",
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            


Degrees of freedom for an \(r \times c\) contingency table:
\[
\text{df} = (r - 1)(c - 1)
\]


35.1.2 The \(\chi^2\) Distribution


Code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from scipy.stats import chi2

x = np.linspace(0, 30, 500)

fig = go.Figure()
for df_, color in zip([1, 2, 4, 6, 9],
                      ["#e63946","#457b9d","#2a9d8f","#e9c46a","#f4a261"]):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x, y=chi2.pdf(x, df_),
        mode="lines", name=f"df = {df_}",
        line=dict(color=color, width=2.5)
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    title="χ² Distribution for Varying Degrees of Freedom",
    xaxis_title="χ²", yaxis_title="Density",
    legend_title="df",
    height=400
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            




35.1.3 Statistical Decision: p-value
The p-value represents the upper-tail probability under \(H_0\):
\[
p = P(\chi^2 \ge \chi^2_{\text{obs}} \mid H_0)
\]


Code
from scipy.stats import chi2
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

gl = 4
chi2_obs = 11.5
x = np.linspace(0, 25, 500)

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x, y=chi2.pdf(x, gl),
    fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(69,123,157,0.2)",
    line=dict(color="#457b9d", width=2),
    name="χ²(4) Distribution"
))

x_tail = x[x >= chi2_obs]
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=np.concatenate([[chi2_obs], x_tail, [x_tail[-1]]]),
    y=np.concatenate([[0], chi2.pdf(x_tail, gl), [0]]),
    fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(230,57,70,0.5)",
    line=dict(color="#e63946", width=2),
    name=f"p-value = {chi2.sf(chi2_obs, gl):.4f}"
))

fig.add_vline(x=chi2_obs, line_dash="dash", line_color="#e63946",
              annotation_text=f"χ²={chi2_obs}",
              annotation_position="top right")

fig.update_layout(
    title="Rejection Region (α = 0.05, df = 4)",
    xaxis_title="χ²", yaxis_title="Density",
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            








ImportantAssumptions for \(\chi^2\) Test Validity




Independent Observations: Each subject appears in exactly one table cell.
Sample Size: \(n \ge 20\).
Expected Frequencies: \(e_{ij} \ge 5\) in at least 80% of cells.
No Zero Expected Frequencies: \(e_{ij} > 0\) for all cells.





35.1.4 Strength of Association: Cramér’s V
To isolate association strength from sample size inflation, Cramér’s V scales \(\chi^2\) between 0 and 1:
\[
V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2 / n}{\min(r-1,\, c-1)}} \in [0, 1]
\]



V Value
Interpretation




0.00 – 0.10
Negligible association


0.10 – 0.20
Weak association


0.20 – 0.40
Moderate association


> 0.40
Strong association





Code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

tables = {
    "Negligible  (V ≈ 0.05)": np.array([[26, 24], [24, 26]]),
    "Weak        (V ≈ 0.15)": np.array([[35, 15], [25, 25]]),
    "Moderate    (V ≈ 0.30)": np.array([[40, 10], [20, 30]]),
    "Strong      (V ≈ 0.55)": np.array([[45,  5], [10, 40]]),
}

colors = {
    "Negligible  (V ≈ 0.05)": ["#d9f0f7", "#a8d8ea"],

35.2 Practical Application: Airline Customer Satisfaction Case Study
An airline seeks to optimize customer satisfaction drivers across 6 candidate features: Class, Travel_Type, Flight_Frequency, Delay_Status, Seat_Selection, and Purchase_Time.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(42)
n = 1000

clase = np.random.choice(["Economy","Business","First"],
                          size=n, p=[0.65, 0.25, 0.10])

tipo_map = {
    "Economy": [0.30, 0.70],
    "Business":  [0.85, 0.15],
    "First":   [0.70, 0.30]
}
tipo = np.array([np.random.choice(["Business_Travel","Vacation"],
                 p=tipo_map[c]) for c in clase])

freq_map = {
    "Economy": [0.15, 0.45, 0.40],
    "Business":  [0.65, 0.30, 0.05],
    "First":   [0.75, 0.20, 0.05]
}
frecuencia = np.array([np.random.choice(["Frequent","Occasional","First_Time"],
                       p=freq_map[c]) for c in clase])

retraso_map = {
    "Business_Travel": [0.50, 0.30, 0.20],
    "Vacation":        [0.45, 0.35, 0.20]
}
retraso = np.array([np.random.choice(["No_Delay","Minor","Severe"],
                    p=retraso_map[t]) for t in tipo])

satisf = []
for c, r in zip(clase, retraso):
    if c == "First" and r == "No_Delay":
        satisf.append(np.random.choice(["Low","Medium","High"], p=[0.05,0.15,0.80]))
    elif c == "Business" and r != "Severe":
        satisf.append(np.random.choice(["Low","Medium","High"], p=[0.10,0.35,0.55]))
    elif c == "Economy" and r == "Severe":
        satisf.append(np.random.choice(["Low","Medium","High"], p=[0.60,0.30,0.10]))
    elif c == "Economy" and r == "No_Delay":
        satisf.append(np.random.choice(["Low","Medium","High"], p=[0.20,0.45,0.35]))
    else:
        satisf.append(np.random.choice(["Low","Medium","High"], p=[0.30,0.40,0.30]))
satisf = np.array(satisf)

asiento = np.random.choice(["Window","Aisle","Middle"],
                            size=n, p=[0.45, 0.40, 0.15])

def p_norm():
    p = np.array([0.50, 0.50]) + np.random.uniform(-0.03, 0.03, 2)
    return p / p.sum()

momento = np.array([np.random.choice(["Early","Last_Minute"],
                    p=p_norm()) for _ in range(n)])

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Class": clase, "Travel_Type": tipo, "Frequency": frecuencia,
    "Delay": retraso, "Satisfaction": satisf,
    "Seat": asiento, "Purchase_Time": momento
})

predictoras = ["Class","Travel_Type","Frequency","Delay","Seat","Purchase_Time"]
resultados = []

for var in predictoras:
    tabla = pd.crosstab(df[var], df["Satisfaction"])
    chi2_v, p_v, dof_v, exp_v = chi2_contingency(tabla)
    n_tot = tabla.values.sum()
    min_dim = min(tabla.shape[0]-1, tabla.shape[1]-1)
    cramer = np.sqrt(chi2_v / (n_tot * min_dim))

    if cramer > 0.3:
        fuerza = "Strong"
    elif cramer > 0.1:
        fuerza = "Moderate"
    else:
        fuerza = "Weak"

    resultados.append({
        "Variable": var, "χ²": round(chi2_v,2),
        "p-value": round(p_v, 4), "Cramér's V": round(cramer, 3),
        "Strength": fuerza
    })

res_df = pd.DataFrame(resultados).sort_values("Cramér's V", ascending=False)

title: 36  Association Rules: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Selection
text:
1 Introduction
In most contexts where transactional data is collected —retail sales, medical records, web browsing histories, digital platform interactions— there is a recurring question that precedes any predictive model: which items tend to appear together? This seemingly simple question gives rise to one of the most thoroughly studied problems in data mining: the discovery of association rules.
The problem was formalized by Agrawal and Srikant (1994) in the context of market basket analysis, where each transaction in a supermarket records the set of products purchased by a customer during a single visit. The original motivation was directly commercial: identifying products that are frequently bought together makes it possible to optimize the physical layout of items in the store, design cross-promotional strategies, and personalize recommendations. The same formalism, however, has since been applied in domains as diverse as bioinformatics —to identify co-expressed genes—, epidemiology —to detect co-occurring symptoms in patients—, and cybersecurity —to recognize access patterns preceding intrusions (Han et al. 2011).
What makes this problem pedagogically valuable is not merely its applicability, but the tension it reveals between two tasks that seem equivalent but are not: generating rules is computationally straightforward; interpreting and selecting useful rules requires genuine statistical judgment. An analyst who generates rules without a critical understanding of the underlying metrics can arrive at erroneous conclusions backed by apparent quantitative rigor. This chapter seeks to progressively build the conceptual tools needed to avoid such mistakes.
The exposition is organized from concrete concepts to formal definitions. We begin with definitions motivated by real-world examples, develop the process of rule generation, and dedicate the largest portion of the chapter to the problem that turns out to be the most challenging: not how to obtain rules, but how to decide which ones are worthwhile.

title: 36  Association Rules: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Selection
text:
2 Fundamental Definitions

2.1 The Data Model: Transactions and Items
The starting point is a set of transactions \(\mathcal{D} = \{T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n\}\), where each transaction \(T_i\) is a subset of a finite universe of items \(\mathcal{I} = \{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_m\}\). In the context of a supermarket, \(\mathcal{I}\) is the complete catalog of products and each \(T_i\) is the set of products purchased in a particular visit. It is important to note that this model does not record quantities or prices: only the presence or absence of each item in each transaction (Tan et al. 2006).
An itemset is any subset \(X \subseteq \mathcal{I}\). An itemset of cardinality \(k\) is called a \(k\)-itemset. For example, \(\{\)milk, bread\(\}\) is a 2-itemset, and \(\{\)milk, bread, butter\(\}\) is a 3-itemset.


2.2 Support
The first fundamental metric is support, which measures the prevalence of a pattern across the dataset.






Definition. The support of an itemset \(X\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) is the fraction of transactions that contain \(X\):
\[\text{supp}(X) = \frac{|\{T_i \in \mathcal{D} : X \subseteq T_i\}|}{|\mathcal{D}|} \tag{1}\]



In probabilistic terms, \(\text{supp}(X) = P(X)\), that is, the empirical probability of observing the itemset \(X\) in a randomly chosen transaction. For a rule \(A \Rightarrow B\), the support is \(P(A \cup B)\): the probability that both the antecedent and the consequent are present in the same transaction.
Support possesses a relevant formal property known as the anti-monotonicity property or Apriori principle: if an itemset \(X\) has a support lower than a minimum threshold \(\sigma_{\min}\), then any superset \(Y \supset X\) will also have a support lower than \(\sigma_{\min}\). Formally proven in Agrawal and Srikant (1994), this property serves as the algorithmic foundation that renders searching for frequent patterns tractable in datasets containing thousands of items.
Interpretation and Intuition. Support answers the question: how common is this pattern in the data? A low support indicates that the pattern is rare, which may be due to a genuinely infrequent relationship or simply because both items are rare individually. A high support is a necessary —yet insufficient— condition for a rule to be useful in practice.


2.3 Confidence
Confidence measures the predictive power of a rule: given that the antecedent occurs, how frequently does the consequent also occur?






Definition. The confidence of the rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) is the empirical conditional probability of \(B\) given \(A\):
\[\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{\text{supp}(A \cup B)}{\text{supp}(A)} = P(B \mid A) \tag{2}\]



A confidence of 0.80 for the rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) means that in 80% of the transactions containing \(A\), \(B\) also appears. This interpretation as conditional probability makes confidence intuitive: it is the accuracy rate of the rule as a prediction rule.
The Fundamental Limitation of Confidence. Despite its intuitiveness, confidence presents a critical limitation that frequently goes unnoticed: it ignores the baseline frequency of the consequent. Consider the following scenario: in a supermarket where 65% of all transactions include whole milk, any rule with whole milk as its consequent will automatically have a confidence of at least 65%, regardless of what the antecedent is. A confidence of 0.70 for the rule \(\{\)bread\(\} \Rightarrow \{\)whole milk\(\}\) is not impressive if whole milk appears in 65% of transactions: bread adds less than 10 percentage points over the baseline rate. The rule possesses minimal predictive power.
This problem —confusing high confidence with a strong relationship— is the most common mistake in association rule analysis and motivates the need for lift as a complementary metric.


2.4 Lift
Lift quantifies how far the relationship between \(A\) and \(B\) deviates from statistical independence.






Definition. The lift of the rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) is the ratio of the observed confidence to the expected confidence under independence:
\[\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(A) \cdot P(B)} \tag{3}\]



The probabilistic interpretation is straightforward: if \(A\) and \(B\) were statistically independent, the probability of their co-occurrence would be \(P(A) \cdot P(B)\). Lift is precisely the factor by which the observed co-occurrence exceeds (or falls below) this expectation under independence (Tan et al. 2006).

\(\text{lift} = 1\): \(A\) and \(B\) are statistically independent. The presence of \(A\) provides no information about \(B\).
\(\text{lift} > 1\): \(A\) and \(B\) co-occur more frequently than expected under independence. The rule indicates a positive association.
\(\text{lift} < 1\): \(A\) and \(B\) co-occur less frequently than expected. The presence of \(A\) inhibits the presence of \(B\).

An important algebraic property is that lift is symmetric: \(\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) = \text{lift}(B \Rightarrow A)\). This has significant practical implications discussed in ?sec-interpretacion.


2.5 A Concrete Example
To ground these definitions, consider the following dataset of five transactions:



Transaction
Items




\(T_1\)
milk, bread, butter


\(T_2\)
milk, bread


\(T_3\)
milk, butter


\(T_4\)
bread, butter


\(T_5\)
milk, bread, cheese



For the rule \(\{\)bread\(\} \Rightarrow \{\)milk\(\}\):
\[\text{supp}(\{\text{bread}, \text{milk}\}) = \frac{3}{5} = 0.60\]
\[\text{conf}(\{\text{bread}\} \Rightarrow \{\text{milk}\}) = \frac{\text{supp}(\{\text{bread}, \text{milk}\})}{\text{supp}(\{\text{bread}\})} = \frac{3/5}{4/5} = 0.75\]
\[\text{lift}(\{\text{bread}\} \Rightarrow \{\text{milk}\}) = \frac{0.75}{P(\{\text{milk}\})} = \frac{0.75}{4/5} = 0.9375\]
The lift of 0.9375 — lower than 1 — reveals that, despite an apparently high confidence of 0.75, the presence of bread actually slightly reduces the probability of finding milk in the same transaction relative to the base rate of milk (which is 0.80). The confidence of 75% was misleading because milk was already very frequent.

title: 36  Association Rules: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Selection
text:
3 Frequent Rule Generation

3.1 From Frequent Itemsets to Rules
The process of discovering association rules is divided into two stages (Agrawal and Srikant 1994; Han et al. 2011):

Frequent Itemset Mining: Identify all itemsets \(X \subseteq \mathcal{I}\) whose support exceeds a minimum threshold \(\sigma_{\min}\) specified by the analyst.
Rule Generation from Frequent Itemsets: For each frequent itemset \(X\) of cardinality \(k \geq 2\), generate all possible rules \(A \Rightarrow B\) where \(A \cup B = X\), \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), \(A \neq \emptyset\), and \(B \neq \emptyset\), retaining only those whose confidence exceeds a minimum threshold \(\gamma_{\min}\).

The separation between these two stages is not arbitrary: the first stage is computationally expensive —the space of all possible subsets of \(\mathcal{I}\) has cardinality \(2^{|\mathcal{I}|}\)— whereas the second stage, once frequent itemsets are known, is relatively fast.


3.2 The Apriori Algorithm
The Apriori algorithm, proposed by Agrawal and Srikant (1994), was the first to efficiently solve the first stage using a breadth-first search strategy that exploits the anti-monotonicity property of support. The core idea is that evaluating the support of a \(k\)-itemset is unnecessary if any of its \((k-1)\)-subsets is already infrequent: by anti-monotonicity, the \(k\)-itemset will also be infrequent. This allows pruning the search space drastically.
The high-level workflow is as follows: in each iteration \(k\), the algorithm generates candidates of size \(k\) from the frequent itemsets of size \(k-1\) (join step), discards those containing infrequent subsets (pruning step), and scans the dataset to compute the support of the remaining candidates. The process terminates when no new frequent candidates can be generated.

It is not the purpose of this chapter to detail the implementation of the algorithm — for that, see Han et al. (2011), Chapter 6, or Tan et al. (2006), Chapter 5. What matters here is understanding its parameters and their impact on the results.


3.3 Parameters as Decisions of the Analyst
Running Apriori requires specifying at least two thresholds:

\(\sigma_{\min}\) (minimum support): Controls how frequent a pattern must be to be considered. A low value produces more frequent itemsets —and potentially more rules— but also more noise. A high value filters aggressively and may eliminate genuine, less frequent patterns.
\(\gamma_{\min}\) (minimum confidence): Controls how predictive a rule must be to be reported. As will be discussed in Section 36.4, this threshold has no direct statistical interpretation: its appropriate value depends on the domain.

A crucial aspect that introductory texts rarely emphasize is that the results depend directly on the chosen parameters. The number of rules obtained can vary by an order of magnitude when changing \(\sigma_{\min}\) by a few percentage points. This implies that reporting rules without disclosing the parameters used to generate them is a methodologically flawed practice.
The following code block empirically illustrates this sensitivity:

This is no coincidence: frequent itemsets with very low support are the most susceptible to being statistical artifacts, and filtering them preserves patterns with higher relative signal.

section: 4 The Problem of Too Many Rules
text:
4 The Problem of Too Many Rules

4.1 Combinatorial Explosion
Suppose a dataset contains 100 distinct items and \(\sigma_{\min} = 0.01\). The number of possible itemsets is \(2^{100} - 1\), an astronomical figure. Even with the pruning of the Apriori algorithm and a reasonably restrictive minimum support, it is possible to generate tens of thousands of rules from moderate-sized datasets. The original Groceries dataset, with 9,835 transactions and 169 items, can generate anywhere from several hundred to several thousand rules depending on the chosen parameters (Han et al. 2011).
This volume of output creates a second-order problem: the proliferation of rules makes manual review infeasible, while automated selection requires criteria that, if poorly chosen, can introduce systematic bias.


4.2 Redundancy and Irrelevance
Part of the issue is structural. Given a frequent itemset \(X = \{A, B, C\}\), the algorithm generates all possible partitions as rules: \(\{A\} \Rightarrow \{B, C\}\), \(\{B\} \Rightarrow \{A, C\}\), \(\{C\} \Rightarrow \{A, B\}\), \(\{A, B\} \Rightarrow \{C\}\), \(\{A, C\} \Rightarrow \{B\}\), \(\{B, C\} \Rightarrow \{A\}\). Many of these rules share the same co-occurrence information and are, to some extent, redundant with respect to each other. The choice of the most appropriate consequent depends on the application context, not the algorithm.
An additional layer of difficulty is irrelevance. A rule can be formally valid —support and confidence above thresholds— while simultaneously failing to offer any actionable insight. This occurs systematically when the consequent is a highly frequent item: the rule appears predictive because its confidence is high, but in reality it reflects the mere ubiquity of the consequent, not a genuine relationship with the antecedent.
This is the central issue that any rigorous association rule analysis methodology must address, and which the evaluation metrics described in the next section attempt to resolve.
crumbs: 36  Association Rules: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Selection

title: 36  Association Rules: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Selection
text:
5 Evaluation Metrics: Deep Interpretation

5.1 Support: Prevalence, Not Interest
Support, as defined in Section 36.2, answers strictly the question how frequent is this pattern? It says nothing about whether the pattern is unexpected, interesting, or actionable. A rule with very high support can be trivial: if 80% of customers buy bottled water, the rule \(\{X\} \Rightarrow \{\text{water}\}\) will have high support for practically any \(X\), without revealing anything useful.
Support does serve an important role as a statistical reliability threshold: a pattern backed by very few observations is unstable and may disappear or alter substantially when adding new data. In a dataset of 50 transactions, a support of 0.10 corresponds to a mere 5 observations — insufficient for robust statistical claims. With larger datasets (on the order of thousands of transactions), support thresholds can and should be more demanding.


5.2 Confidence: Conditional Predictivity with Structural Bias
Confidence measures \(P(B \mid A)\): the probability that the consequent is present given the antecedent. Its interpretation as conditional probability is clear and directly useful in recommendation systems: if 80% of customers who buy bread also buy butter, that confidence directly justifies recommending butter to someone who just placed bread in their cart.
However, confidence carries a well-documented structural bias (Tan et al. 2006): it is monotonically increasing in \(P(B)\). For a fixed antecedent \(A\):
\[\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(A)} \leq \frac{P(B)}{P(A)} \cdot P(A) = P(B) \cdot \frac{1}{P(A)}\]
Confidence depends directly on \(P(B)\). A highly frequent item \(B\) will, ceteris paribus, yield high-confidence rules for any antecedent \(A\), simply because \(B\) appears in nearly all transactions. This dependency makes confidence non-comparable across rules with consequents of vastly different frequencies, introducing a systematic source of bias if used as the sole selection criterion.
The practical takeaway is this: before declaring that a rule has “high confidence,” it is necessary to compare that confidence with \(P(B)\). Only if \(\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) \gg P(B)\) can we assert that the presence of \(A\) genuinely contributes to predicting \(B\).






Important



Nontrivial Confidence Threshold. For the rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) to have lift \(> k\), it is required that: \[\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) > k \cdot P(B)\] In particular, for a rule to be simply nontrivial (lift \(> 1\)), confidence must exceed the base frequency of the consequent: \(\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) > P(B)\).




5.3 Lift: The Central Metric of Interest
Lift, defined in Eq. 39.4, corrects the bias of confidence by normalizing by \(P(B)\). Its interpretation as a likelihood ratio makes it directly comparable across rules with different consequents.
From a probability perspective, lift is the ratio of observed joint probability to expected joint probability under independence:
\[\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(A) \cdot P(B)}\]
A lift significantly greater than 1 constitutes evidence in favor of a genuine association between \(A\) and \(B\). A lift close to 1 indicates that knowing \(A\) does not alter the probability of \(B\), rendering the rule informationally void (Tan et al. 2006).
Symmetry of Lift. As noted at the end of Section 36.2, lift is symmetric: \(\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) = \text{lift}(B \Rightarrow A)\). This may be surprising since confidence is asymmetric. The reason is algebraic: lift compares \(P(A \cup B)\) with \(P(A) \cdot P(B)\), treating \(A\) and \(B\) symmetrically.
This symmetry has practical implications: when generating the rules \(A \Rightarrow B\) and \(B \Rightarrow A\), both have the exact same lift but can have very different confidences. Which direction to prefer in a real application depends on the context: if the goal is to recommend \(B\) given \(A\), the confidence of \(A \Rightarrow B\) is the relevant metric; if the goal is to recommend \(A\) given \(B\), \(\text{conf}(B \Rightarrow A)\) is key.
Limitations of Lift. Despite its superiority over confidence for detecting nontrivial associations, lift has two major limitations:

Instability with low support. In small datasets or with rare items, lift can be artificially inflated. If \(A\) and \(B\) are rare items —\(P(A) = P(B) = 0.01\)— and co-occur only once, their support is \(P(A \cup B) = 0.01\) and their lift is \(1/0.01 = 100\). This value is huge but backed by a single observation, making it statistically insignificant.
Variable ceiling. The maximum value lift can reach is not universal: it depends on the individual supports of \(A\) and \(B\). The theoretical maximum lift is \(1/\max(P(A), P(B))\), implying that comparing lifts across rules with different frequency levels is invalid without this correction.

These limitations motivate the use of complementary metrics, introduced in Section 36.7.


5.4 Comparative Summary
Table 36.1 synthesizes the properties of the three fundamental metrics.

6 Visual Interpretation of the Rule Space

6.1 Representation in Support-Confidence-Lift Space
The set of rules generated by Apriori can be visualized as a point cloud in a three-dimensional space defined by support, confidence, and lift. This representation allows immediate identification of different types of rules —useful, misleading, and trivial— and guides selection more effectively than inspecting tables alone.
The most convenient way to project this 3D space onto a 2D chart is plotting confidence and lift along Cartesian axes while encoding support in marker size. Using color to represent lift adds visual redundancy that highlights regions of interest.


Show code
fig = px.scatter(
    reglas,
    x="confidence",
    y="lift",
    size="support",
    hover_data={
        "regla": True,
        "support": ":.3f",
        "confidence": ":.3f",
        "lift": ":.3f",
    },
    color="lift",
    color_continuous_scale="RdYlGn",
    labels={
        "confidence": "Confidence",
        "lift": "Lift",
        "support": "Support",
    },
    size_max=28,
)

fig.add_hline(
    y=1.0,
    line_dash="dash",
    line_color="crimson",
    annotation_text="Lift = 1 (statistical independence)",
    annotation_position="top left",
    annotation_font_color="crimson",
)

fig.update_layout(
    height=500,
    xaxis=dict(range=[0, 1.05], title="Confidence"),
    yaxis=dict(title="Lift"),
    coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="Lift"),
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Rule space: confidence (horizontal axis) vs. lift (vertical axis), with support encoded in marker size and lift in color. The dashed red line marks lift = 1, the boundary of statistical independence. Rules below this line are spurious or trivial. Hovering over any point reveals the complete rule.






6.2 Reading the Plot: Four Quadrants
Figure 36.1 implicitly defines four interpretation zones:
Zone I — Desirable quadrant (high lift, high confidence, large marker). Rules in this region are the strongest candidates: they possess predictive power (high confidence), represent a genuine association unexplained by base frequencies (lift > 1), and are supported by a reasonable volume of transactions (high support). These are the most actionable patterns.
Zone II — High confidence, low lift (below the red line). This is the highest risk area for an uncritical analyst. Rules here may exhibit impressive confidence values —0.70, 0.80, or higher— but a lift near or below 1. In most cases, this is due to the base frequency problem: the consequent is so ubiquitous that it appears regardless of the antecedent. Relying on these rules for decision-making is at best useless and at worst counterproductive.
Zone III — High lift, low support (small markers above the line). These rules signal potentially strong associations but are backed by few observations. Their high lift could be a statistical artifact: in a dataset of 50 transactions, two items co-occurring just 5 times might show high lift purely by chance. The rule may be genuine, but caution and validation with additional data are required.
Zone IV — Low across all metrics. Rules lacking support, relevant confidence, and with lift near 1. There is no argument for retaining them.


6.3 Raw Co-occurrence: The Transaction Matrix
Before interpreting formal metrics, a useful complementary visualization is the co-occurrence matrix among the most frequent items. This matrix records, for each pair of items, the absolute number of transactions in which both appear simultaneously.


Show code
freq = df.sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
top_items = freq.head(10).index.tolist()
df_top = df[top_items]
cooc = df_top.T.dot(df_top)
np.fill_diagonal(cooc.values, 0)

fig = px.imshow(
    cooc,
    color_continuous_scale="Oranges",
    labels={"color": "Co-occurrences"},
    aspect="auto",
    text_auto=True,
)
fig.update_layout(height=430)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Co-occurrence matrix among the top 10 most frequent items in the dataset. The diagonal is set to zero (an item does not co-occur with itself). High-intensity orange cells should be interpreted with caution when involving items with high base frequency.




An important observation regarding Figure 36.2: cells with higher intensity tend to correspond to pairs involving the most frequent items —in this case, whole milk and bread. This is not evidence of a particularly strong association between them; it is largely a consequence of their high individual frequencies. Raw co-occurrence is the numerator of \(P(A \cup B)\), but it excludes the denominators \(P(A)\) and \(P(B)\) necessary to evaluate whether the relationship is nontrivial. The most informative cells are those with high intensity between items of moderate frequency, such as the granola-yogurt-fruit cluster.

7 Selection of Useful Rules

7.1 Practical Filtering Criteria
Selecting useful rules is not an entirely automated procedure: it requires analyst decisions informed by domain context. However, a general set of guidelines serves as a solid starting point (Tan et al. 2006; Han et al. 2011):
Criterion 1: Substantially greater lift than 1. A rule whose lift does not noticeably exceed the baseline of independence (1.0) reveals no genuine association between antecedent and consequent. A pragmatic threshold is lift \(\geq 1.2\) for weak relationships and lift \(\geq 1.5\) for moderate relationships. In large datasets and applications where decision costs are high, stricter values (lift \(\geq 2.0\)) are appropriate.
Criterion 2: Support backed by sufficient observations. Minimum support should translate to an absolute number of transactions that is statistically sensible. In a 50-transaction dataset, support \(= 0.10\) corresponds to just 5 observations — highly unstable. In a 9,000-transaction dataset, that same support represents 900 observations, which is robust.
Criterion 3: Confidence exceeding the consequent’s base frequency. As derived in Section 36.5, the condition \(\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) > P(B)\) is equivalent to lift \(> 1\). A good practice is explicitly calculating the “nontrivial confidence threshold” for every potential consequent prior to evaluating rules, as illustrated below:

This table serves as a diagnostic tool: before getting excited about a rule with whole milk as consequent, verify that confidence exceeds 0.58 (for lift > 1) or 0.87 (for lift > 1.5). If observed confidence falls short of these values, the rule provides no value.


7.2 Complementary Metrics
Data mining literature proposes numerous alternative metrics to lift for evaluating rule interest (Tan et al. 2006). Three of the most widely used in practice are:
Leverage.
\[\text{lev}(A \Rightarrow B) = P(A \cup B) - P(A) \cdot P(B)\]
Leverage measures the absolute difference between observed co-occurrence and expected co-occurrence under independence. Its interpretation is more direct than lift: it measures how many additional transactions, beyond the independence baseline, contain both \(A\) and \(B\). A leverage of 0.05 in a 1,000-transaction dataset means roughly 50 additional transactions contain both \(A\) and \(B\) beyond expectation. The range of leverage is \([-P(A) \cdot P(B), \min(P(A), P(B)) - P(A) \cdot P(B)]\).
Conviction.
\[\text{conv}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{1 - P(B)}{1 - \text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B)}\]
Conviction measures how often the rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) is “wrong” — that is, how often \(A\) occurs without \(B\) — relative to expectation under independence. Unlike lift, conviction is asymmetric: \(\text{conv}(A \Rightarrow B) \neq \text{conv}(B \Rightarrow A)\) in general, making it more appropriate for evaluating directional rules. As confidence approaches 1, conviction approaches infinity, indicating a quasi-deterministic rule. Conviction \(= 1\) indicates independence.
Zhang’s Metric.
\[Z(A, B) = \frac{P(A \cup B) - P(A) \cdot P(B)}{\max\{P(A \cup B)(1 - P(A)),\; P(A)(P(B) - P(A \cup B))\}}\]
Proposed to address limitations of lift, Zhang’s metric ranges from \([-1, 1]\) and is symmetric. Its main advantage is normalizing correctly across both high and low co-occurrence regimes, making it more robust against highly frequent items. A Zhang value near 0 indicates independence; positive values near 1 indicate strong association.

Rules in the second group, even with modest absolute confidence, are far more informative because they represent real deviations from expected behavior under independence.


7.4 Systematic Selection Pipeline
The following procedure condenses these criteria into an evaluation function applicable to any set of rules:


Show code
def evaluar_regla(row, n_transacciones=50, verbose=True):
    """
    Evaluates association rule quality across four criteria.
    Returns a qualitative classification: ROBUST, CANDIDATE, or DISCARD.
    """
    observaciones = []
    puntos = 0

    # Criterion 1: Lift
    if row["lift"] > 1.5:
        observaciones.append("Strong lift (> 1.5)")
        puntos += 3
    elif row["lift"] > 1.1:
        observaciones.append("Moderate lift (1.1 – 1.5)")
        puntos += 1
    else:
        observaciones.append("Weak lift (≤ 1.1) — nontrivial")

    # Criterion 2: Absolute support
    n_obs = int(row["support"] * n_transacciones)
    if n_obs >= 10:
        observaciones.append(f"Solid support ({n_obs} transactions)")
        puntos += 2
    elif n_obs >= 5:
        observaciones.append(f"Minimum support ({n_obs} transactions)")
        puntos += 1
    else:
        observaciones.append(f"Insufficient support ({n_obs} transactions)")

    # Criterion 3: Zhang
    if row["zhang"] > 0.3:
        observaciones.append("Robust Zhang (> 0.3)")
        puntos += 2
    elif row["zhang"] > 0.1:
        observaciones.append("Moderate Zhang (0.1 – 0.3)")
        puntos += 1
    else:
        observaciones.append("Weak Zhang (≤ 0.1)")

    # Criterion 4: Conviction
    if row["conviction"] > 1.5:
        observaciones.append("High conviction (> 1.5)")
        puntos += 1

    clasificacion = (
        "ROBUST" if puntos >= 6
        else "CANDIDATE" if puntos >= 3
        else "DISCARD"
    )

    if verbose:
        print(f"Rule: {row['regla']}")
        for obs in observaciones:
            print(f"  • {obs}")
        print(f"  → Classification: {clasificacion} (score: {puntos}/8)\n")
    return clasificacion

# Apply to top 5 rules by lift
print("Evaluation of top 5 rules by lift:\n")
for _, row in reglas.sort_values("lift", ascending=False).head(5).iterrows():
    evaluar_regla(row)

This pipeline should not be viewed as a rigid algorithm: threshold values and weights should be adapted to the domain. title: 36  Association Rules: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Selection
text:
8 Limitations of the Approach

8.1 The Causality Issue
Perhaps the most significant limitation of association rule analysis, and the most frequently ignored, is that rules are descriptive and correlational, never causal (Pearl 2009). The rule \(\{\)bread\(\} \Rightarrow \{\text{butter}\}\) with high lift indicates that buyers of bread tend to buy butter more often than expected. It does not imply that buying bread causes buying butter, nor that placing bread next to butter will cause more joint purchases. Confusing correlation with causation in data analysis is a well-documented source of costly business and policy mistakes (Pearl 2009).
This distinction is especially crucial in high-stakes fields like medicine or epidemiology. Identifying that certain symptoms co-occur with a diagnosis is not equivalent to understanding the causal mechanism connecting them. Inferring causality requires experimental designs or formal frameworks such as causal graphs (Pearl 2009).


8.2 Dominant Items and Base Frequency Bias
As analyzed throughout this chapter, items with very high support introduce structural bias into rule mining. In the Groceries dataset, whole milk appears in roughly 26% of all 9,835 original transactions —and 58% of the 50-transaction sample used in our computational examples. This dominance causes whole milk to appear as consequent in numerous high-confidence rules, most of which do not represent genuine associations.
A practical mitigation strategy is removing or special-handling items exceeding a high support threshold (e.g., 40–50%) prior to mining, or analyzing sub-segments of the dataset with more homogeneous item distributions.


8.3 Lack of Temporal Structure
The transaction data model —unordered sets— cannot capture temporal sequences. If sequential behavior matters (e.g., customers buy a primary item first and an accessory in a later visit), Apriori ignores it. Sequential pattern mining algorithms like GSP (Generalized Sequential Patterns) and PrefixSpan extend Apriori principles to handle ordered itemset sequences (Han et al. 2011).


8.4 Instability with Small Datasets
The computational examples in this chapter use 50 transactions, suitable for illustrating concepts but insufficient for robust statistical claims. On small datasets, support is highly sensitive to minor fluctuations: adding or removing a single transaction alters itemset support by 2 percentage points (1/50), potentially pushing patterns across threshold boundaries. In practice, association rule mining requires at least several hundred transactions to be reliable, and preferably thousands.


8.5 Parameter Sensitivity
As demonstrated in Section 36.3, rule quantity and character depend heavily on user parameters. This sensitivity has two methodological consequences: (1) results are not objective in the sense of being independent of analyst choices, and (2) two analyses of the same dataset with different parameters can yield superficially contradictory conclusions. Best practice calls for systematically exploring parameter space and reporting how robust findings are to reasonable parameter shifts.

title: 36  Association Rules: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Selection
text:
9 Conceptual Summary
This chapter developed the foundations of association rule analysis with an emphasis on critical interpretation. Key takeaways include:
On Fundamental Definitions:

Support measures pattern prevalence; confidence measures conditional predictivity; lift measures deviation from statistical independence.
No single metric suffices on its own: high support does not imply interest, high confidence does not imply a genuine relationship, and high lift with low support may be noise.

On Rule Generation:

Rule generation is automated and yields massive rule sets; selection requires statistical judgment and domain expertise.
Apriori parameters (\(\sigma_{\min}\), \(\gamma_{\min}\)) are analyst decisions without intrinsic statistical foundations; they must always be reported alongside results.

On the Core Problem:

High confidence does not equal a strong relationship when the consequent is frequent. Lift corrects for this bias.
The minimum confidence threshold for a rule to be nontrivial is \(\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) > P(B)\).

On Selecting Useful Rules:

The lift-vs-confidence scatter plot with support-encoded marker size is the most informative visualization for exploring rule space.
Complementary metrics such as leverage, conviction, and Zhang’s metric validate or challenge what lift suggests. Robust rules demonstrate strength across multiple criteria simultaneously.
Rule direction matters for decision making: lift is symmetric, but confidence is asymmetric.

On Limitations:

Association rules are descriptive, correlational tools; they do not infer causality.
The approach lacks temporal structure; ordered sequences require specialized algorithms.
Results are unstable on small datasets and highly sensitive to parameter choices.

The ultimate goal is not to maximize the number of rules discovered, but to identify the small subset of rules representing genuinely nontrivial patterns, supported by sufficient observations, and consistent across multiple evaluation metrics. Achieving this requires, beyond algorithmic mastery, a solid understanding of the statistical principles underlying each metric.

title: 37  Beyond Lift: Advanced Metrics, Sensitivity, and Rule Structure
text:
1 Introduction
The previous chapter established the foundations of association rule analysis: definitions of support, confidence, and lift, the rule generation process via the Apriori algorithm, and basic criteria for distinguishing genuine rules from trivial ones. The central argument was that generating rules is algorithmically simple, but critical evaluation of their validity demands moving beyond confidence as the sole criterion.
This chapter continues that line of reasoning and explores four directions that introductory treatments leave open. First, we rigorously analyze the structural limitations of lift as an evaluation metric: although lift corrects the bias of confidence, it possesses its own deficiencies that specialized literature has documented in detail, which are often ignored in introductory presentations. Second, we introduce a set of complementary metrics —leverage, conviction, and Zhang’s metric— whose mathematical properties allow evaluating aspects of rules that lift fails to capture, and whose combination yields more robust evaluations. Third, we address the issue of parameter sensitivity: we empirically demonstrate that the number, nature, and quality of rules obtained depend non-trivially on thresholds set by the analyst when invoking the algorithm, carrying direct methodological consequences. Finally, we propose representing the rule set as a relationship graph between items, enabling identification of the global structure of rule space and distinguishing core patterns from peripheral ones.
The common thread running through all these sections is identical to the one that motivated the previous chapter: the objective is not to maximize the number of reported rules, but to identify the small subset of rules representing nontrivial patterns, backed by consistent evidence from multiple perspectives.
crumbs: 37  Beyond Lift: Advanced Metrics, Sensitivity, and Rule Structure

title: 37  Beyond Lift: Advanced Metrics, Sensitivity, and Rule Structure
text:
2 Structural Limitations of Lift

2.1 The Symmetry of Lift and the Asymmetry of Decisions
An algebraic property of lift that few introductory presentations discuss in depth is its symmetry: for any pair of itemsets \(A\) and \(B\),
\[\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(A) \cdot P(B)} = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(B) \cdot P(A)} = \text{lift}(B \Rightarrow A) \tag{1}\]
Symmetry follows directly from the commutativity of multiplication in the denominator. Lift measures the deviation of joint probability \(P(A \cup B)\) from expected value under independence \(P(A) \cdot P(B)\), and this deviation is identical regardless of which set is designated as antecedent or consequent.
This symmetry has a major practical consequence that frequently goes unnoticed. When the algorithm generates the two rules \(A \Rightarrow B\) and \(B \Rightarrow A\) from the same frequent itemset \(\{A, B\}\), both rules will have the exact same lift. However, their confidences will, in general, differ:
\[\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(A)}, \qquad \text{conf}(B \Rightarrow A) = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(B)}\]
The rule with higher confidence is the one whose antecedent has lower individual support. If \(P(A) < P(B)\), then \(\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) > \text{conf}(B \Rightarrow A)\): predicting the more frequent item from the less frequent item is “easier” in terms of confidence, precisely because the consequent occurs with higher baseline frequency.
Table 37.1 illustrates this phenomenon with empirical data for the yogurt — whole milk pair:

    (reglas_base["antecedents_str"].isin(["whole milk", "yogurt"])) &
    (reglas_base["consequents_str"].isin(["whole milk", "yogurt"])) &
    (reglas_base["antecedents"].apply(len) == 1)
][["regla", "antecedent support", "consequent support", "support",
   "confidence", "lift"]].round(3)

Table 1: The two directions of the yogurt — whole milk relationship share the same lift but different confidences. The direction {yogurt} → {whole milk} exhibits higher confidence because whole milk is the more frequent item of the pair.




The practical implication is direct: when the objective is taking an action conditioned on observing an item —“what should I recommend to someone buying \(X\)?”— rule direction matters, and lift alone cannot guide that choice. Confidence, despite its documented limitations, remains the relevant metric for directing that choice. A recommendation engine sorting rules purely by lift and picking the first direction encountered may be recommending the suboptimal direction.


2.2 Theoretical Ceiling of Lift and Cross-Rule Comparability
A second limitation of lift, equally critical and less widely known, is that its scale is not universal: the maximum achievable lift for a given pair depends on individual item frequencies. This property makes comparing lifts across rules with different individual support levels methodologically flawed in a strict sense.
To derive the theoretical ceiling, observe that co-occurrence support \(P(A \cup B)\) is bounded above by the support of the rarer item: if \(P(A) \leq P(B)\), then \(P(A \cup B) \leq P(A)\) (no more transactions can co-occur than those containing the rarer item). Therefore:
\[\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(A) \cdot P(B)} \leq \frac{P(A)}{P(A) \cdot P(B)} = \frac{1}{P(B)} = \frac{1}{\max(P(A), P(B))} \tag{2}\]
The maximum theoretical lift for the pair \((A, B)\) is:
\[\text{lift}_{\max}(A, B) = \frac{1}{\max(P(A), P(B))} \tag{3}\]
This result has an immediate consequence: two frequent items —say, with support 0.50 each— have a maximum theoretical lift of just 2.0. Two rare items —with support 0.05 each— have a maximum theoretical lift of 20. An observed lift of 1.8 for the first pair represents 90% of its achievable maximum; the same lift of 1.8 for the second pair represents only 9%. The exact same figure signals a near-optimal rule in one case and a weak rule in the other.
To correct for this scale asymmetry, one can compute relative lift, defined as the fraction of theoretical maximum achieved by the observed lift:
\[\text{lift}_{\text{rel}}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B)}{\text{lift}_{\max}(A, B)} = \text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) \cdot \max(P(A), P(B)) \tag{4}\]
Relative lift spans the range \((0, 1]\) and is directly comparable across rules with different frequency levels. A relative lift near 1 indicates that items co-occur with maximum possible frequency given their individual supports.


Show code
freq_rel = df.mean()

def lift_max_teorico(row):
    pa = freq_rel.get(row["antecedents_str"], np.nan)
    pb = freq_rel.get(row["consequents_str"], np.nan)
    if pd.isna(pa) or pd.isna(pb):
        return np.nan
    return 1.0 / max(pa, pb)

reglas_simples = reglas_base[
    reglas_base["antecedents"].apply(len) == 1
].copy()
reglas_simples["lift_max_teorico"] = reglas_simples.apply(lift_max_teorico, axis=1)
reglas_simples["lift_relativo"] = (
    reglas_simples["lift"] / reglas_simples["lift_max_teorico"]
).round(3)

title: 37  Beyond Lift: Advanced Metrics, Sensitivity, and Rule Structure
text:
3 Complementary Metrics to Lift
The catalog of proposed metrics for evaluating association rule interest is extensive: Tan et al. (2006) systematically enumerate and compare over twenty distinct measures. None is universally superior; each captures a distinct facet of what we intuitively call “interest.” This section details three metrics whose mathematical properties and complementarity with lift make them especially valuable in practice.

3.1 Leverage: Absolute Difference Above Chance
Leverage for a rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) measures the absolute difference between observed co-occurrence frequency and expected frequency under statistical independence:
\[\text{lev}(A \Rightarrow B) = P(A \cup B) - P(A) \cdot P(B) \tag{5}\]
This definition shares the exact structure of lift’s numerator, minus the normalization by \(P(A) \cdot P(B)\). Consequently, leverage preserves probability units, giving it an operationally direct interpretation: a leverage of 0.05 in a 1,000-transaction dataset means roughly 50 transactions contain both \(A\) and \(B\) beyond expectation under independence. This is the additional transaction count attributable to the association.
The theoretical range of leverage is \([-\min(P(A), P(B)) \cdot (1 - \max(P(A), P(B))),\; \min(P(A), P(B)) \cdot (1 - \max(P(A), P(B)))]\), centered at zero. Positive leverage indicates positive association; negative indicates inhibition; zero indicates independence —just like lift, but on an absolute rather than relative scale.
The key distinction between leverage and lift lies in scale. Lift normalizes deviation from independence into a dimensionless number comparable across rules with different consequents. Leverage gives the absolute magnitude of that deviation, which is more interpretable when quantifying rule impact: in recommendation engines, leverage is proportional to additional transactions generated by acting on the rule. However, this reliance on absolute frequencies makes leverage systematically low for rare items, even when their relative relationship is very strong —the exact inverse problem of absolute lift.


3.2 Conviction: Asymmetry and Quasi-Determinism
Conviction for a rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) was introduced to create a directional, asymmetric metric like confidence that simultaneously reflects departure from statistical independence (Tan et al. 2006):
\[\text{conv}(A \Rightarrow B) = \frac{1 - P(B)}{1 - \text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B)} = \frac{P(A) \cdot (1 - P(B))}{P(A) - P(A \cup B)} \tag{6}\]
Conviction’s interpretation is less intuitive than lift or leverage, but warrants careful examination. The numerator \(1 - P(B)\) is the expected frequency of rule “errors” —transactions where \(B\) does not occur— under independence: if \(A\) and \(B\) were independent, a fraction \(1 - P(B)\) of transactions containing \(A\) would lack \(B\). The denominator \(1 - \text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B)\) is the observed frequency of those errors. The ratio measures how many times fewer errors the rule makes compared to expectation under independence.
Several notable properties follow:

When \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, \(\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) = P(B)\), and conviction \(= (1 - P(B)) / (1 - P(B)) = 1\). Conviction equals 1 if and only if there is independence —just as lift equals 1 under independence.
As confidence approaches 1, the denominator approaches 0, and conviction approaches infinity. A rule with very high conviction is quasi-deterministic: observing \(A\) predicts \(B\) with near certainty.
When confidence is lower than \(P(B)\) (negative association), conviction is less than 1.
Unlike lift, conviction is asymmetric: \(\text{conv}(A \Rightarrow B) \neq \text{conv}(B \Rightarrow A)\) in general, making it well-suited for evaluating rule strength in its specific direction.

This asymmetry is particularly valuable when rule direction carries operational meaning: in recommendation systems, medical diagnostics, or any domain where acting on an antecedent predicts a consequent.


3.3 Zhang’s Metric: Bounded Range and Robustness
Proposed to address limitations of lift, Zhang’s metric is defined as (Tan et al. 2006):
\[Z(A, B) = \frac{P(A \cup B) - P(A) \cdot P(B)}{\max\left\{P(A \cup B)\cdot[1 - P(A)],\; P(A)\cdot[P(B) - P(A \cup B)]\right\}} \tag{7}\]
The numerator matches leverage: observed co-occurrence minus independence. The denominator normalizes the metric to ensure \(Z \in [-1, 1]\) for any item pair, regardless of individual frequencies. This property —lacking in lift— makes Zhang’s metric directly comparable across rules with varying frequency levels.
The denominator selects the maximum of two terms: \(P(A \cup B) \cdot [1 - P(A)]\), which dominates under high co-occurrence (strong positive association), and \(P(A) \cdot [P(B) - P(A \cup B)]\), which dominates under low co-occurrence (negative association or inhibition). This design guarantees a symmetric scale: \(Z = 1\) corresponds to maximum co-occurrence (\(A\) and \(B\) co-occur whenever the rarer item occurs), while \(Z = -1\) corresponds to minimum co-occurrence (mutual exclusion).
Zhang’s metric is symmetric —like lift— and exceptionally robust against highly frequent items, which cause the most severe bias in confidence and leverage. For these reasons, Tan et al. (2006) recommend Zhang’s metric as one of the most reliable measures for ranking rules by general interest when no prior domain knowledge is available.

3.5 Correlation Between Metrics: Agreement and Discrepancy
Given multiple metrics, a natural question is whether they are redundant: if lift, leverage, and Zhang always rank rules identically, choice of metric is irrelevant. Correlation analysis provides an empirical answer.


Show code

    corr_matrix,

    color_continuous_scale="RdBu_r",

    zmax=1,

Figure 2: Pearson correlation matrix among the six evaluation metrics across the full rule set. Values are displayed inside each cell. Red-white-blue scale: deep red = high positive correlation, deep blue = high negative correlation, white = no correlation.




Figure 37.2 reveals several structural relationships. First, lift and Zhang show high positive correlation: both measure essential deviation from independence, differing in scale and extreme-value behavior. Second, leverage and support show moderate positive correlation: frequent items produce higher absolute leverage, reflecting leverage’s dependence on base frequencies. Third, conviction can exhibit low correlation with other metrics in certain datasets, precisely because it is sensitive to confidence values near 1 —where minor confidence shifts produce large conviction changes— while other metrics change smoothly.
Regions of low or negative correlation in this matrix are analytically most informative: where two metrics disagree, the analyst must decide which to weight higher based on context. A rule with high lift but low leverage involves infrequent items whose relative association is strong but whose absolute impact is limited. A rule with high Zhang but moderate conviction may be robust in overall association while not quasi-deterministic in direction.


3.6 The Multimetric Profile of a Rule
A method for visually summarizing a rule’s behavior across all metrics simultaneously is the normalized radar plot. For each rule, metrics are min-max scaled to \([0, 1]\) —for visualization purposes only, without assuming equal metric importance— and the resulting polygon is plotted.

top5 = reglas_norm.loc[top5_idx]

for _, row in top5.iterrows():
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar(
        r=[row[m] for m in metricas_viz] + [row[metricas_viz[0]]],
        theta=metricas_viz + [metricas_viz[0]],
        fill="toself",
        name=row["regla"][:38],
        opacity=0.55,
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    polar=dict(radialaxis=dict(visible=True, range=[0, 1])),
    height=500,
    showlegend=True,
    legend=dict(x=1.05, y=1.0),
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Normalized profile of top 5 rules by lift. Each axis corresponds to a metric min-max scaled to [0,1]. A larger, more regular polygon indicates a rule that is robust across multiple criteria simultaneously. Normalization is for display only and does not imply equal weighting.




Figure 37.3 compares five rules across five dimensions simultaneously. A rule with a large, regular polygon is robust: all metrics agree it is interesting. A rule with an asymmetric polygon —large on one axis, small on others— is strong under one criterion but weak under others, calling for cautious interpretation.

title: 37  Beyond Lift: Advanced Metrics, Sensitivity, and Rule Structure
text:
4 Sensitivity to Algorithm Parameters

4.1 Thresholds as Decisions Lacking Intrinsic Statistical Basis
When invoking Apriori with specific parameters —e.g., min_support = 0.10 and minimum lift of 1.0— decisions are made that, unlike parameters in formal statistical models, carry no intrinsic statistical justification. No theory establishes that the “correct” minimum support is 0.10 rather than 0.08 or 0.12. Analysts select these thresholds based on practical considerations —compute time, manageable result set size, domain knowledge— but the algorithm accepts them blindly.
This circumstance carries serious methodological consequences: the resulting rule set is not an objective property of the dataset, but a joint function of the dataset and chosen parameters. Two analysts working on the same dataset with slightly different thresholds can arrive at substantially different rule sets, potentially reaching conflicting conclusions if unaware of this dependence. Sound methodology requires exploring result stability across reasonable parameter shifts —termed sensitivity analysis— and reporting those parameters alongside findings.


4.2 Sensitivity to Minimum Support
The first sensitivity experiment systematically varies \(\sigma_{\min}\) while fixing minimum lift at 1.0, tracking changes in rule counts and median rule quality.


Show code
soportes_grid = [0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12, 0.14, 0.16, 0.18, 0.20]
resultados_sens = []

for s in soportes_grid:
    its = apriori(df, min_support=s, use_colnames=True)
    if len(its) == 0:
        resultados_sens.append({
            "σ_min": s, "Frequent itemsets": 0,
            "Rules": 0, "Median lift": np.nan, "Max lift": np.nan
        })
        continue
    r = association_rules(its, metric="lift", min_threshold=1.0)
    resultados_sens.append({
        "σ_min": round(s, 2),
        "Frequent itemsets": len(its),
        "Rules": len(r),
        "Median lift": round(r["lift"].median(), 3) if len(r) > 0 else np.nan,
        "Max lift": round(r["lift"].max(), 3) if len(r) > 0 else np.nan,
    })

The behavior in Figure 37.4 is neither accidental nor dataset-specific: it is a structural property of rule mining. Raising \(\sigma_{\min}\) excludes less frequent itemsets. Many of these involve rare items co-occurring by chance in the sample —precisely the patterns most vulnerable to statistical instability. Filtering them leaves a remaining rule set with higher average support and higher median lift. Informally: patterns surviving stricter filters are, on average, more robust.
The tension between these curves reflects the fundamental trade-off in association rule mining: one cannot simultaneously maximize rule quantity and average quality. Every support threshold represents a choice within this trade-off space, governed by the relative cost of two error types: including spurious rules (false positives) versus omitting genuine but rare patterns (false negatives).


4.3 Sensitivity to Lift Threshold
The second experiment fixes support at 0.10 and varies minimum lift across a wide range. The result yields a rule set survival curve: for each threshold, how many rules survive.


Show code

lifts_umbral = np.round(np.arange(0.5, 2.6, 0.1), 1)
curva_supervivencia = []

for lt in lifts_umbral:
    r = association_rules(its_fijo, metric="lift", min_threshold=float(lt))
    curva_supervivencia.append({
        "Minimum lift threshold": lt,
        "Surviving rules": len(r),
    })

df_surv = pd.DataFrame(curva_supervivencia)

fig = px.line(
    df_surv,
    x="Minimum lift threshold",
    y="Surviving rules",
    markers=True,
    color_discrete_sequence=["#2a9d8f"],
)
fig.add_vline(
    x=1.0, line_dash="dash", line_color="crimson",
    annotation_text="lift = 1 (independence)",
    annotation_position="top right",
    annotation_font_color="crimson",
)
fig.update_layout(height=390)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 5: Rule set survival curve vs. minimum lift threshold. Each point answers: if lift ≥ x is required, how many rules remain? A steep drop at value x indicates many rules cluster just above that threshold.




Curve shape in Figure 37.5 reveals lift distribution characteristics. A steep drop in \([1.0, 1.3]\) indicates many rules exhibit lift barely above independence —formally nontrivial but marginally interesting. A gradual drop suggests lifts are more evenly distributed over a wide range. In both cases, the curve identifies the lift threshold where the rule set stabilizes at a manageable size without discarding top patterns.


4.4 Full Map of Parameter Space
The comprehensive sensitivity analysis explores both key parameters simultaneously: minimum support and minimum confidence. The result is a 2D surface depicting rule counts generated for each parameter combination.


Show code
grid_support = np.round(np.arange(0.06, 0.22, 0.02), 2)
grid_conf    = np.round(np.arange(0.20, 1.00, 0.10), 2)
heatmap_data = []

for s in grid_support:
    for c in grid_conf:
        its = apriori(df, min_support=float(s), use_colnames=True)
        if len(its) == 0:
            heatmap_data.append({"min_support": s, "min_confidence": c, "n_reglas": 0})
            continue
        r = association_rules(its, metric="confidence", min_threshold=float(c))
        heatmap_data.append({
            "min_support": s,
            "min_confidence": c,
            "n_reglas": len(r),
        })

df_hm = pd.DataFrame(heatmap_data)
pivot = df_hm.pivot(index="min_confidence", columns="min_support", values="n_reglas")

fig = px.imshow(
    pivot,
    color_continuous_scale="YlOrRd",
    labels={"x": "Minimum support", "y": "Minimum confidence", "color": "No. of rules"},
    aspect="auto",
    text_auto=True,
)
fig.update_layout(height=450)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 6: Heatmap of rule counts vs. minimum support (horizontal axis) and minimum confidence (vertical axis). Bottom-left region —loose thresholds— yields maximum rules with lowest average quality. Top-right region —strict thresholds— yields few or no rules, but high reliability. Analysts must deliberately navigate this trade-off.




Figure 37.6 summarizes the analyst’s decision space. Each cell answers: selecting these thresholds yields how many rules? High-density regions (bottom-left, deep red) represent loose thresholds yielding high rule counts —along with high numbers of spurious rules. Low-density regions (top-right, pale yellow/white) represent strict thresholds yielding few rules, each backed by high frequency and strong predictive power.
The critical methodological lesson is: no single point on this map is correct in the abstract. Threshold choices are always relative to problem context. In retail with millions of daily transactions, min_support = 0.01 is justified because 1% represents thousands of observations. In a medical dataset with 200 patients, that same threshold equals just 2 cases —statistically inadequate for any claim. Correct selection requires translating support percentages into absolute observation counts and judging whether that sample size supports the intended claim.

section: 5 Global Structure of Rule Space: Graph Representation
text:
5 Global Structure of Rule Space: Graph Representation

5.1 Motivation for a Network Representation
Previous sections represented rules as tables and metric scatter plots. Both forms help evaluate individual rules or small subsets, but obscure the relational structure connecting items globally. An item can participate in many rules as antecedent or consequent; two items may connect directly via a rule or indirectly through an intermediate item. This topological structure is invisible in tabular form.
Graph representations make this structure explicit. Formally, we construct a graph \(G = (V, E)\) where vertex set \(V\) comprises unique items participating in at least one filtered rule, and edge set \(E\) contains directed edge \((A, B)\) for every rule \(A \Rightarrow B\) exceeding minimum lift and support thresholds. To maintain readability, we restrict focus to single-item antecedents and consequents (1-itemsets).


5.2 Centrality, Hubs, and Bridge Nodes
In graph theory, node centrality measures relative importance in the network. Among multiple definitions, a natural metric in association rules is the sum of lifts for all rules involving the item as antecedent or consequent. This weights items participating in many strong associations, rather than merely many associations.


Show code
reglas_grafo = reglas_base[
    (reglas_base["lift"] > 1.1) &
    (reglas_base["support"] >= 0.10) &
    (reglas_base["antecedents"].apply(len) == 1) &
    (reglas_base["consequents"].apply(len) == 1)
].copy()

nodos = list(set(
    reglas_grafo["antecedents_str"].tolist() +
    reglas_grafo["consequents_str"].tolist()
))
n_nodos = len(nodos)
nodo_idx = {nd: i for i, nd in enumerate(nodos)}

angulos = [2 * math.pi * i / n_nodos for i in range(n_nodos)]
xs = [math.cos(a) for a in angulos]
ys = [math.sin(a) for a in angulos]

# Centrality by sum of lifts
centralidad = {}
for nd in nodos:
    r_sub = reglas_grafo[
        (reglas_grafo["antecedents_str"] == nd) |
        (reglas_grafo["consequents_str"] == nd)
    ]
    centralidad[nd] = r_sub["lift"].sum()

edge_x, edge_y = [], []
for _, row in reglas_grafo.iterrows():
    x0 = xs[nodo_idx[row["antecedents_str"]]]
    y0 = ys[nodo_idx[row["antecedents_str"]]]
    x1 = xs[nodo_idx[row["consequents_str"]]]
    y1 = ys[nodo_idx[row["consequents_str"]]]
    edge_x += [x0, x1, None]
    edge_y += [y0, y1, None]

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=edge_x, y=edge_y,
    mode="lines",
    line=dict(width=1.2, color="#cccccc"),
    hoverinfo="none",
    showlegend=False,
))

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=xs, y=ys,
    mode="markers+text",
    text=nodos,
    textposition="top center",
    textfont=dict(size=10),

Figure 7: Association rule graph for single items with lift > 1.1 and support ≥ 0.10. Each node is an item; each edge is a rule meeting thresholds. Node size and color depict centrality (sum of lifts for connected rules). Large, bright nodes represent items involved in multiple strong associations; small, dark nodes are peripheral.




Figure 37.7 visualizes rule space topology. Highly central nodes participate in multiple strong associations, not simply high edge counts. An item can become a hub for two distinct reasons: being genuinely central to market basket co-purchases —its co-occurrences far exceed expectations from individual frequencies— or being so ubiquitous that it co-occurs with nearly everything, albeit with low lift.
Distinguishing genuine centrality from frequency-driven spurious centrality parallels the confidence issue: just as high confidence can artifactually arise from consequent base frequency, high network centrality can stem from sheer item ubiquity. Weighting centrality by lift —rather than raw co-occurrence counts— serves to correct this bias.
Equally important is the bridge node or broker: an item with few network neighbors connecting item clusters that would otherwise remain disconnected. In basket analysis, a bridge node might represent a niche item acting as a trigger for a specific purchasing chain. Such nodes are invisible in frequency-only analyses but offer high marketing actionability.


5.3 The “Whole Milk Problem”: A Case Study
Analyzing whole milk in Groceries concretely illustrates these challenges. Present in ~58% of sample transactions, whole milk is a dominant item whose high frequency systematically distorts metrics for every rule targeting it as consequent.

\[\text{conf}(A \Rightarrow B) > k \cdot P(B) \qquad \text{equivalently,} \qquad \text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) > k \tag{8}\]

title: 37  Beyond Lift: Advanced Metrics, Sensitivity, and Rule Structure
text:
6 An Integrated Evaluation Framework

6.1 From Fragmentation to Coherence
The concepts developed across this chapter —lift limitations, complementary metrics, parameter sensitivity, graph structure— are not isolated components. They form a unified framework answering a core question: how much confidence does a specific rule warrant?
Answering this question involves multiple dimensions:

Relative Dimension: How far does observed lift deviate from independence relative to theoretical maximum given item supports? Relative lift addresses this.
Absolute Dimension: How many additional transactions beyond baseline independence exhibit co-occurrence? Leverage answers this.
Directional Predictive Dimension: How deterministic is the rule in its specific direction? Conviction addresses this.
Normalized Robustness Dimension: Is the association strong on a scale comparable across varying item frequencies? Zhang’s metric resolves this.
Parametric Stability Dimension: Does the rule persist across reasonable threshold choices, or vanish under slight \(\sigma_{\min}\) tightening? Sensitivity analysis addresses this.

A rule showing strength across all dimensions earns high confidence. A rule succeeding in only one or two calls for caution. The following function systematically executes this multidimensional evaluation:


Show code
def evaluar_regla_completa(row, n_transacciones=50, verbose=True):
    """
    Multidimensional evaluation of an association rule.
    Returns qualitative classification: ROBUST / CANDIDATE / DISCARD
    """
    criterios = []
    puntos = 0

    # Dimension 1: Lift
    if row["lift"] > 1.5:
        criterios.append("Strong lift (> 1.5)")
        puntos += 3
    elif row["lift"] > 1.1:
        criterios.append("Moderate lift (1.1 – 1.5)")
        puntos += 1
    else:
        criterios.append("Weak lift (≤ 1.1) — indistinguishable from chance")

    # Dimension 2: Absolute support
    n_obs = int(row["support"] * n_transacciones)
    if n_obs >= 10:
        criterios.append(f"Solid support ({n_obs} of {n_transacciones} transactions)")
        puntos += 2
    elif n_obs >= 5:
        criterios.append(f"Minimum support ({n_obs} of {n_transacciones} transactions)")
        puntos += 1
    else:
        criterios.append(f"Insufficient support ({n_obs} of {n_transacciones} transactions)")

    # Dimension 3: Zhang (normalized robustness)
    if row["zhang"] > 0.3:
        criterios.append("Robust Zhang (> 0.3)")
        puntos += 2
    elif row["zhang"] > 0.1:
        criterios.append("Moderate Zhang (0.1 – 0.3)")
        puntos += 1
    else:
        criterios.append("Weak Zhang (≤ 0.1) — likely base frequency artifact")

    # Dimension 4: Conviction (directional determinism)
    if row["conviction"] > 1.5:
        criterios.append("High conviction (> 1.5) — quasi-deterministic rule")
        puntos += 1

    clasificacion = (
        "ROBUST"    if puntos >= 6 else
        "CANDIDATE"  if puntos >= 3 else
        "DISCARD"
    )

    if verbose:
        print(f"{'─'*55}")
        print(f"Rule:  {row['regla']}")
        print(f"{'─'*55}")
        for c in criterios:
            print(f"  • {c}")
        print(f"\n  → Classification: {clasificacion}  ({puntos}/8 points)\n")

    return clasificacion

# Evaluate top 6 rules by lift
print("Evaluation of top 6 rules by lift:\n")
for _, row in reglas_base.sort_values("lift", ascending=False).head(6).iterrows():
    evaluar_regla_completa(row)

The difference between basic association rule analysis in introductory texts and the critical framework developed here lies not in code: mlxtend functions remain identical. The difference lies in the questions asked before interpreting results and the conceptual tools applied.

title: 37  Beyond Lift: Advanced Metrics, Sensitivity, and Rule Structure
text:
7 Conceptual Summary
This chapter explored association rule mining beyond fundamental metrics. Key takeaways:
On Structural Limitations of Lift:

Lift is symmetric: \(\text{lift}(A \Rightarrow B) = \text{lift}(B \Rightarrow A)\). Selecting rule direction for practical applications relies on confidence —an asymmetric metric.
Lift has a theoretical ceiling dependent on individual supports: \(\text{lift}_{\max} = 1 / \max(P(A), P(B))\). Comparing raw lifts across rules with differing supports can be misleading. Relative lift —ratio of observed to maximum lift— provides a fairer basis for comparison.

On Complementary Metrics:

Leverage measures absolute difference between observed co-occurrence and independence. It reflects additional transactions attributable to association, but is systematically low for rare items.
Conviction is asymmetric and measures rule quasi-determinism in direction: very high values signal confidence near 1.
Zhang’s metric spans \([-1, 1]\), is symmetric, and resists frequent-item bias. It is recommended for comparing rules across varying frequency regimes.
Metrics are non-redundant: imperfect correlations mean metric discrepancies offer key analytical signals.

On Parameter Sensitivity:

Apriori thresholds carry no intrinsic statistical justification. Resulting rule sets are a joint function of dataset and chosen parameters.
Sensitivity analysis —systematic exploration of parameter space— is a mandatory methodological practice.
The support-confidence map visualizes full decision space, letting analysts deliberately position choices along the quantity vs. quality curve.

On Graph Representations:

Rule graphs reveal network topology: hubs, bridge nodes, and item clusters.
Lift-weighted centrality —rather than raw edge counts— distinguishes genuinely central items from frequency-driven artifacts.
The “Whole Milk Problem” demonstrates how high consequent frequency makes discovering informative rules nearly impossible regardless of thresholds.

On the Integrated Framework:

Robust rule evaluation requires examining at least four dimensions simultaneously: relative lift, leverage, Zhang, and conviction.
Robust rules show convergence across multiple metrics; candidate rules show partial convergence; discarded rules fail under stricter metrics.
