title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.1 Introduction
Association rule mining seeks to uncover regularities in transactional databases: products frequently bought together, web pages visited in the same session, words co-occurring in documents, or events recorded in tandem. In this context, a transaction represents an observation made up of multiple items; for instance, a supermarket basket might contain {Bread, Milk, Diapers}. The goal is not to predict a target label, but rather to identify co-occurrence structures that allow extracting interpretable knowledge from discrete data (Agrawal and Srikant 1994; Han et al. 2012).
The FP-Growth (Frequent Pattern Growth) algorithm was proposed as an efficient alternative to Apriori for discovering frequent itemsets. Its core idea is to avoid explicit candidate generation by compressing the transaction database into a compact data structure called the FP-tree (Frequent Pattern Tree). From this tree, the algorithm mines frequent patterns using conditional pattern bases and conditional trees (Han et al. 2000; Borgelt 2005).
This chapter develops FP-Growth in a step-by-step fashion. First, we review the concepts of transactions, itemsets, support, and frequency. Next, we illustrate how to build an FP-tree using a toy market basket example. Finally, we explain how to extract frequent patterns via conditional prefix paths, compare FP-Growth with Apriori, and implement a practical pipeline in Python.
crumbs: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.2 Basic Concepts
In association mining, we work with a collection of transactions. Each transaction contains a subset of items drawn from a finite universe of possible products, terms, or events. This representation is natural for set-based data: a purchase contains products, a document contains words, a web session contains visited pages.






Definition. Let \(I = \{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_m\}\) be a finite set of items. A transaction \(T\) is a subset of \(I\), i.e.: \[
T \subseteq I.
\] A transaction database is a collection \(\mathcal{D} = \{T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n\}\) of transactions.









Definition. An itemset is any subset \(X \subseteq I\). We say that a transaction \(T_i\) contains \(X\) if all items in \(X\) appear in \(T_i\): \[
X \subseteq T_i.
\]



The key metric for assessing pattern relevance is support. It is commonly reported either as an absolute count or as a relative proportion. Absolute count indicates how many transactions contain the pattern; relative support divides that count by the total number of transactions.






Definition. The absolute support of an itemset \(X\) in a transaction database \(\mathcal{D}\) is the number of transactions containing \(X\): \[
\operatorname{supp}_{\#}(X)=\left|\{T_i \in \mathcal{D}: X \subseteq T_i\}\right|.
\] Relative support is defined as: \[
\operatorname{supp}(X)=\frac{\operatorname{supp}_{\#}(X)}{|\mathcal{D}|}.
\tag{1}\]









Definition. Given a minimum support threshold \(\text{min\_sup}\), an itemset \(X\) is frequent if its absolute support satisfies: \[
\operatorname{supp}_{\#}(X) \geq \text{min\_sup}.
\tag{2}\]



The threshold \(\text{min\_sup}\) controls the granularity of the analysis. Setting it too low yields an excessive number of patterns, many of which are trivial or uninterpretable. Setting it too high can eliminate interesting but less common patterns. Consequently, in real-world applications, it is typically chosen through exploratory analysis, domain knowledge, and computational constraints.
crumbs: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.3 From Apriori to FP-Growth
The Apriori algorithm relies on a fundamental property: if an itemset is frequent, all of its subsets must also be frequent. Equivalently, if an itemset is infrequent, none of its supersets can be frequent (Agrawal and Srikant 1994). This anti-monotonicity property allows pruning the search space, but Apriori still needs to generate candidate itemsets and scan the database multiple times.
FP-Growth follows a different strategy. Instead of explicitly generating and evaluating candidates, it performs two main passes over the database: one to compute individual item supports and another to construct a compact tree. It then mines frequent patterns directly from this compressed structure (Han et al. 2000).
This approach offers significant advantages when many transactions share prefixes. When items are sorted globally in descending frequency order, similar transactions tend to share the initial branches of the tree. Thus, the FP-tree stores aggregated information rather than repeating each full transaction independently.

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining

39.5 Frequency Ordering
The FP-tree relies on a global item ordering. The standard rule is ordering items by descending frequency. Ties can be broken deterministically, such as alphabetically. This ordering ensures that transactions containing frequent items share prefixes, maximizing tree compactness.
In our example, the global ordering is:
\[
\text{Milk} \succ \text{Bread} \succ \text{Diapers} \succ \text{Beer}.
\]
Applying this order transforms the original transactions as follows:



Original Transaction
Ordered Transaction

{Bread, Milk, Diapers, Beer}

{Milk, Diapers, Beer}
[Milk, Diapers, Beer]


{Bread, Milk, Diapers, Beer}
[Milk, Bread, Diapers, Beer]


{Bread, Milk, Diapers}
[Milk, Bread, Diapers]





Show code

order = sorted(frequent_items, key=lambda item: (-item_counts[item], item))
rank = {item: position for position, item in enumerate(order)}

ordered_transactions = []
for transaction in transactions:
    filtered = [item for item in transaction if item in frequent_items]
    ordered = sorted(filtered, key=lambda item: rank[item])
    ordered_transactions.append(ordered)

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.6 Construction of the FP-tree
An FP-tree is a rooted tree initialized with a null root node. Each node stores an item, a count, and child pointers. To insert an ordered transaction, we traverse it from left to right. If the next item already exists as a child of the current node, its count is incremented. Otherwise, a new child node is created with an initial count of one.






Definition. An FP-tree is a tree structure \(\mathcal{T}\) where each non-root node represents an item and maintains a count. The count of node \(v\) reflects the number of transactions sharing the path prefix from the root to \(v\): \[
\operatorname{count}(v)=\left|\{T_i \in \mathcal{D}: \operatorname{path}(v) \subseteq T_i\}\right|.
\]



The construction algorithm proceeds as follows:

Create a null root node.
Sort items in each transaction according to global frequency order.
Insert each transaction sequentially into the tree.
Increment node counts along matching existing paths.
Allocate new nodes whenever a prefix path deviates.



Show code
class FPNode:
    def __init__(self, item=None, count=0, parent=None):
        self.item = item
        self.count = count
        self.parent = parent
        self.children = {}

    def add_child(self, item):
        child = FPNode(item=item, count=0, parent=self)
        self.children[item] = child
        return child


def insert_transaction(root, transaction):
    current = root
    for item in transaction:
        if item not in current.children:
            current.add_child(item)
        current = current.children[item]
        current.count += 1


def build_fp_tree(ordered_transactions):
    root = FPNode(item="null", count=0)
    for transaction in ordered_transactions:
        insert_transaction(root, transaction)
    return root


def print_tree(node, indent=0):
    label = f"{node.item}: {node.count}" if node.item != "null" else "null"
    print("  " * indent + label)
    for child in node.children.values():
        print_tree(child, indent + 1)

root = build_fp_tree(ordered_transactions)
print_tree(root)


null
  Milk: 5
    Bread: 4
      Diapers: 3
        Beer: 2
    Diapers: 1
      Beer: 1


In this example, the primary branch begins with Milk because it occurs across all transactions. From Milk, several transactions continue to Bread, while others branch directly to Diapers. Compression is achieved by accumulating counts along shared prefixes rather than storing each transaction independently.

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
section: 39.7 Prefix Paths and Conditional Pattern Base
text:
39.7 Prefix Paths and Conditional Pattern Base
Once the FP-tree is built, FP-Growth extracts frequent patterns by processing items from least to most frequent. For each target item, all prefix paths terminating at that item are gathered. Removing the target item from these paths yields its conditional pattern base.






Definition. Given an item \(a\), the conditional pattern base of \(a\), denoted \(\mathcal{B}_a\), is the multiset of prefix paths preceding \(a\) in the FP-tree, weighted by the node count of \(a\): \[
\mathcal{B}_a = \{(P_j,c_j): P_j \text{ is a prefix path of } a \text{ with count } c_j\}.
\]

With \(\text{min\_sup}=3\), Bread is pruned from the conditional base of Beer, while Milk and Diapers remain frequent. Thus, the frequent patterns containing Beer are:
\[
\{\text{Beer}\}, \quad
\{\text{Milk},\text{Beer}\}, \quad
\{\text{Diapers},\text{Beer}\}, \quad
\{\text{Milk},\text{Diapers},\text{Beer}\}.
\]


Show code
def collect_prefix_paths(node, target_item):
    """Returns prefix paths leading to target_item in a basic FP-tree."""
    paths = []

    def traverse(current):
        for child in current.children.values():
            if child.item == target_item:
                path = []
                parent = child.parent
                while parent is not None and parent.item != "null":
                    path.append(parent.item)
                    parent = parent.parent
                path.reverse()
                if path:
                    paths.append((path, child.count))
            traverse(child)

    traverse(node)
    return paths

prefix_paths_cerveza = collect_prefix_paths(root, "Beer")
prefix_paths_cerveza


[(['Milk', 'Bread', 'Diapers'], 2), (['Milk', 'Diapers'], 1)]

def conditional_counts(prefix_paths):
    counts = Counter()
    for path, weight in prefix_paths:
        for item in path:
            counts[item] += weight
    return counts

conditional_counts(prefix_paths_cerveza)

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.8 Conditional Tree
After building an item’s conditional pattern base, items failing to meet minimum support are pruned, and a new sub-tree is constructed for that base. This is the conditional tree. For Beer, the conditional tree reduces to:
\[
\text{Milk}:3 \rightarrow \text{Diapers}:3.
\]
This indicates that across transactions containing Beer, Milk co-occurs 3 times and Diapers co-occurs 3 times. The joint branch confirms that {Milk, Diapers, Beer} is also a frequent pattern.






Definition. The conditional FP-tree of an item \(a\) is the FP-tree constructed from its conditional pattern base \(\mathcal{B}_a\) after removing items whose conditional count falls below \(\text{min\_sup}\): \[
\mathcal{T}_a = \operatorname{FPtree}\left(\{P_j \in \mathcal{B}_a: \operatorname{count}_{\mathcal{B}_a}(i) \geq \text{min\_sup}\}\right).
\]





Show code
def expand_weighted_paths(prefix_paths):
    expanded = []
    for path, weight in prefix_paths:
        expanded.extend([path] * weight)
    return expanded

conditional_item_counts = conditional_counts(prefix_paths_cerveza)
conditional_frequent = {
    item for item, count in conditional_item_counts.items()
    if count >= min_sup
}

conditional_order = sorted(
    conditional_frequent,
    key=lambda item: (-conditional_item_counts[item], item)
)
conditional_rank = {item: pos for pos, item in enumerate(conditional_order)}

conditional_transactions = []
for path in expand_weighted_paths(prefix_paths_cerveza):
    filtered_path = [item for item in path if item in conditional_frequent]
    ordered_path = sorted(filtered_path, key=lambda item: conditional_rank[item])
    if ordered_path:
        conditional_transactions.append(ordered_path)

conditional_root = build_fp_tree(conditional_transactions)
print_tree(conditional_root)

39.9 Frequent Patterns for the Base Example
Repeating this mining procedure for all items in ascending order of frequency yields the complete set of frequent itemsets:







Base Item
Associated Frequent Patterns




Beer
{Beer}, {Milk, Beer}, {Diapers, Beer}, {Milk, Diapers, Beer}


Diapers
{Diapers}, {Milk, Diapers}, {Bread, Diapers}, {Milk, Bread, Diapers}


Bread
{Bread}, {Milk, Bread}


Milk
{Milk}



Aggregating and deduplicating, the frequent itemsets for \(\text{min\_sup}=3\) are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\{\text{Milk}\},\{\text{Bread}\},\{\text{Diapers}\},\{\text{Beer}\},\\
&\{\text{Milk},\text{Bread}\},\{\text{Milk},\text{Diapers}\},\{\text{Milk},\text{Beer}\},\\
&\{\text{Bread},\text{Diapers}\},\{\text{Diapers},\text{Beer}\},\\
&\{\text{Milk},\text{Bread},\text{Diapers}\},\{\text{Milk},\text{Diapers},\text{Beer}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Note that FP-Growth does not generate association rules directly; it outputs frequent itemsets. Association rules are generated subsequently from these itemsets by evaluating metrics such as confidence, lift, or conviction (Tan et al. 2019; Han et al. 2012).

From frequent itemsets, rules are derived. For example, a rule \(X \Rightarrow Y\) states: “when \(X\) occurs, \(Y\) also tends to occur.”






Definition. The confidence of an association rule \(X \Rightarrow Y\) (where \(X \cap Y = \varnothing\)) measures the fraction of transactions containing \(X\) that also contain \(Y\): \[
\operatorname{conf}(X \Rightarrow Y)=\frac{\operatorname{supp}(X \cup Y)}{\operatorname{supp}(X)}.
\tag{3}\]









Definition. The lift of a rule \(X \Rightarrow Y\) compares observed co-occurrence of \(X\) and \(Y\) against expected co-occurrence under statistical independence: \[
\operatorname{lift}(X \Rightarrow Y)=\frac{\operatorname{supp}(X \cup Y)}{\operatorname{supp}(X)\operatorname{supp}(Y)}.
\tag{4}\]

FP-Growth is preferred when datasets are large and contain dense frequent patterns. Apriori remains useful for educational purposes or lightweight tasks requiring straightforward candidate generation. In practice, algorithm selection depends on transaction density, support threshold, available memory, and the need to inspect intermediate candidate steps.
crumbs: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.12 Applications
FP-Growth is widely applied across domains where data is naturally set-structured:

Market basket analysis: identifying products frequently bought together.
Recommender systems: suggesting items, articles, or services based on co-occurrence patterns.
Customer behavior analysis: discovering purchasing habits in physical retail or e-commerce.
Web usage mining: detecting common navigation paths or clickstream sequences.
Text mining: discovering words, terms, or phrases co-occurring in documents.

In all cases, frequent patterns must be interpreted cautiously. Co-occurrence does not imply causation. A rule may be statistically valid yet offer no practical value if it represents an obvious, redundant, or data-collection-biased pattern.
crumbs: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.13 Pros and Cons
Key advantages of FP-Growth include:

Eliminates explicit candidate generation.
Reduces full database scans to two passes.
Compresses transactions via shared prefix paths.
Efficiently mines long, complex frequent patterns.
Scales well on dense datasets where Apriori generates combinatorial explosions of candidates.

Main limitations include:

FP-tree memory overhead can be substantial on sparse, uncompressible datasets.
Implementation complexity is higher than Apriori.
Recursive conditional mining can be memory-heavy when frequent patterns abound.
Lacks native support for incremental updates: changing data requires rebuilding the tree.

These constraints do not invalidate the algorithm, but highlight the need to carefully configure support thresholds, clean input data, and evaluate pattern actionability.
crumbs: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.14 Best Practices for Analysis
Applying FP-Growth in real projects requires a structured, reproducible workflow:

Formally define what constitutes a transaction.
Clean and normalize items.
Inspect single-item frequency distributions prior to pattern mining.
Experiment with multiple minimum support thresholds.
Inspect frequent itemsets before attempting rule generation.
Evaluate support, confidence, and lift jointly.
Validate patterns using domain knowledge.
Document all decisions, thresholds, and data preprocessing assumptions.

The most critical step is not running the algorithm, but defining a coherent transaction model. In text mining, choosing words vs. lemmas vs. n-grams fundamentally alters pattern meaning. In e-commerce, defining a transaction as an order vs. a session vs. a user account completely reshapes support interpretation.
crumbs: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining

title: 38  FP-Growth and Frequent Pattern Mining
text:
39.15 Conclusions
FP-Growth is a cornerstone algorithm in frequent pattern mining. Its primary contribution is replacing candidate generation with a compact data structure —the FP-tree— that stores shared prefix paths and enables mining patterns via conditional bases. This strategy drastically reduces database scans and outperforms Apriori on large or dense datasets.
Conceptually, FP-Growth highlights a fundamental principle in data science: computational efficiency depends heavily on data representation. Transforming flat transaction lists into a compressed prefix tree renders frequent itemset mining manageable without sacrificing complete information retrieval.
In real-world deployment, algorithmic output must be paired with rigorous domain interpretation. Frequent patterns provide valuable starting points for building hypotheses and recommendation engines, but co-occurrence does not constitute causal proof. Thus, association mining should be integrated into broader exploratory workflows informed by domain expertise and practical utility.

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
1 Introduction
Classification is one of the fundamental tasks in supervised learning. Its goal is to learn a decision rule from previously observed examples capable of assigning a categorical label to new observations. Unlike numerical prediction (regression), where the output belongs to a continuous or ordered discrete space, in classification the output belongs to a finite set of discrete classes: for example, spam or non-spam, approve or reject, positive, negative, or neutral (Hastie et al. 2009; James et al. 2021).
In general terms, a classification problem starts with a training dataset composed of pairs
\[
\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n},
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{X}\) represents the predictor variables or available observations, while \(y_i \in \mathcal{Y}\) represents the target class. The objective is to construct a function
\[
\hat{f}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}
\]
that generalizes well to unseen data.
This chapter explores decision trees as interpretable classification models. The exposition focuses on the general logic of tree induction, Hunt’s algorithm, the ID3 algorithm, entropy, information gain, and the extraction of classification rules.

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
2 Classification as a Supervised Problem
In a classification problem, historical examples are available where the true class is known. The model leverages these examples to learn patterns connecting explanatory variables to target labels.
Typical examples include:

Classifying an email as spam or non-spam;
Deciding whether a credit application should be approved or rejected;
Identifying whether a patient presents hypertension;
Categorizing a review as positive, negative, or neutral;
Predicting whether a customer will purchase a laptop.

The distinction between classification and regression depends on the type of target variable. If the output is categorical, it is a classification problem. If the output is numerical, it is a regression problem.



Task
Output Type
Example




Classification
Categorical
Pass / Fail


Regression
Numerical
Tomorrow’s Temperature









Definition. A supervised classification problem consists of estimating a function \(\hat{f}\) that maps each observation \(\mathbf{x}\) to a class \(y\) within a finite set of labels \(\mathcal{Y}\): \[
\hat{f}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}, \qquad |\mathcal{Y}| < \infty.
\tag{1}\]

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
3 Training, Testing, and Generalization
Classification workflows are typically divided into two main phases: training and testing. During training, the algorithm adjusts its internal rules using labeled data. During testing, the model is evaluated on unseen data to estimate its generalization capability.
This separation is essential because a model can memorize training data without learning useful underlying patterns. This phenomenon is known as overfitting. In decision trees, overfitting occurs when a tree grows too deep, creating highly specific partitions for individual training cases (Breiman et al. 1984; Quinlan 1986).






Definition. Given a training set \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\) and a test set \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}\), the generalization capability of a classifier is evaluated by estimating its performance on examples not used during model fitting: \[
\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \cup \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}, \qquad
\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \cap \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}} = \varnothing.
\tag{2}\]

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
4 Data Preparation Before Classifier Building
Before training a classifier, data preparation is required. Model quality depends directly on feature quality. Three common tasks are data cleaning, transformation, and dimensionality reduction.
Data cleaning involves correcting invalid or inconsistent entries (such as negative ages or misspelled categories) and deciding how to handle missing values. Data transformation includes encoding categorical variables, scaling numerical features, and parsing dates into usable features. Dimensionality reduction removes redundant, irrelevant, or noisy features.
For decision trees, feature scaling is less critical than in linear models or neural networks, as trees are invariant to monotonic feature transformations. However, category quality, missing value strategies, and handling of continuous features remain important considerations (James et al. 2021; Géron 2022).

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
5 Decision Trees
A decision tree is a predictive model that organizes sequential decisions in a hierarchical structure. Each internal node represents a test on an attribute, each branch represents a test outcome, and each leaf node assigns a class. Predicting a new observation involves traversing the tree from the root to a leaf.
Decision trees are particularly valued for their interpretability. Unlike opaque models, a tree can be translated directly into human-readable IF-THEN rules (Breiman et al. 1984; Quinlan 1993).






Definition. A classification decision tree is a hierarchical structure composed of internal nodes, branches, and leaves. Each internal node applies a test \(h_j(\mathbf{x})\), each branch corresponds to a test outcome, and each leaf assigns a class \(c \in \mathcal{Y}\): \[
T(\mathbf{x}) = c, \qquad c \in \mathcal{Y}.
\tag{3}\]



Core elements of a tree include:







Element
Description




Root Node
The topmost node containing all training examples before splitting.


Internal Node
A node where an attribute test is evaluated to split the dataset.


Branch
A outcome path originating from a node test.


Leaf Node
A terminal node assigning a final class label.

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
6 Data Partitioning in Decision Trees
Tree induction relies on recursively partitioning data. At each node, an attribute is chosen to split the dataset into subsets.
For categorical attributes, the tree may create one branch per category. For instance, if Outlook takes values Sunny, Overcast, and Rain, three branches are formed. In binary trees, categories are evaluated via boolean tests like “Is color red?”.
For continuous attributes, a split threshold must be selected. For example, Income might be split into Income <= 25000 and Income > 25000. Although ID3 was designed primarily for categorical features, extensions such as C4.5 handle continuous variables smoothly (Quinlan 1986, 1993).

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
7 Hunt’s Algorithm
Hunt’s algorithm outlines a general recursive framework for building decision trees. The core logic is simple: if all examples reaching a node belong to the same class, the node becomes a leaf. Otherwise, an attribute test is chosen to partition the data, and the procedure recurses on each subset.
Let \(D_t\) be the set of training records reaching node \(t\). The algorithm proceeds as follows:

If all records in \(D_t\) belong to class \(y\), create a leaf node with label \(y\).
If \(D_t\) is empty, create a leaf node labeled with a default class (typically the majority class of the parent node).
If records belong to multiple classes, select an attribute test to split \(D_t\).
Partition \(D_t\) into subsets based on test outcomes.
Recursively apply the algorithm to each subset.

This approach is top-down (moving from root to leaves) and follows a divide-and-conquer strategy.






Definition. Let \(D_t\) be the set of examples reaching node \(t\). A node is pure if all examples in \(D_t\) belong to the exact same class: \[
\exists c \in \mathcal{Y} \; \text{such that} \; y_i = c \quad \forall (\mathbf{x}_i,y_i) \in D_t.
\tag{4}\]

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
39  Classification and Decision Trees
section: 9 ID3: Feature Selection via Information Gain
text:
9 ID3: Feature Selection via Information Gain
ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3) is a classic decision tree algorithm proposed by Quinlan. It uses information gain at each node to select the attribute that best separates the target classes (Quinlan 1986).
The intuition is that a good splitting attribute produces subsets that are purer (more homogeneous) than the original set. To quantify impurity, ID3 uses entropy from information theory (Shannon 1948).
The workflow is:

Start with all training records at the root node.
Calculate current dataset entropy.
Evaluate all available candidate attributes.
Compute weighted average entropy after splitting for each attribute.
Select the attribute yielding highest Information Gain.
Recurse on child branches.

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
10 Entropy as an Impurity Measure
Entropy measures the degree of randomness or impurity in a dataset. If all examples belong to a single class, entropy is 0. If classes are evenly split, entropy reaches its maximum value.






Definition. Let \(S\) be a dataset with \(c\) target classes, and let \(p_i\) be the proportion of examples belonging to class \(i\). The entropy of \(S\) is defined as: \[
H(S) = -\sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i \log_2(p_i).
\tag{5}\]



By convention, \(0\log_2(0)=0\), since \(\lim_{p \to 0^+} p\log_2(p) = 0\).
For example, if \(S\) contains 15 records with 9 Yes and 6 No labels:
\[
p(\text{Yes}) = \frac{9}{15}, \qquad p(\text{No}) = \frac{6}{15}.
\]
Thus,
\[
H(S) = -\frac{9}{15}\log_2\left(\frac{9}{15}\right)
       -\frac{6}{15}\log_2\left(\frac{6}{15}\right)
       \approx 0.971.
\]


Show code
import numpy as np

def entropy(labels):
    values, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / counts.sum()
    return -np.sum(probs * np.log2(probs))

labels = ["Yes"] * 9 + ["No"] * 6
entropy(labels)


np.float64(0.9709505944546686)

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
11 Information Gain
Information Gain measures the reduction in entropy achieved by partitioning a dataset on a given attribute. A split producing pure child nodes yields high information gain.






Definition. Let \(S\) be a dataset and \(A\) an attribute taking values \(v \in \operatorname{Values}(A)\). If \(S_v\) denotes the subset of examples where attribute \(A\) takes value \(v\), Information Gain is defined as: \[
\operatorname{Gain}(S,A) = H(S) - \sum_{v\in \operatorname{Values}(A)} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(S_v).
\tag{6}\]



The first term, \(H(S)\), represents initial dataset impurity. The second term represents expected entropy after splitting, weighted by subset sizes. Information Gain reflects the impurity reduction obtained by splitting on \(A\).

def information_gain(data, attribute, target):
    total_entropy = entropy(data[target])
    weighted_entropy = 0.0
    for value, subset in data.groupby(attribute):
        weight = len(subset) / len(data)
        weighted_entropy += weight * entropy(subset[target])
    return total_entropy - weighted_entropy

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
15 Extracting Classification Rules
A primary benefit of decision trees is their direct conversion into classification rules. Each root-to-leaf path produces a single IF-THEN rule.
From the tree above, we extract:

IF Outlook = Sunny AND Humidity = High, THEN Play = No.
IF Outlook = Sunny AND Humidity = Normal, THEN Play = Yes.
IF Outlook = Overcast, THEN Play = Yes.
IF Outlook = Rain AND Wind = Weak, THEN Play = Yes.
IF Outlook = Rain AND Wind = Strong, THEN Play = No.







Definition. A classification rule extracted from a decision tree is a logical implication comprising conditions along a root-to-leaf path: \[
\text{IF } (A_1=v_1) \land (A_2=v_2) \land \cdots \land (A_k=v_k) \text{ THEN } y=c.
\tag{7}\]



These rules are intuitive and easy to communicate to non-technical domain experts. Consequently, decision trees are widely applied in medical diagnostics, credit scoring, predictive maintenance, and customer churn analysis (Breiman et al. 1984; James et al. 2021).

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
16 Implementation with scikit-learn
While the preceding examples computed entropy and information gain manually, production environments utilize optimized machine learning libraries. In Python, scikit-learn provides efficient decision tree implementations (scikit-learn developers 2026).
Categorical features are typically one-hot encoded before fitting a tree configured with criterion="entropy".


Show code
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report

X = df.drop(columns="Play")
y = df["Play"]

categorical_features = X.columns.tolist()

preprocess = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features)
    ]
)

model = DecisionTreeClassifier(
    criterion="entropy",
    max_depth=3,
    random_state=42
)

clf = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("preprocess", preprocess),
    ("model", model)
])

clf.fit(X, y)
clf.predict(X)

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
18 Computational Complexity
The computational complexity of tree building depends on the number of records \(n\), number of attributes \(m\), number of classes, and split evaluation costs. For categorical features, a simplified per-node split evaluation cost is \(O(mn)\).
Summing across tree levels, a balanced tree of depth \(d\) processes roughly \(n\) examples per level, yielding a total induction complexity estimate of:
\[
O(mn d),
\]
where \(d\) is tree depth. In the worst case, depth can reach \(n\), incurring higher costs and producing non-generalizable unpruned trees. Continuous features require sorting or threshold scanning, modifying training complexity (Hastie et al. 2009; scikit-learn developers 2026).






Definition. For \(n\) examples, \(m\) attributes, and tree depth \(d\), a simplified computational complexity estimate for categorical tree induction is: \[
T(n,m,d) = O(mnd).
\tag{8}\]



Inference with a trained tree is highly efficient: classifying a new record requires traversing a single path from root to leaf, taking \(O(d)\) time.

title: 39  Classification and Decision Trees
39  Classification and Decision Trees
text:
20 Conclusions
Supervised classification aims to assign categorical labels to new instances based on historical observations. Decision trees offer an intuitive, interpretable framework for solving classification tasks through sequential feature tests.
Hunt’s algorithm provides the general recursive blueprint for tree construction. ID3 specifies a split selection criterion grounded in entropy and Information Gain. Entropy measures class impurity, while Information Gain quantifies impurity reduction following a split.
The baseball example illustrated how initial entropy is computed, candidate features are evaluated, root nodes selected, and branches recursively grown until pure leaves are reached. Converting trained trees into IF-THEN rules bridges the gap between quantitative predictive modeling and human explainability.
In real-world machine learning pipelines, decision trees require careful hyperparameter tuning and regularization to avoid overfitting. Nevertheless, they remain a foundational model family in data science due to their unique balance of simplicity, transparency, and competitive predictive capability.

title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Introduction
The evaluation of classification models constitutes one of the most strategically complex problems in Data Mining. It is not enough to build a model that “works”: it is necessary to quantify precisely and contextually how well it works, in which scenarios it fails, and what types of errors it makes, since as we will see below, classifier quality is completely determined by the model’s objective and application context (Han et al. 2011).
This distinction carries direct consequences in real-world environments: a medical diagnostic model that confuses “statistical accuracy” with “clinical utility” may leave sick patients untreated; a fraud detection system optimizing the wrong metric may block legitimate transactions and damage customer relations.
Consequently, specialized literature has produced a robust set of metrics and evaluation tools extending far beyond intuitive accuracy percentages. Understanding these metrics is a core competency of the data scientist (Provost and Fawcett 2013).
This chapter systematically develops the most important metrics for evaluating binary and multiclass classifiers, integrating them with the KDD (Knowledge Discovery in Databases) process and decision-making logic in high-stakes contexts. Each section combines mathematical rigor with executable Python code, following the principle that deep understanding of a metric requires formal derivation as well as implementation and visualization on real data.
crumbs: 40  Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation

title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Errors
In this chapter we define an error as a situation where a classification model assigns an incorrect label to an instance.
We define the error rate as the proportion of incorrectly classified instances over total evaluated instances.






Definition. The error rate of a classifier with \(k\) errors on a test set of \(n\) instances is defined as:
\[
\epsilon = \frac{k}{n}
\tag{1}\]



At first glance, this definition may seem sufficient for evaluating any classifier, given that in most cases the objective is minimizing the total number of errors committed by the model. However, as we will explore throughout this chapter, not all errors are created equal; depending on context, different mistakes carry radically different consequences.

title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Error Types and Their Costs

The Confusion Matrix: The Foundation of All Classifier Evaluation
Generally speaking, we designate a class as positive (1) when it represents the target class of interest, and negative (0) when it is the complementary class. For instance, in a fraud detection system, the positive class is “fraud” and the negative class is “legitimate transaction”. In a medical diagnostic system, the positive class is “sick” and the negative class is “healthy”.
We can organize the errors of a binary classifier using the confusion matrix, a tabular representation that synthesizes binary classifier performance (Han et al. 2011). Formally, it is defined as:






Definition. For a classifier with positive (1) and negative (0) classes, the confusion matrix is defined as:
\[
M = \begin{pmatrix} TN & FP \\ FN & TP \end{pmatrix}
\tag{2}\]
where rows represent actual ground-truth classes and columns represent predicted classes. The four components are:

TP (True Positive): Model predicted positive and actual instance is positive. Correct classification of the target class.
TN (True Negative): Model predicted negative and actual instance is negative. Correct classification of the majority/normal class.
FP (False Positive): Model predicted positive but actual instance is negative. Also called Type I Error.
FN (False Negative): Model predicted negative but actual instance is positive. Also called Type II Error.




Visually, the error types can be represented in the following diagram:



Visual representation of a confusion matrix and binary classification metrics. The diagram illustrates the relationship between actual ground truth (Positive/Negative columns) and model predictions (central circle). True Positives (TP) and False Positives (FP) fall within the prediction area, while False Negatives (FN) and True Negatives (TN) lie in the exclusion area.


As detailed below, the confusion matrix forms the bedrock of classifier evaluation, as all performance metrics are derived from it. Furthermore, interpreting each element carries direct strategic implications for model-driven decision making.


Synthetic Datasets Generation
Throughout this chapter, two synthetic datasets replicating the statistical characteristics of real-world problems are used.

The Medical Dataset simulates detecting a severe medical condition with ~8% prevalence, reflecting typical class imbalance in screening studies.
The Financial Dataset simulates transactions with a ~3% fraud rate, matching industry benchmarks (Pedregosa et al., 2011).

Both datasets are generated using sklearn.datasets.make_classification, controlling the number of informative features, label noise, and class imbalance.


Show code
# ── Global Setup and Imports ───────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.figure_factory as ff
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import (
    confusion_matrix, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score,
    f1_score, fbeta_score, roc_curve, auc, precision_recall_curve,
    average_precision_score, classification_report,
)

SEED = 42

# ── Medical Dataset: 92% healthy, 8% sick ──────────────────────────────────
X_med, y_med = make_classification(
    n_samples=1000, n_features=10, n_informative=5,
    weights=[0.92, 0.08],   # strong imbalance
    flip_y=0.02,            # 2% label noise
    random_state=SEED,
)
X_tr_m, X_te_m, y_tr_m, y_te_m = train_test_split(
    X_med, y_med, test_size=0.3, stratify=y_med, random_state=SEED
)

# ── Financial Dataset: 97% legitimate, 3% fraud ────────────────────────────
X_fin, y_fin = make_classification(
    n_samples=5000, n_features=15, n_informative=7,
    weights=[0.97, 0.03],
    flip_y=0.01,
    random_state=SEED,
)
X_tr_f, X_te_f, y_tr_f, y_te_f = train_test_split(
    X_fin, y_fin, test_size=0.3, stratify=y_fin, random_state=SEED
)

# ── Model 1: Logistic Regression — Medical dataset ────────────────────────
modelo_lr = LogisticRegression(random_state=SEED, max_iter=500)
modelo_lr.fit(X_tr_m, y_tr_m)
y_pred_lr = modelo_lr.predict(X_te_m)
y_prob_lr = modelo_lr.predict_proba(X_te_m)[:, 1]

# ── Model 2: Random Forest — Medical dataset ──────────────────────────────
modelo_rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=SEED)
modelo_rf.fit(X_tr_m, y_tr_m)
y_pred_rf = modelo_rf.predict(X_te_m)
y_prob_rf = modelo_rf.predict_proba(X_te_m)[:, 1]

# ── Model 3: Logistic Regression — Financial dataset ──────────────────────
modelo_fin = LogisticRegression(
    random_state=SEED, max_iter=500, class_weight="balanced"
)
modelo_fin.fit(X_tr_f, y_tr_f)
y_pred_fin = modelo_fin.predict(X_te_f)
y_prob_fin = modelo_fin.predict_proba(X_te_f)[:, 1]

print("Class distribution — Medical test set    :",
      dict(zip(*np.unique(y_te_m, return_counts=True))))
print("Class distribution — Financial test set  :",
      dict(zip(*np.unique(y_te_f, return_counts=True))))

Class distribution — Financial test set  : {np.int64(0): np.int64(1449), np.int64(1): np.int64(51)}


To evaluate models throughout the chapter, we fit three binary classifiers: Logistic Regression and Random Forest on the medical dataset, and a class-weighted Logistic Regression on the financial dataset.
Below is the confusion matrix for the Logistic Regression model on the medical dataset:


Show code
# ── Reusable Function: Interactive Confusion Matrix ────────────────────────
def plot_confusion_matrix(cm,
                          titulo=" ",
                          etiquetas=None):
    """
    Visualizes a 2×2 confusion matrix using Plotly.

    Displays absolute counts and row-wise percentages
    (accuracy/error rate per true class).
    """
    if etiquetas is None:
        etiquetas = ["Negative (0)", "Positive (1)"]

    cm_pct = cm.astype(float) / cm.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) * 100
    texto = [
        [f"{cm[i,j]}<br>({cm_pct[i,j]:.1f} %)" for j in range(2)]
        for i in range(2)
    ]
    z_plot     = cm[::-1, :]
    texto_plot = texto[::-1]
    y_labels   = etiquetas[::-1]

    fig = ff.create_annotated_heatmap(
        z=z_plot,
        x=etiquetas,
        y=y_labels,
        annotation_text=texto_plot,
        colorscale=[[0, "#f8f9fa"], [0.5, "#4a90d9"], [1, "#e74c3c"]],
        showscale=True,
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        title=titulo,
        xaxis_title="Model Prediction",
        yaxis_title="Actual Class",
        height=430, width=530,
        font=dict(size=13),
    )
    etq = {(0, 0): ("TN", "gray"),    (0, 1): ("FP", "#e67e22"),
           (1, 0): ("FN", "#e74c3c"), (1, 1): ("TP", "#27ae60")}
    for (ri, ci), (label, color) in etq.items():
        ri_plot = 1 - ri
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=etiquetas[ci], y=y_labels[ri_plot],
            text=f"<b>{label}</b>",
            showarrow=False,
            font=dict(size=11, color=color),
            yshift=-22,
        )
    return fig


# ── Apply to medical classifier ─────────────────────────────────────────────

TP = int(cm_lr[1, 1]); TN = int(cm_lr[0, 0])
FP = int(cm_lr[0, 1]); FN = int(cm_lr[1, 0])

print("Confusion Matrix — Logistic Regression (Medical):")
print(cm_lr)
print(f"\nTP={TP}, TN={TN}, FP={FP}, FN={FN}")

fig_cm = plot_confusion_matrix(
    cm_lr,

From this confusion matrix, all subsequent performance metrics are derived. Furthermore, interpreting each cell carries direct strategic consequences.


Asymmetric Cost of Errors: Real-World Contexts
The single most important characteristic of classification errors is not their raw frequency, but their differential cost. In almost all real data mining applications, FP and FN do not carry equal costs; optimizing for one inevitably trades off against the other (James et al., 2021).

Healthcare: The Devastating Cost of False Negatives
In a lung cancer screening system, a False Negative means predicting “benign” for a malignant nodule. The patient leaves untreated. This asymmetry means clinical screening prioritizes high Recall (low FN rate), even at the expense of lower Precision. A False Positive means predicting “malignant” for a benign nodule: the patient undergoes an unnecessary biopsy —an invasive and costly procedure— but compared to missing cancer, an FP is the tolerable error.


Finance: The Operational Cost of False Positives
In fraud detection, a False Positive blocks a legitimate credit card transaction: the customer cannot complete their purchase, risking customer attrition. A False Negative allows fraudulent transactions to pass, but the monetary loss is typically insured or subject to chargebacks. This inverse asymmetry means fraud systems prioritize high Precision, accepting that some frauds slip through undetected (Provost & Fawcett, 2013).

title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Performance Metrics: Beyond Error Rate
Properly evaluating a classifier requires analyzing not just the total number of errors, but their type and cost. A suite of metrics derived from the confusion matrix quantifies different facets of model performance. These metrics are complementary rather than mutually exclusive, and should be evaluated jointly. Below are the primary metrics for binary classification, complete with formal definitions, calculations, and contextual interpretations.

Accuracy: Definition, Utility, and Limitations

Formal Definition
\[
\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}
\]
Accuracy measures the proportion of correctly classified instances across all classes (Han et al., 2011).


Calculation and Basic Interpretation


Show code
# ── Real Model Accuracy vs. Trivial Baseline ───────────────────────────────
acc_lr      = accuracy_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr)
y_trivial   = np.zeros_like(y_te_m)          # always predicts "healthy"
acc_trivial = accuracy_score(y_te_m, y_trivial)

print(f"Accuracy — Logistic Regression : {acc_lr:.4f}  ({acc_lr*100:.2f} %)")
print(f"Accuracy — Trivial Baseline    : {acc_trivial:.4f}  ({acc_trivial*100:.2f} %)")
print()
print("Does the trivial baseline (always 'healthy') detect any sick patients?")
print(f"  Sick patients detected: {((y_trivial==1) & (y_te_m==1)).sum()} / {y_te_m.sum()}")


Accuracy — Logistic Regression : 0.9300  (93.00 %)
Accuracy — Trivial Baseline    : 0.9167  (91.67 %)

Does the trivial baseline (always 'healthy') detect any sick patients?
  Sick patients detected: 0 / 25




The Accuracy Paradox
The most severe flaw of accuracy emerges under class imbalance, an extremely prevalent scenario in real-world data mining (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). In our financial dataset with 97% legitimate transactions, a dummy classifier predicting “legitimate” for all transactions achieves ~97% accuracy while detecting zero fraud:


Show code
# ── Accuracy Paradox — Financial Dataset ───────────────────────────────────
y_trivial_fin   = np.zeros_like(y_te_f)
acc_trivial_fin = accuracy_score(y_te_f, y_trivial_fin)
acc_modelo_fin  = accuracy_score(y_te_f, y_pred_fin)
recall_trivial  = recall_score(y_te_f, y_trivial_fin, zero_division=0)
recall_modelo   = recall_score(y_te_f, y_pred_fin)

print("Financial Dataset (97% legitimate, 3% fraud)")
print("─" * 52)
print(f"Accuracy — Trivial Model : {acc_trivial_fin:.4f}  ({acc_trivial_fin*100:.1f} %)")
print(f"Accuracy — Real Model    : {acc_modelo_fin:.4f}  ({acc_modelo_fin*100:.1f} %)")
print()
print(f"Recall   — Trivial Model : {recall_trivial:.4f}  → 0 frauds detected")
print(f"Recall   — Real Model    : {recall_modelo:.4f}  → detects real frauds")
print()
print("Takeaway: higher accuracy ≠ better model on imbalanced data.")
print("(Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015)")


Financial Dataset (97% legitimate, 3% fraud)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Accuracy — Trivial Model : 0.9660  (96.6 %)
Accuracy — Real Model    : 0.7820  (78.2 %)

Recall   — Trivial Model : 0.0000  → 0 frauds detected
Recall   — Real Model    : 0.7255  → detects real frauds

Takeaway: higher accuracy ≠ better model on imbalanced data.
(Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015)

modelos    = ["Real Model\n(LR + class_weight)", "Trivial Model\n(always negative)"]
accuracies = [acc_modelo_fin, acc_trivial_fin]
recalls    = [recall_modelo, recall_trivial]

fig = go.Figure(data=[
    go.Bar(name="Accuracy", x=modelos, y=accuracies,
           marker_color=["#4a90d9", "#e74c3c"],
           text=[f"{v:.2%}" for v in accuracies], textposition="auto"),
    go.Bar(name="Recall (fraud class)", x=modelos, y=recalls,

    barmode="group",

    ),
    yaxis=dict(title="Value", range=[0, 1.1], tickformat="%"),
    height=420,
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            





Precision: Reliability of Positive Predictions

Formal Definition
\[
\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}
\]
Precision measures the proportion of positive predictions that are truly positive (James et al., 2021).


Detailed Calculation


Show code
# ── Precision: Manual Calculation and sklearn ──────────────────────────────
precision_manual = TP / (TP + FP) if (TP + FP) > 0 else 0
precision_sk     = precision_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr, zero_division=0)

print(f"Manual Calculation — Precision = {TP} / ({TP}+{FP}) = {precision_manual:.4f}")
print(f"sklearn            — Precision = {precision_sk:.4f}")
print()
print(f"Interpretation: for every 10 'sick' alerts,")
print(f"  approximately {precision_sk*10:.1f} correspond to truly sick patients.")


Manual Calculation — Precision = 6 / (6+2) = 0.7500
sklearn            — Precision = 0.7500

Interpretation: for every 10 'sick' alerts,
  approximately 7.5 correspond to truly sick patients.




Limitation: High Precision \(\neq\) Good Classifier
Precision measures prediction quality. A system that is ultra-conservative and only triggers alerts under absolute certainty achieves perfect Precision (1.0): every alert issued is correct. However, the price of perfection is silence: the system ignores many actual positive cases out of caution.
Conversely, if a system alerts indiscriminately, its Precision drops. Fawcett (2006) notes that extremely low precision causes alarm fatigue: users receive so many false alarms that they lose trust and ignore the system entirely.


Example: Spam Filtering

High Precision (Conservative): The spam filter only flags messages containing “100% FREE GUARANTEED CASH”. Precision is 1.0 (no important emails sent to spam), but the inbox fills with uncaught spam.
Low Precision (Alarm Fatigue): The filter flags any email containing exclamation marks or capital letters. It catches all spam, but sends legitimate invoices to spam as well. Users end up checking the spam folder daily, defeating the filter’s purpose.



Show code
# ── Conservative Model: High Precision, Low Recall ─────────────────────────
umbral_alto = 0.90
y_conserv   = (y_prob_lr >= umbral_alto).astype(int)

p_c  = precision_score(y_te_m, y_conserv, zero_division=0)
r_c  = recall_score(y_te_m, y_conserv, zero_division=0)
f1_c = f1_score(y_te_m, y_conserv, zero_division=0)

print(f"Threshold = {umbral_alto}  (conservative model)")
print(f"  Precision : {p_c:.4f}  (rarely wrong when alerting)")
print(f"  Recall    : {r_c:.4f}  (misses many true sick cases)")
print(f"  F1-Score  : {f1_c:.4f}")
print(f"  Alerts issued: {y_conserv.sum()} out of {y_te_m.sum()} true sick cases")


Threshold = 0.9  (conservative model)
  Precision : 1.0000  (rarely wrong when alerting)
  Recall    : 0.0400  (misses many true sick cases)
  F1-Score  : 0.0769
  Alerts issued: 1 out of 25 true sick cases





Recall (Sensitivity): Coverage of True Positives

Formal Definition
\[
\text{Recall} = \text{Sensitivity} = \text{TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}
\]
Recall measures the proportion of actual positive cases successfully identified by the classifier (Fawcett, 2006).


Calculation and Relationship to False Negative Rate


Show code
# ── Recall Calculation and FNR Relationship ────────────────────────────────
recall_manual = TP / (TP + FN) if (TP + FN) > 0 else 0
recall_sk     = recall_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr)
fnr           = FN / (TP + FN)   # False Negative Rate = 1 − Recall

print(f"Manual Calculation — Recall = {TP} / ({TP}+{FN}) = {recall_manual:.4f}")
print(f"sklearn            — Recall = {recall_sk:.4f}")
print(f"FNR (1 − Recall)            = {fnr:.4f}")
print()
print(f"Out of {y_te_m.sum()} actual sick patients in the test set,")
print(f"  the model detects {TP} and misses {FN}.")


Manual Calculation — Recall = 6 / (6+19) = 0.2400
sklearn            — Recall = 0.2400
FNR (1 − Recall)            = 0.7600

Out of 25 actual sick patients in the test set,
  the model detects 6 and misses 19.




Limitation: High Recall \(\neq\) Good Classifier
While Precision focuses on alert quality, Recall focuses on coverage: how effectively the system catches all true positive cases.
A system with Recall = 1.0 catches 100% of target cases. However, achieving perfect recall often requires predicting positive aggressively, dragging along numerous False Positives and degrading Precision.


Example: Smoke Alarm

High Recall (Total Sensitivity): A smoke alarm triggers at the slightest hint of water vapor or toast. Recall is 1.0 (no real fire goes undetected), but occupants suffer constant false alarms (low precision).
Low Recall (Strict Threshold): A smoke detector only activates when flames directly touch the sensor. Precision is high (if it sounds, there is a fire), but Recall is low: by the time it alerts, the room is consumed.




Precision–Recall Trade-off across Decision Thresholds
As noted by Fawcett (2006), both extremes represent failure: a low-recall system is blind, while a low-precision system generates alarm fatigue. Data scientists balance this trade-off primarily through the decision threshold: the probability cut-off mapping continuous probabilities into binary predictions.
The table below demonstrates the empirical trade-off between Recall and Precision across decision thresholds (Provost & Fawcett, 2013):


Show code
# ── P-R Trade-off across thresholds — Medical Dataset ──────────────────────
rows = []
for u in [0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80]:
    y_u  = (y_prob_lr >= u).astype(int)
    tp_u = int(((y_u==1) & (y_te_m==1)).sum())
    fp_u = int(((y_u==1) & (y_te_m==0)).sum())
    fn_u = int(((y_u==0) & (y_te_m==1)).sum())
    tn_u = int(((y_u==0) & (y_te_m==0)).sum())
    rows.append({
        "Threshold θ": u,
        "TP": tp_u, "FP": fp_u, "FN": fn_u, "TN": tn_u,
        "Recall":    round(tp_u/(tp_u+fn_u), 3) if (tp_u+fn_u)>0 else 0,
        "Precision": round(tp_u/(tp_u+fp_u), 3) if (tp_u+fp_u)>0 else 0,
        "F1":        round(f1_score(y_te_m, y_u, zero_division=0), 3),
    })

df_tradeoff = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Precision–Recall Trade-off across Decision Thresholds")
print("Medical Dataset — Logistic Regression")
print("(Provost & Fawcett, 2013)\n")
print(df_tradeoff.to_string(index=False))

Specificity: Protection of True Negatives

Formal Definition
\[
\text{Specificity} = \text{TNR} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}
\]
Specificity measures the proportion of actual negative instances correctly identified as negative (Han et al., 2011).


Calculation and Relationship to FPR


Show code
# ── Specificity Calculation and FPR Relationship ───────────────────────────
specificity = TN / (TN + FP) if (TN + FP) > 0 else 0
fpr_val     = FP / (TN + FP)   # 1 − Specificity = FPR

print(f"Specificity = {TN} / ({TN}+{FP}) = {specificity:.4f}")
print(f"FPR (1 − Specificity) = {fpr_val:.4f}")
print()
print("Summary table of relevance metrics:")
print(f"  Precision   = {precision_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr):.4f}  "
      f"— reliability of positive predictions")
print(f"  Recall      = {recall_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr):.4f}  "
      f"— coverage of true positives")
print(f"  Specificity = {specificity:.4f}  "
      f"— protection of true negatives")


Specificity = 273 / (273+2) = 0.9927
FPR (1 − Specificity) = 0.0073

Summary table of relevance metrics:
  Precision   = 0.7500  — reliability of positive predictions
  Recall      = 0.2400  — coverage of true positives
  Specificity = 0.9927  — protection of true negatives





Negative Predictive Value (NPV): Reliability of Negative Predictions
While Precision focuses on positive alert reliability (“Positive!”), Negative Predictive Value (NPV) measures confidence in negative predictions (“Negative”). It answers: If the model predicts negative, how likely is the instance truly negative?

Formal Definition
\[
\text{NPV} = \frac{TN}{TN + FN}
\]
A high NPV allows users to act confidently on negative predictions. A low NPV means negative predictions are unreliable, carrying high risks of unflagged positive cases.


Code Calculation


Show code
# ── Negative Predictive Value (NPV) ────────────────────────────────────────
vpn = TN / (TN + FN) if (TN + FN) > 0 else 0

print(f"NPV = {TN} / ({TN}+{FN}) = {vpn:.4f}")
print("Indicates the probability that an instance is truly negative given a negative prediction.")


NPV = 273 / (273+19) = 0.9349
Indicates the probability that an instance is truly negative given a negative prediction.





Summary of the “Four Classic” Metrics








Model State
Metric Name
User Perspective




Model predicts “Positive!”
Precision (PPV)
“Is this a real case or a false alarm?”


Model predicts “Negative”
NPV
“Can I rest easy or am I missing something?”


True state is Positive
Sensitivity (Recall)
“Can the model catch this instance?”


True state is Negative
Specificity
“Will the model leave normal cases alone?”





The SnNout / SpPin Clinical Rules
James et al. (2021) introduce clinical mnemonics:

SnNout (High Snsensitivity \(\implies\) Negative result rules out disease): Screening tests require high Sensitivity to avoid missing sick patients.
SpPin (High Specificity \(\implies\) Positive result rules in disease): Confirmatory tests require high Specificity to avoid falsely confirming non-cases.

text:
F1-Score and Multiclass Variants

The Need for a Composite Metric
The Precision–Recall trade-off highlights the need for a metric combining both into a single scalar score. F1-Score resolves this using the harmonic mean (Han et al., 2011).


Formal Definition
\[
F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} = \frac{2 \cdot TP}{2 \cdot TP + FP + FN}
\]


Why Harmonic Mean over Arithmetic Mean
The arithmetic mean can mask extreme imbalances. The harmonic mean heavily penalizes classifiers that sacrifice either Precision or Recall:


Show code
# ── Demo: Arithmetic vs. Harmonic Mean ─────────────────────────────────────
def f1_manual(p, r):
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r) if (p + r) > 0 else 0

def media_aritmetica(p, r):
    return (p + r) / 2

casos = [
    ("Model A — balanced",               0.90, 0.90),
    ("Model B — Precision only",         0.99, 0.01),
    ("Model C — Recall only",            0.01, 0.99),
    ("Model D — moderate high threshold",0.85, 0.60),
]

print(f"{'Model':<35}  {'P':>5}  {'R':>5}  {'Arithmetic':>11}  {'F1 (Harmonic)':>14}")
print("─" * 78)
for nombre, p, r in casos:
    print(f"{nombre:<35}  {p:>5.2f}  {r:>5.2f}  "
          f"{media_aritmetica(p,r):>11.4f}  {f1_manual(p,r):>14.4f}")

print()
print("Harmonic mean pulls strongly toward the lower value: heavily penalizing extreme trade-offs.")
print("(Han et al., 2011)")


Model                                    P      R   Arithmetic   F1 (Harmonic)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Model A — balanced                    0.90   0.90       0.9000          0.9000
Model B — Precision only              0.99   0.01       0.5000          0.0198
Model C — Recall only                 0.01   0.99       0.5000          0.0198
Model D — moderate high threshold     0.85   0.60       0.7250          0.7034

Harmonic mean pulls strongly toward the lower value: heavily penalizing extreme trade-offs.
(Han et al., 2011)




Generalization: F-Beta Score
\[
F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2) \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\beta^2 \cdot \text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}
\]
Choosing \(\beta\) explicitly weights the relative importance of FP vs. FN (James et al., 2021):


Show code
# ── F-beta: Parameter β as Priority Indicator ──────────────────────────────
p_lr = precision_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr, zero_division=0)
r_lr = recall_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr)

print(f"Medical LR Model — P = {p_lr:.3f}, R = {r_lr:.3f}\n")
print(f"{'β':>5}  {'Priority Focus':<40}  {'F-beta':>8}")
print("─" * 58)
for beta, desc in [
    (0.5, "Precision weighted 2× (FP more costly)"),
    (1.0, "Precision = Recall     (Standard F1)"),
    (2.0, "Recall weighted 2×    (FN more costly)"),
    (5.0, "Recall dominates      (Critical: catastrophic FN)"),
]:
    fb = fbeta_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr, beta=beta, zero_division=0)
    print(f"{beta:>5}  {desc:<40}  {fb:>8.4f}")


Medical LR Model — P = 0.750, R = 0.240

    β  Priority Focus                              F-beta
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  0.5  Precision weighted 2× (FP more costly)      0.5263
  1.0  Precision = Recall     (Standard F1)        0.3636
  2.0  Recall weighted 2×    (FN more costly)      0.2778
  5.0  Recall dominates      (Critical: catastrophic FN)    0.2464




Multiclass F1 Variants
\[F1_{\text{macro}} = \frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C} F1_c \qquad F1_{\text{micro}} = \frac{2\sum TP_c}{2\sum TP_c + \sum FP_c + \sum FN_c} \qquad F1_{\text{weighted}} = \sum_{c=1}^{C} w_c \cdot F1_c\]


Show code

print("F1-Score Variants:")
for avg in ["macro", "micro", "weighted", "binary"]:
    val = f1_score(y_te_m, y_pred_lr, average=avg, zero_division=0)
    print(f"  F1 {avg:<10}: {val:.4f}")

print()
print("Full Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(
    y_te_m, y_pred_lr,
    target_names=["Healthy (0)", "Sick (1)"],
))

section: ROC Curve and Area Under the Curve (AUC)
text:
ROC Curve and Area Under the Curve (AUC)

Motivation
Binary classification metrics depend on decision threshold \(\theta\). A single model may achieve high sensitivity under low thresholds while triggering more false positives. The ROC curve (Receiver Operating Characteristic) analyzes this trade-off without fixing a single threshold, evaluating classifier performance across all possible thresholds (Fawcett, 2006).


Formal Definition
Let \(\hat{p}(x)\) be the predicted probability of observation \(x\) belonging to the positive class. For threshold \(\theta\), the model predicts:

positive class if \(\hat{p}(x) \ge \theta\),
negative class if \(\hat{p}(x) < \theta\).

This yields:
\[
\text{TPR}(\theta) = \frac{TP(\theta)}{TP(\theta) + FN(\theta)},
\qquad
\text{FPR}(\theta) = \frac{FP(\theta)}{FP(\theta) + TN(\theta)} = 1 - \text{Specificity}(\theta)
\]
where:

\(\text{TPR}(\theta)\) is True Positive Rate,
\(\text{FPR}(\theta)\) is False Positive Rate.

The ROC curve is the parametric curve
\[
\big(\text{FPR}(\theta), \text{TPR}(\theta)\big)
\]
traced across all \(\theta \in [0, 1]\).


Axis Interpretation

1. True Positive Rate (TPR)
TPR equals Recall or Sensitivity, representing the proportion of actual positive cases correctly identified.

Common Name: Sensitivity or Recall.
In Plain Terms: Given a true positive case, how likely is the model to detect it?



2. False Positive Rate (FPR)
FPR is the complement of Specificity (\(1 - \text{Specificity}\)). It represents the proportion of actual negative cases incorrectly flagged as positive.

Common Name: False Positive Rate or Fall-out.
In Plain Terms: Given a true negative case, how likely is the model to raise a false alarm?




What Does the ROC Curve Represent?
The ROC curve illustrates the trade-off between:

detecting positives (increasing TPR),
avoiding false alarms (keeping FPR low).

An ideal classifier hugs the top-left corner of the ROC space, combining high Sensitivity with low False Positive Rate.
Reference lines:

The diagonal line \(\text{TPR} = \text{FPR}\) represents a random classifier (no discriminative ability);
Curves further above the diagonal indicate superior class separation capability.



Area Under the Curve (AUC)
AUC (Area Under the Curve) summarizes the ROC curve into a single scalar score:
\[
\text{AUC} = \int_0^1 \text{TPR}(u)\,du
\quad \text{where } u = \text{FPR}
\]
AUC measures global ranking ability: how effectively the model ranks positive instances higher than negative instances across all thresholds.
Interpretation guidelines:

\(\text{AUC} \approx 0.5\): Random guessing,
\(\text{AUC} > 0.5\): Better than chance,
\(\text{AUC} \to 1\): Near-perfect discrimination.



Probabilistic Interpretation of AUC
Bamber (1975) established that AUC carries a natural probabilistic interpretation:
\[
\text{AUC} = P\!\left(\hat{p}(x^+) > \hat{p}(x^-)\right)
\]
where \(x^+\) is a randomly chosen positive instance and \(x^-\) is a randomly chosen negative instance.
AUC represents the probability that the model assigns a higher score to a randomly chosen positive instance than to a randomly chosen negative instance. An \(\text{AUC} = 0.85\) means an 85% probability of correctly ranking a positive-negative pair.


Advantages of ROC and AUC

Threshold-agnostic evaluation.
Enables global classifier comparisons.
Evaluates overall discriminative capacity independently of operational cut-offs.



Critical Limitation
ROC and AUC can provide overly optimistic assessments on severely imbalanced datasets. In such scenarios, the Precision–Recall curve is far more informative because it directly penalizes false positives relative to a rare positive class.


Show code
# ── ROC Curve: Logistic Regression vs. Random Forest ───────────────────────
fpr_lr, tpr_lr, thresholds_roc = roc_curve(y_te_m, y_prob_lr)
fpr_rf, tpr_rf, _              = roc_curve(y_te_m, y_prob_rf)

auc_lr = auc(fpr_lr, tpr_lr)
auc_rf = auc(fpr_rf, tpr_rf)

print(f"AUC — Logistic Regression : {auc_lr:.4f}")
print(f"AUC — Random Forest       : {auc_rf:.4f}")
print()
print(f"LR Interpretation: P(score(sick) > score(healthy)) = {auc_lr:.1%}")
print(f"(Bamber, 1975; Fawcett, 2006)")


AUC — Logistic Regression : 0.7219
AUC — Random Forest       : 0.9201

LR Interpretation: P(score(sick) > score(healthy)) = 72.2%
(Bamber, 1975; Fawcett, 2006)




Interactive Visualization: Comparative ROC Curves


Show code
# ── Interactive ROC Curve with Shaded Area ──────────────────────────────────
fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[0, 1], y=[0, 1], mode="lines",
    name="Random (AUC = 0.50)",
    line=dict(color="#aaa", width=1.5, dash="dash"),
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[0, 0, 1], y=[0, 1, 1], mode="lines",
    name="Perfect (AUC = 1.00)",
    line=dict(color="#27ae60", width=1.5, dash="dot"),
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=fpr_lr, y=tpr_lr, mode="lines",
    name=f"Logistic Reg (AUC = {auc_lr:.3f})",
    line=dict(color="#4a90d9", width=2.5),
    fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(74,144,217,0.10)",
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=fpr_rf, y=tpr_rf, mode="lines",
    name=f"Random Forest (AUC = {auc_rf:.3f})",
    line=dict(color="#e74c3c", width=2.5),
    fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(231,76,60,0.08)",
))

fig.update_layout(
    title=(
        "ROC Curve — Model Comparison (Medical Dataset)<br>"
        "<sup>Fawcett (2006); Bamber (1975)</sup>"
    ),
    xaxis_title="False Positive Rate (FPR = 1 − Specificity)",
    yaxis_title="True Positive Rate (Recall)",
    xaxis=dict(range=[0, 1]), yaxis=dict(range=[0, 1.02]),
    height=460,
    legend=dict(x=0.55, y=0.15),
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            




Limitations of ROC-AUC on Imbalanced Data
Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015) demonstrated that under severe class imbalance, ROC-AUC can overstate performance because FPR includes TN in its denominator: when negatives dominate, large absolute numbers of false positives yield small FPR values, artificially smoothing the ROC curve.

title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Precision–Recall Curve and Average Precision

Motivation
When the target class is rare, evaluating overall accuracy is insufficient. Key operational questions include:

When the model predicts positive, how reliable is that alert?
Out of all true positive instances, what fraction does the model recover?

The Precision–Recall (PR) curve evaluates this trade-off. True Negatives (TN) do not appear in PR calculations, focusing evaluation strictly on positive class performance under class imbalance (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015).


Formal Definition
For predicted positive probabilities \(\hat{p}(x)\) and decision threshold \(\theta\):
\[
\text{Precision}(\theta) = \frac{TP(\theta)}{TP(\theta) + FP(\theta)},
\qquad
\text{Recall}(\theta) = \frac{TP(\theta)}{TP(\theta) + FN(\theta)}
\]
where:

Precision measures predicted positive purity;
Recall measures true positive recovery coverage.

The Precision–Recall curve plots
\[
\big(\text{Recall}(\theta), \text{Precision}(\theta)\big)
\]
across varying thresholds \(\theta\).


Axis Interpretation

1. Precision
Precision evaluates prediction purity. It remains high when positive predictions are overwhelmingly true positives.


2. Recall
Recall measures the model’s capacity to avoid missing positive instances.



What Does the Precision–Recall Curve Represent?
The PR curve illustrates the trade-off between:

recovering positive cases (increasing Recall),
maintaining reliable positive alerts (preserving high Precision).

As decision thresholds relax, the model captures more positives (Recall rises), but false positives increase, driving Precision down. An optimal model keeps its PR curve near the top-right corner.


PR Baseline
Unlike ROC curves (where random guessing equals the diagonal line), the PR baseline equals positive class prevalence:
\[
\text{PR Baseline} = P(\text{positive}) = \frac{TP + FN}{N}
\]
If positive prevalence is 10%, a random classifier yields a baseline Precision of ~0.10. PR curves and AP values above baseline demonstrate meaningful predictive capability.


Average Precision (AP)
Average Precision (AP) summarizes the PR curve into a single scalar score, computing weighted average precision across recall increments:
\[
\text{AP} = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\, P_k
\]
where \(R_k\) and \(P_k\) represent Recall and Precision at threshold step \(k\).


AP Interpretation

AP near 1 indicates high precision across almost all recall levels.
AP near class prevalence indicates performance no better than random guessing.
Larger gaps between AP and prevalence indicate stronger positive-class prioritization.



Utility in Imbalanced Settings
Under class imbalance, models may exhibit misleadingly strong ROC curves while generating unacceptable volumes of false positives. PR curves and AP ignore TNs, concentrating evaluation on true positive retrieval without false alarm contamination.


Show code
# ── Precision-Recall Curve: LR vs. RF ──────────────────────────────────────
prec_lr_c, rec_lr_c, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_te_m, y_prob_lr)
prec_rf_c, rec_rf_c, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_te_m, y_prob_rf)

ap_lr = average_precision_score(y_te_m, y_prob_lr)
ap_rf = average_precision_score(y_te_m, y_prob_rf)
prevalencia = y_te_m.mean()

print(f"Average Precision — Logistic Reg : {ap_lr:.4f}")
print(f"Average Precision — Random Forest : {ap_rf:.4f}")
print(f"Baseline (Positive Class Prevalence) : {prevalencia:.4f}")
print()
print("AP values above prevalence indicate performance superior to random guessing.")
print("(Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015)")

title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Decision Threshold Optimization

Threshold as a Strategic Parameter
Probabilistic classifiers output continuous probabilities \(\hat{p}(x) \in [0, 1]\). Default cut-off \(\theta = 0.5\) is a convention, rarely optimal for specific business cases (Provost & Fawcett, 2013). When error costs are known, optimal threshold \(\theta^*\) can be derived analytically (James et al., 2021):
\[\theta^* = \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}}\]

Healthcare (\(C_{FN} = 100 \cdot C_{FP}\)): \(\theta^* = 1/101 \approx 0.01\) (flag almost any positive signal for review)
Finance (\(C_{FP} = 10 \cdot C_{FN}\)): \(\theta^* = 10/11 \approx 0.91\) (require high confidence before blocking)



Threshold Impact on Performance Metrics


Show code
# ── Threshold Impact on Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 ───────────────
umbrales_demo  = np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.02)
metricas_umbral = []

for u in umbrales_demo:
    y_u  = (y_prob_lr >= u).astype(int)
    tp_u = int(((y_u==1) & (y_te_m==1)).sum())
    tn_u = int(((y_u==0) & (y_te_m==0)).sum())
    fp_u = int(((y_u==1) & (y_te_m==0)).sum())
    fn_u = int(((y_u==0) & (y_te_m==1)).sum())
    n    = tp_u + tn_u + fp_u + fn_u
    metricas_umbral.append({
        "umbral":    u,
        "accuracy":  (tp_u + tn_u) / n if n > 0 else 0,
        "precision": tp_u / (tp_u + fp_u) if (tp_u + fp_u) > 0 else 0,
        "recall":    tp_u / (tp_u + fn_u) if (tp_u + fn_u) > 0 else 0,
        "f1":        2*tp_u / (2*tp_u+fp_u+fn_u) if (2*tp_u+fp_u+fn_u)>0 else 0,
    })

df_umb = pd.DataFrame(metricas_umbral)

fig = go.Figure()
for col, color, name in [
    ("accuracy",  "#4a90d9", "Accuracy"),
    ("precision", "#27ae60", "Precision"),
    ("recall",    "#e74c3c", "Recall"),
    ("f1",        "#e67e22", "F1-Score"),
]:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=df_umb["umbral"], y=df_umb[col],
        name=name, line=dict(color=color, width=2.2), mode="lines",
    ))

idx_best = df_umb["f1"].idxmax()
best_u   = df_umb.loc[idx_best, "umbral"]
fig.add_vline(x=0.5, line_dash="dash", line_color="gray",
              annotation_text="θ=0.5 (default)")
fig.add_vline(x=best_u, line_dash="dot", line_color="#e67e22",
              annotation_text=f"θ*_F1 = {best_u:.2f}")

fig.update_layout(
    title=(
        "Decision Threshold Impact on Evaluation Metrics<br>"
        "<sup>Provost & Fawcett (2013)</sup>"
    ),
    xaxis_title="Decision Threshold (θ)",
    yaxis_title="Metric Value",
    yaxis=dict(range=[0, 1.05]),
    height=430,
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            




Optimal Threshold Search Strategies


Show code
# ── Three Threshold Selection Strategies ──────────────────────────────────
print("Strategy 1: Maximize F1-Score")
f1_arr = [f1_score(y_te_m, (y_prob_lr >= u).astype(int), zero_division=0)
          for u in np.arange(0.01, 0.99, 0.01)]
u_best_f1  = np.arange(0.01, 0.99, 0.01)[np.argmax(f1_arr)]
y_best_f1  = (y_prob_lr >= u_best_f1).astype(int)
print(f"  θ* = {u_best_f1:.2f}  →  F1={max(f1_arr):.4f}, "
      f"P={precision_score(y_te_m, y_best_f1, zero_division=0):.4f}, "
      f"R={recall_score(y_te_m, y_best_f1):.4f}\n")

print("Strategy 2 (Clinical): Highest θ achieving Recall ≥ 0.90")
best_med_u = None
for u in np.arange(0.01, 0.99, 0.01):
    if recall_score(y_te_m, (y_prob_lr >= u).astype(int), zero_division=0) >= 0.90:
        best_med_u = u
if best_med_u is not None:
    y_med_u = (y_prob_lr >= best_med_u).astype(int)
    print(f"  θ* = {best_med_u:.2f}  →  "
          f"P={precision_score(y_te_m, y_med_u, zero_division=0):.4f}, "
          f"R={recall_score(y_te_m, y_med_u):.4f}\n")

print("Strategy 3: Youden's J Statistic (max TPR − FPR)")
J        = tpr_lr - fpr_lr
idx_yo   = np.argmax(J)
u_youden = thresholds_roc[idx_yo]
y_yo     = (y_prob_lr >= u_youden).astype(int)
print(f"  θ* = {u_youden:.2f}  →  J={J[idx_yo]:.4f}, "
      f"P={precision_score(y_te_m, y_yo, zero_division=0):.4f}, "
      f"R={recall_score(y_te_m, y_yo):.4f}")
print("  (James et al., 2021)")

text:
Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls

Relying Solely on Accuracy Under Class Imbalance
The most widespread and damaging mistake (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). As demonstrated in Section 4.3, the accuracy paradox makes accuracy misleadingly high on imbalanced datasets. Rule of thumb: Always report Precision, Recall, and F1 when class proportions exceed an 80/20 split.


Confusing Precision with Recall
Precision measures positive prediction reliability; Recall measures true positive recovery coverage. They are orthogonal and complementary metrics. Confusing them leads to misinterpreting high precision as high sensitivity, ignoring missed cases (Fawcett, 2006).


Assuming Higher AUC Guarantees Superior Operational Performance


Show code
# ── High AUC but Low F1 at Operational Threshold ─────────────────────────
np.random.seed(99)
y_fake_prob = np.where(
    y_te_m == 1,
    np.random.beta(3, 1, size=y_te_m.shape),
    np.random.beta(1, 2, size=y_te_m.shape),
)
y_fake_pred = (y_fake_prob >= 0.50).astype(int)

fpr_fk, tpr_fk, _ = roc_curve(y_te_m, y_fake_prob)
auc_fk = auc(fpr_fk, tpr_fk)

print("Model with High AUC but Poor Probability Calibration (Low F1 at default threshold):")
print(f"  AUC             : {auc_fk:.4f}")
print(f"  F1  (θ = 0.50)  : {f1_score(y_te_m, y_fake_pred, zero_division=0):.4f}")
print(f"  Recall          : {recall_score(y_te_m, y_fake_pred, zero_division=0):.4f}")
print()
print("Takeaway: AUC measures ranking capacity, not operational cut-off performance.")
print("Always validate metrics at the target deployment threshold.")
print("(Fawcett, 2006)")


Model with High AUC but Poor Probability Calibration (Low F1 at default threshold):
  AUC             : 0.9340
  F1  (θ = 0.50)  : 0.3962
  Recall          : 0.8400

Takeaway: AUC measures ranking capacity, not operational cut-off performance.
Always validate metrics at the target deployment threshold.
(Fawcett, 2006)




Optimizing Thresholds Directly on Test Data (Data Leakage)
Tuning decision thresholds on the test set constitutes data leakage, producing over-optimistic performance estimates (James et al., 2021). Thresholds must be selected on a validation set and evaluated strictly on a held-out test set.


Reporting Macro F1 to Mask Poor Minority Class Performance


Show code
# ── Macro F1 Masking Poor Positive Class Performance ──────────────────────
y_casi_trivial       = np.zeros_like(y_te_m)
idx_top2             = np.argsort(y_prob_lr)[-2:]
y_casi_trivial[idx_top2] = 1

f1_macro_mal = f1_score(y_te_m, y_casi_trivial, average="macro")
f1_pos_mal   = f1_score(y_te_m, y_casi_trivial, average="binary")

print("Model detecting almost no sick cases (only 2 positive predictions):")
print(f"  Macro F1          = {f1_macro_mal:.4f}  ← looks deceptively 'acceptable'")
print(f"  Positive Class F1 = {f1_pos_mal:.4f}  ← exposes true failure")
print()
print("Always inspect per-class F1 scores rather than relying solely on global averages.")
print("(Han et al., 2011)")


Model detecting almost no sick cases (only 2 positive predictions):
  Macro F1          = 0.5540  ← looks deceptively 'acceptable'
  Positive Class F1 = 0.1481  ← exposes true failure

Always inspect per-class F1 scores rather than relying solely on global averages.
(Han et al., 2011)
