title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Metric Selection Decision Guide
Selecting appropriate evaluation metrics requires analyzing domain requirements prior to computing scores (Provost & Fawcett, 2013):
Step 1 — Quantify Class Imbalance: If class ratios exceed 80/20, discard accuracy as the primary evaluation metric (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015).
Step 2 — Identify Differential Error Costs: Catastrophic FNs \(\implies\) Recall/Sensitivity. High-cost FPs \(\implies\) Precision. Balanced error costs \(\implies\) F1-Score (James et al., 2021).
Step 3 — Determine Objective (Global Ranking vs. Cut-off Deployment): Model comparison \(\implies\) ROC-AUC or PR-AUC. Production deployment \(\implies\) Threshold-specific metrics (Fawcett, 2006).
Step 4 — Multiclass Setting: Equal business class importance \(\implies\) Macro F1. Total error volume \(\implies\) Micro F1. Prevalence-weighted \(\implies\) Weighted F1 (Han et al., 2011; Pedregosa et al., 2011).
Step 5 — Translate to Business Impact: Connect statistical metrics directly to operational decisions: How many sick patients are treated? How much fraud is prevented? (Provost & Fawcett, 2013).

title: Classifier Evaluation: Essential Metrics and Their Interpretation
text:
Conclusions
Evaluating classification models in Data Mining is not a mechanical step at the end of the KDD pipeline (Fayyad et al., 1996): it is a strategic analysis bridging statistical quality and domain utility.
The metrics presented in this chapter form a cohesive framework (Han et al., 2011). Accuracy provides general context but fails under class imbalance (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). Precision and Recall quantify the trade-off between error types under asymmetric domain costs (Provost & Fawcett, 2013). The F1-Score synthesizes this trade-off via the harmonic mean (James et al., 2021). ROC curves and AUC provide threshold-agnostic discriminative assessments (Bamber, 1975; Fawcett, 2006), complemented by Precision-Recall curves under positive-class scarcity (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). Finally, decision thresholds represent strategic levers derived from differential error costs (Provost & Fawcett, 2013).
A data scientist’s core competency lies in understanding what each metric asserts about a model and selecting metrics that align statistical optimization with business objectives.

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.1 Introduction
Model evaluation is a central phase of supervised classification. In classification tasks, a dataset is available where both predictor variables and ground-truth target labels are known for every instance. From these observations, the goal is to learn a decision rule capable of assigning correct class labels to unseen future data (hastie2009elements?; james2021introduction?).
In practical terms, evaluating a classifier goes far beyond counting correct predictions. Model quality depends on how errors are distributed, class balance, relative costs of false positives and false negatives, and operational context. For example, in a spam filter, allowing a few unsolicited emails into the primary inbox may be tolerable, but incorrectly sending an urgent email to the spam folder is a severe error. In medical diagnostics, conversely, generating false positives is far preferable to missing true cases of disease (fawcett2006introduction?; saito2015precision?).
This chapter establishes the core concepts required to evaluate classification models. First, we examine data partitioning methods such as holdout and \(K\)-fold cross-validation. Next, we introduce the confusion matrix and key metrics derived from it: accuracy, error rate, precision, recall, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score. Finally, we explore the ROC curve, Area Under the Curve (AUC), and metric selection strategies suited to specific problem constraints.

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.2 Supervised Learning and Evaluation
Supervised learning operates on labeled datasets. Each observation contains a feature vector \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and an associated target class \(y_i\). In binary classification, \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\), where \(1\) denotes the positive class and \(0\) denotes the negative class.






Definition. A supervised dataset is a collection of input-output pairs: \[
\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n},
\qquad
\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^p,\quad y_i \in \mathcal{Y}
\]



A classification model can be conceptualized as a trainable function: \[
f_\theta:\mathbb{R}^p \to \mathcal{Y},
\] where \(\theta\) represents parameters learned from data. In probabilistic models, the classifier outputs estimated probabilities or confidence scores: \[
\hat{p}_i = P_\theta(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i).
\] Converting continuous scores into discrete class assignments requires a decision threshold \(\tau\): \[
\hat{y}_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & \hat{p}_i \geq \tau,\\
0, & \hat{p}_i < \tau.
\end{cases}
\]
Evaluation must be performed on data withheld during training to reliably estimate generalization performance on unseen instances. Evaluating a model solely on its training set yields overly optimistic estimates due to overfitting (hastie2009elements?; bishop2006pattern?).

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.3 Data Partitioning
Standard methodology splits datasets into disjoint subsets with distinct operational roles: training, validation, and testing.






Definition. A train-validation-test split partitions dataset \(\mathcal{D}\) into three pairwise disjoint subsets: \[
\mathcal{D} =
\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}
\cup
\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}
\cup
\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}},
\qquad
\mathcal{D}_{a} \cap \mathcal{D}_{b} = \varnothing
\quad (a \neq b)
\]



The training set fits model parameters. The validation set compares hyperparameter configurations and selects candidate models. The test set remains strictly untouched until final evaluation to provide an unbiased estimate of generalization capability.
A typical split distribution:



Subset
Typical Ratio
Primary Function




Training
70 %
Fit model parameters


Validation
15 %
Tune hyperparameters & select model


Testing
15 %
Estimate final generalization performance



Alternatively, a 50 % train / 25 % validation / 25 % test split is used when higher validation and testing stability is required. Choice of split ratio depends on overall dataset size, computational cost, and expected evaluation variance.

42.3.1 Holdout Method
The holdout method partitions a dataset a single time into static subsets (e.g., 80 % training and 20 % testing).






Definition. The holdout method constructs a single partition: \[
\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \cup \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}},
\qquad
\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \cap \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}} = \varnothing
\]



Its primary advantage is computational simplicity and speed, making it scalable to massive datasets. Its primary limitation is high variance: evaluation results depend heavily on the specific random split. If the test set happens to contain disproportionately easy cases, reported performance will be artificially high; if it contains unusually hard cases, performance will appear artificially poor.
Under class imbalance, unstratified holdout risks creating test sets with insufficient representation of the minority class. For example, in a dataset with 950 healthy and 50 diseased records, random splitting might place almost no positive cases in test sets, rendering metrics like recall highly unstable.


42.3.2 Stratified Random Sampling
Stratified sampling mitigates unrepresentative split risks by preserving overall class proportions within each subset. If class A makes up 80 % of the dataset and class B makes up 20 %, training, validation, and test subsets maintain matching 80/20 proportions.






Definition. A stratified partition preserves marginal class distributions across subsets: \[
P_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}(Y=y)
\approx
P_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}}(Y=y)
\approx
P_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}}(Y=y)
\approx
P_{\mathcal{D}}(Y=y)
\]



Stratification is essential under class imbalance. However, while preserving proportions, single stratified splits can still suffer from sample variance on small datasets.


42.3.3 Repeated Holdout
Repeated holdout performs multiple independent random splits and averages evaluated metrics across runs, smoothing out single-split variance.






Definition. In repeated holdout, \(R\) independent partitions are generated and metric \(M\) is reported as the mean across runs: \[
\bar{M}
=
\frac{1}{R}
\sum_{r=1}^{R}
M^{(r)}
\]



For example, if 5 repetitions yield accuracy scores of 85 %, 82 %, 88 %, 84 %, and 86 %, the mean holdout accuracy is: \[
\bar{M}
=
\frac{85 + 82 + 88 + 84 + 86}{5}
=
85\%.
\]
While more reliable than single holdout, repeated holdout can overlap test instances across runs. For small datasets, \(K\)-fold cross-validation provides a more systematic approach.


42.3.4 K-fold Cross-Validation
\(K\)-fold cross-validation partitions data into \(K\) equal-sized folds. The model is trained \(K\) times: in each iteration \(k\), fold \(k\) serves as the test set while the remaining \(K-1\) folds serve as training data (stone1974cross?; kohavi1995study?).






Definition. In \(K\)-fold cross-validation, overall metric \(M\) is estimated as the mean score across all \(K\) test folds: \[
\widehat{M}_{\text{CV}}
=
\frac{1}{K}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
M_k
\]



For instance, with \(K=5\), each fold contains 20 % of data. Iteration 1 evaluates on fold 1 while training on folds 2–5; iteration 2 evaluates on fold 2 while training on folds 1, 3, 4, 5; and so forth.
If test fold accuracy scores are 82 %, 80 %, 84 %, 81 %, and 83 %, the 5-fold cross-validation accuracy is: \[
\widehat{M}_{\text{CV}}
=
\frac{82 + 80 + 84 + 81 + 83}{5}
=
82\%.
\]
Cross-validation maximizes data utilization because every observation is evaluated in a test fold exactly once and used for training in \(K-1\) folds. Its primary cost is computational (\(K\) training passes). In practice, \(K=5\) or \(K=10\) are standard choices (kohavi1995study?).

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.4 Python Example: Holdout and Cross-Validation
The following Python example uses scikit-learn to fit a Logistic Regression classifier on a synthetic binary problem, comparing stratified holdout and 5-fold cross-validation.


Show code
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=1000,
    n_features=10,
    n_informative=5,
    n_redundant=2,
    weights=[0.85, 0.15],
    random_state=42
)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.20,
    stratify=y,
    random_state=42
)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

metricas_holdout = {
    "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
    "precision": precision_score(y_test, y_pred),
    "recall": recall_score(y_test, y_pred),
    "f1": f1_score(y_test, y_pred),
}

metricas_holdout


{'accuracy': 0.87,
 'precision': 0.7777777777777778,
 'recall': 0.22580645161290322,
 'f1': 0.35}




Show code
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

scores = cross_validate(
    model,
    X,
    y,
    cv=cv,
    scoring=["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1"],
    return_train_score=False
)

{metrica: scores[f"test_{metrica}"].mean()
 for metrica in ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1"]}


{'accuracy': np.float64(0.859),
 'precision': np.float64(0.5909090909090909),
 'recall': np.float64(0.29290322580645156),
 'f1': np.float64(0.3833043294837315)}


This example highlights why accuracy alone is insufficient: on imbalanced data, high accuracy can be achieved simply by favoring the majority class while missing positive cases (low recall).

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.5 Confusion Matrix
The confusion matrix cross-tabulates actual ground-truth labels against model predictions. In binary classification, it tracks four counts: true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.






Definition. For positive class \(1\) and negative class \(0\), the confusion matrix is structured as: \[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& \hat{y}=0 & \hat{y}=1\\
\hline
y=0 & TN & FP\\
y=1 & FN & TP
\end{array}
\]



Count interpretations:








Symbol
Name
Description




\(TP\)
True Positive
Actual positive correctly predicted as positive


\(TN\)
True Negative
Actual negative correctly predicted as negative


\(FP\)
False Positive
Actual negative incorrectly predicted as positive


\(FN\)
False Negative
Actual positive incorrectly predicted as negative



In spam filtering, a false positive occurs when legitimate email is misclassified as spam. A false negative occurs when spam bypasses the filter into the main inbox.

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.8 Metric Selection Guidelines
Metric selection depends on domain goals and relative error costs:








Metric
Primary Use Case
Key Decision Question




Accuracy
Balanced classes, equal error costs
Are all classification errors equally costly?


Error rate
Overall error percentage tracking
What overall failure rate is acceptable?


Precision
Minimizing False Positives
When the model predicts positive, how reliable is it?


Recall / Sensitivity
Minimizing False Negatives
How many true positive cases can we afford to miss?


Specificity
Minimizing False Alarms on Negatives
How effectively are true negative cases preserved?


F1-score
Imbalanced classes, balancing P & R
Is there a direct trade-off between FP and FN costs?



Consider medical cancer screening models:



Model
TPR
FPR




Model A
0.92
0.35


Model B
0.81
0.08



Model A captures more true cancers (high sensitivity) at the expense of higher false alarms. In initial screening, Model A may be preferred to avoid missed diagnoses. However, if follow-up biopsies carry high physical or financial costs, Model B offers a cleaner balance. Metric selection must align with operational domain realities (fawcett2006introduction?).

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.9 Decision Thresholds
Probabilistic models output continuous confidence scores \(\hat{p}(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1]\). Converting scores into class predictions depends on decision threshold \(\tau\).






Definition. Given probability score \(\hat{p}(\mathbf{x})\), a binary decision rule with threshold \(\tau\) is: \[
\hat{y}(\mathbf{x};\tau)
=
\mathbb{I}\{\hat{p}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \tau\}
\]



Lowering \(\tau\) from 0.70 to 0.30 classifies more instances as positive. This raises TPR (catching more positive cases) while simultaneously raising FPR (generating more false alarms).


Show code
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

probs = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

for tau in [0.70, 0.50, 0.30]:
    y_pred_tau = (probs >= tau).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_tau).ravel()
    tpr = tp / (tp + fn)
    fpr = fp / (fp + tn)
    print(f"threshold={tau:.2f} | TPR={tpr:.3f} | FPR={fpr:.3f}")


threshold=0.70 | TPR=0.129 | FPR=0.000
threshold=0.50 | TPR=0.226 | FPR=0.012
threshold=0.30 | TPR=0.613 | FPR=0.041

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.10 ROC Curve and AUC
The ROC curve evaluates classifier trade-offs across all decision thresholds by plotting True Positive Rate vs. False Positive Rate (fawcett2006introduction?).






Definition. The ROC curve is the parametric set of points: \[
\text{ROC}
=
\left\{
\left(
\text{FPR}(\tau),
\text{TPR}(\tau)
\right)
:
\tau \in \mathbb{R}
\right\}
\]



An ideal classifier hugs the top-left corner (\(\text{TPR}=1, \text{FPR}=0\)). The diagonal line represents random guessing.
AUC summarizes the area under the ROC curve into a single scalar, representing the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance receives a higher prediction score than a randomly chosen negative instance (fawcett2006introduction?).






Definition. Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is: \[
\text{AUC}
=
\int_{0}^{1}
\text{TPR}(\text{FPR})\,d(\text{FPR})
\]



General AUC guidelines:



AUC Range
General Interpretation




0.90–1.00
Outstanding


0.80–0.90
Good / Excellent


0.70–0.80
Acceptable


0.60–0.70
Poor


0.50–0.60
No discriminative value



High AUC does not guarantee optimal performance at a specific operational threshold. Furthermore, under severe class imbalance, Precision–Recall curves offer superior analytical insight (saito2015precision?).

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
section: 42.11 Python Example: ROC Curve and AUC
text:
42.11 Python Example: ROC Curve and AUC


Show code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import RocCurveDisplay, roc_auc_score

auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, probs)

RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, probs)
plt.title(f"ROC Curve (AUC = {auc:.3f})")
plt.show()

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.12 Precision–Recall Curves
When the positive class is rare, ROC curves can present overly optimistic performance views. Precision–Recall curves evaluate positive class recovery without True Negative domination (saito2015precision?).






Definition. The Precision–Recall curve plots: \[
\text{PR}
=
\left\{
\left(
\text{Recall}(\tau),
\text{Precision}(\tau)
\right)
:
\tau \in \mathbb{R}
\right\}
\]





Show code
from sklearn.metrics import PrecisionRecallDisplay, average_precision_score

ap = average_precision_score(y_test, probs)

PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, probs)
plt.title(f"Precision-Recall Curve (AP = {ap:.3f})")
plt.show()









Average Precision (AP) computes weighted precision across recall increments. Unlike ROC-AUC, its baseline equals positive class prevalence.

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.13 Recommended Classifier Evaluation Workflow
A reproducible evaluation pipeline follows these steps:

Formally define the target positive class and operational goal.
Reserve a test set before hyperparameter tuning.
Apply stratified partitioning under class imbalance.
Fit candidate models on training data.
Tune hyperparameters using cross-validation.
Evaluate the selected model once on the held-out test set.
Report confusion matrices and domain-aligned metrics.
Tune decision thresholds for continuous probability outputs.
Fully document random seeds, split protocols, and library versions.

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.14 Full Python Evaluation Example


Show code
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    balanced_accuracy_score,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
    f1_score,
    roc_auc_score,
    confusion_matrix,
)

def evaluar_clasificador(y_true, y_score, threshold=0.5):
    y_pred = (y_score >= threshold).astype(int)

    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()

    return {
        "threshold": threshold,
        "TP": tp,
        "TN": tn,
        "FP": fp,
        "FN": fn,
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
        "balanced_accuracy": balanced_accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
        "precision": precision_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(y_true, y_pred),
        "specificity": tn / (tn + fp),
        "f1": f1_score(y_true, y_pred),
        "auc": roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score),
    }

for tau in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]:
    print(evaluar_clasificador(y_test, probs, threshold=tau))

title: 41  Evaluating a Classification Model
text:
42.15 Conclusions
Evaluating classification models requires moving beyond simple accuracy calculations. Proper data partitioning ensures reliable generalization estimates. Holdout splits are fast but can suffer from split variance. \(K\)-fold cross-validation provides robust, low-variance estimates at higher computational cost.
The confusion matrix provides the foundation for derived performance metrics: precision, recall, specificity, F1-score, and balanced accuracy. Each metric evaluates distinct performance aspects and must be aligned with domain error costs. High sensitivity minimizes missed positive cases in screening; high precision minimizes false alarms in fraud detection.
Finally, ROC and Precision–Recall curves analyze model performance across all thresholds, enabling threshold selection tailored to specific operational requirements.

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
1 Introduction
Decision trees constitute a fundamental family of supervised learning models designed to learn decision rules from labeled training data. In classification, these rules assign an observation to a categorical class label; in regression, they estimate a continuous numerical value. Within this family, the CART (Classification and Regression Trees) algorithm occupies a central position because it formalizes the construction of strictly binary trees capable of handling both categorical and numerical features while incorporating cost-complexity pruning mechanisms to control model complexity (Breiman et al. 1984; Hastie et al. 2009).
Unlike algorithms such as ID3, which was originally formulated for classification trees with multi-way splits on categorical features, CART builds strictly binary trees. At each internal node, the algorithm evaluates a boolean question (“does a specific condition hold?”) to split data into two disjoint subsets: those meeting the condition and those that do not. The fundamental goal is selecting splits that recursively yield increasingly homogeneous child nodes with respect to the target variable.
In classification tasks, node homogeneity is measured using an impurity function. CART typically employs the Gini index, though entropy is also widely supported. In regression tasks, split criteria rely on variance reduction or Mean Squared Error (MSE) minimization. This chapter focuses primarily on CART for classification, exploring binary tree structure, Gini index calculations, categorical and continuous variable splitting rules, impurity reduction, pruning, and computational complexity.

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
crumbs: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
3 Classification, Purity, and Impurity
Supervised classification starts with a training set:
\[
D = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n},
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{X}\) represents predictor features for observation \(i\) and \(y_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, K\}\) is its target class label. The goal is learning a mapping \(f: \mathcal{X} \to \{1, 2, \dots, K\}\) predicting target labels for new observations.
A node is pure if all contained observations belong to a single class, making leaf prediction unambiguous. Conversely, if a node mixes observations across multiple classes, it is impure, warranting further splits if informative candidate questions remain available.






Definition. Let \(D_t\) be the subset of training instances reaching node \(t\). The proportion of class \(k\) instances in node \(t\) is: \[
p_{k,t} = \frac{1}{|D_t|}\sum_{(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)\in D_t}\mathbf{1}(y_i=k).
\]



If \(p_{k,t}=1\) for some class \(k\), the node is pure. As class proportions spread across multiple classes, impurity increases. This intuition is formalized by the Gini index.
crumbs: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
4 Gini Index
The Gini index measures node impurity based on class distribution. For \(K\) target classes, it is defined as:






Definition. The Gini index of node \(D_t\) with class proportions \(p_{1,t},\dots,p_{K,t}\) is: \[
Gini(D_t)=1-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k,t}^{2}.
\tag{1}\]



This expression can be interpreted as the probability of incorrectly classifying a randomly chosen node element if it were randomly labeled according to the empirical class distribution of the node (Breiman et al. 1984; James et al. 2021).
In binary classification with classes “Yes” and “No”, if \(p\) is the proportion of positive instances:
\[
Gini(D_t)=1-p^2-(1-p)^2=2p(1-p).
\]
The minimum Gini value is \(0\), achieved when \(p=0\) or \(p=1\) (pure node). The maximum binary Gini value is \(0.5\), achieved when \(p=0.5\) (equal 50/50 mixture).


Show code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def gini_from_counts(counts):
    counts = np.asarray(counts, dtype=float)
    probs = counts / counts.sum()
    return 1 - np.sum(probs**2)

# Example: 9 "Yes" records and 5 "No" records
gini_raiz = gini_from_counts([9, 5])
print(f"Root Gini = {gini_raiz:.3f}")


Root Gini = 0.459


In this example, initial impurity is approximately \(0.459\), indicating that the root node contains a mixture of both classes.
crumbs: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
5 Evaluating Binary Splits
In CART, a split divides node dataset \(D_t\) into left (\(D_L\)) and right (\(D_R\)) child subsets. Split quality is evaluated by computing the weighted average impurity of both child nodes, rather than evaluating child purity in isolation. This prevents favoring splits that isolate tiny pure nodes at the expense of overall dataset purity.






Definition. The weighted Gini impurity of a binary split \(s\) partitioning \(D_t\) into \(D_L\) and \(D_R\) is: \[
Gini_s(D_t)=\frac{|D_L|}{|D_t|}Gini(D_L)+\frac{|D_R|}{|D_t|}Gini(D_R).
\tag{2}\]



CART selects the candidate split \(s\) that minimizes weighted Gini impurity. Equivalently, this maximizes impurity reduction (Gini gain).






Definition. The impurity reduction achieved by split \(s\) at node \(D_t\) is: \[
\Delta Gini(s,D_t)=Gini(D_t)-Gini_s(D_t).
\tag{3}\]



Both formulations yield identical split rankings for a given node: minimizing \(Gini_s(D_t)\) is mathematically equivalent to maximizing \(\Delta Gini(s,D_t)\) because parent impurity \(Gini(D_t)\) is constant during evaluation.
crumbs: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
6 Binary Splits for Categorical Features
Suppose a categorical feature \(A\) takes values in a finite set:
\[
\mathcal{A}=\{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_m\}.
\]
Rather than creating an \(m\)-way branch, CART constructs binary questions of the form:
\[
A \in S_A,
\]
where \(S_A\) is a non-empty proper subset of \(\mathcal{A}\). For example, if:
\[
\text{income} \in \{\text{low}, \text{medium}, \text{high}\},
\]
candidate split subsets include:
\[
\text{income} \in \{\text{low}\}, \qquad \text{income} \in \{\text{medium}\}, \qquad \text{income} \in \{\text{low}, \text{medium}\}.
\]
Each question partitions observations into two subsets: matching instances and non-matching instances.






Definition. For a categorical feature \(A\) taking \(m\) distinct categories, the number of distinct, non-trivial binary splits is: \[
\frac{2^m-2}{2}=2^{m-1}-1.
\tag{4}\]



We subtract 2 because empty and full set subsets do not form valid splits. We divide by 2 because subset \(S_A\) and its complement \(\mathcal{A} \setminus S_A\) define the exact same physical data partition (simply swapping left and right branch assignments).


Show code
from itertools import combinations


def binary_partitions(values):
    values = tuple(values)
    m = len(values)
    partitions = []
    seen = set()
    full = frozenset(values)
    for r in range(1, m):
        for comb in combinations(values, r):
            left = frozenset(comb)
            right = full - left
            key = frozenset([left, right])
            if key not in seen:
                seen.add(key)
                partitions.append((set(left), set(right)))
    return partitions

for left, right in binary_partitions(["low", "medium", "high"]):
    print(left, "vs", right)

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
7 Binary Splits for Continuous Features
For continuous numerical features, CART evaluates candidate cut-points. For continuous feature \(A\), a split takes the form:
\[
A < c \quad \text{vs.} \quad A \geq c.
\]
Standard procedure sorts unique observed values of \(A\), computes midpoints between consecutive sorted values, and evaluates each midpoint as a candidate threshold \(c\).






Definition. Given sorted unique values \(a_{(1)}<a_{(2)}<\dots<a_{(r)}\) of a continuous numerical feature \(A\), candidate cut-points are: \[
c_j=\frac{a_{(j)}+a_{(j+1)}}{2}, \qquad j=1,\dots,r-1.
\tag{5}\]



Consider the toy dataset:
\[
(20,\text{Yes}),\quad (25,\text{Yes}),\quad (30,\text{No}),\quad (40,\text{No}).
\]
Sorted values are \(20, 25, 30, 40\), yielding candidate midpoints:
\[
22.5, \qquad 27.5, \qquad 35.
\]
For each threshold \(c\), child subsets are formed:
\[
D_L=\{A<c\}, \qquad D_R=\{A\geq c\},
\]
and weighted Gini impurity is computed.


Show code
import pandas as pd

edad = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": [20, 25, 30, 40],
    "target": ["Yes", "Yes", "No", "No"]
})


def gini(labels):
    counts = pd.Series(labels).value_counts().to_numpy()
    return gini_from_counts(counts)


def weighted_gini_for_cut(df, feature, target, c):
    left = df[df[feature] < c]
    right = df[df[feature] >= c]
    n = len(df)
    return (len(left)/n)*gini(left[target]) + (len(right)/n)*gini(right[target])

values = sorted(edad["age"].unique())
cuts = [(values[i] + values[i+1]) / 2 for i in range(len(values)-1)]

resultados = pd.DataFrame({
    "cutpoint": cuts,
    "weighted_gini": [weighted_gini_for_cut(edad, "age", "target", c) for c in cuts]
})

def weighted_gini_categorical(df, feature, target, left_values):
    left_values = set(left_values)
    left = df[df[feature].isin(left_values)]
    right = df[~df[feature].isin(left_values)]
    n = len(df)
    return (len(left)/n)*gini(left[target]) + (len(right)/n)*gini(right[target])


def best_categorical_split(df, feature, target):
    values = sorted(df[feature].unique())

        rows.append({

            "left_subset": tuple(sorted(left)),
            "right_subset": tuple(sorted(right)),
            "weighted_gini": wg,
            "gini_reduction": gini(df[target]) - wg
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("weighted_gini")

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
9 Impurity Reduction and Interpretation
Gini reduction measures absolute purity improvement relative to parent node impurity. For instance, if root impurity is:
\[
Gini(D)=0.459,
\]
and a candidate split produces:
\[
Gini_s(D)=0.357,
\]
the Gini reduction is:
\[
\Delta Gini = 0.459-0.357=0.102.
\]
Higher Gini reduction signals a better split. CART systematically tests all available feature splits at a node, selecting the one with maximum impurity reduction, and repeats this process recursively on each child node.

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
11 Cost-Complexity Pruning
A key architectural feature of CART is cost-complexity pruning. The tree is initially allowed to grow deep, after which weak branches providing minimal predictive gain relative to tree complexity are pruned (Breiman et al. 1984).
For tree \(T\), cost-complexity objective combines empirical error with a complexity penalty:






Definition. The cost-complexity criterion for tree \(T\) parameterized by \(\alpha \geq 0\) is: \[
R_{\alpha}(T)=R(T)+\alpha |T|,
\tag{6}\]



where \(R(T)\) is empirical training error, \(|T|\) is the number of terminal leaf nodes, and \(\alpha \ge 0\) controls complexity penalty. Setting \(\alpha=0\) keeps the unpruned full tree. Larger \(\alpha\) values favor smaller, simpler trees.
Pruning yields simpler, more interpretable models less prone to overfitting. In scikit-learn, cost-complexity pruning is configured via ccp_alpha (scikit-learn developers 2026).


Show code
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

X = datos[["age", "income", "student", "credit_rating"]]
y = datos["buy_laptop"]

preprocess = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), X.columns)]
)

modelo = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("preprocess", preprocess),
    ("tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="gini", random_state=42))
])

modelo.fit(X, y)
pred = modelo.predict(X)
print(f"Training Accuracy = {accuracy_score(y, pred):.3f}")

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
13 Extracting Classification Rules
Trees translate directly into IF-THEN rules. Each root-to-leaf path forms a single rule. For example:
\[
\text{IF age} \neq \text{middle\_aged AND student} = \text{yes THEN buy\_laptop} = \text{yes}.
\]
Extracted rules make model logic transparent to non-technical stakeholders, allowing auditability for bias or counter-intuitive logic.

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
14 CART for Regression
While this chapter focuses on classification, CART applies equally to regression tasks. For regression trees, leaf nodes predict continuous numerical values (typically node mean target values).
Split selection in regression minimizes node variance or Residual Sum of Squares (RSS):






Definition. In a regression tree, for split \(s\) partitioning \(D_t\) into \(D_L\) and \(D_R\), RSS error is: \[
RSS(s)=\sum_{i\in D_L}(y_i-\bar{y}_L)^2+\sum_{i\in D_R}(y_i-\bar{y}_R)^2.
\tag{7}\]



Thus, CART unifies classification and regression under a common framework: recursively partitioning feature space into internally homogeneous regions.
crumbs: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
15 Computational Complexity
CART training complexity depends on sample size \(n\), feature count \(m\), feature types, and final tree depth. For numerical features, sorting values at each node takes \(O(mn \log n)\) initial time.
Overall training complexity for balanced binary trees can be estimated as:
\[
O(mn\log n).
\]
Factors influencing complexity:

\(n\) dictates training instance evaluation counts;
\(m\) dictates feature evaluations per split;
Tree depth dictates partitioning iterations;
Categorical features with many categories scale as \(2^{m-1}-1\) candidate binary splits.

Hyperparameters like max_depth, min_samples_split, and ccp_alpha keep computational and structural complexity in check.
crumbs: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
crumbs: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees

title: 42  CART Trees: Classification and Regression Trees
text:
17 Conclusions
CART is a cornerstone decision tree algorithm. Its core mechanic is recursively partitioning feature space using binary splits to minimize node impurity. In classification, the Gini index provides an effective impurity measure; in regression, RSS minimization guides partitioning.
The CART framework combines interpretability, versatility, and mathematical clarity. Impurity-weighted split selection, Gini gain maximization, and cost-complexity pruning allow building accurate models while controlling overfitting. Beyond its standalone utility, CART provides the essential foundation for state-of-the-art ensemble techniques across modern data science.

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
1 From Linear Regression to Region-Based Models
Decision trees represent a family of rule-based supervised learning methods. Unlike global linear models that describe an entire dataset using a single global equation, a decision tree partitions predictor space into smaller regions and fits a simple localized prediction in each one. This approach is particularly effective when relationships between explanatory variables and continuous target responses are non-linear, vary across feature space subregions, or involve complex interactions (Breiman et al. 1984; Hastie et al. 2009).
In regression tasks, the objective is predicting a numerical response. For example, we might estimate laptop prices based on RAM, screen size, processor specs, and brand; or forecast housing prices based on surface area, location, and property age. A regression tree learns decision rules of the form “if a feature falls below a specific threshold, follow one branch; otherwise, follow another”. At the end of each branch lies a terminal leaf node, where the response prediction is typically the average of training observations reaching that specific region.
This chapter develops the core logic of regression trees, their geometric interpretation as piecewise constant functions, split evaluation criteria, pruning techniques to prevent overfitting, and basic evaluation metrics. Subsequently, tree-based ensemble methods are introduced, specifically bagging, random forests, and boosting. Finally, the nearest neighbor algorithm is presented as a contrast to decision trees: a memory-based, distance-driven lazy learning method.
Multiple linear regression models a continuous target \(y\) as a global linear combination of predictor features \(x_1, \ldots, x_p\):
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1}+\dots+\beta_p x_{ip}+\varepsilon_i.
\]
Its primary advantage is coefficient interpretability: each \(\beta_j\) quantifies the expected change in \(y\) given a one-unit increase in \(x_j\), holding all other features constant. However, this structure enforces a global functional form. When the true relationship between \(X\) and \(y\) varies across different regions of feature space, a single linear equation can prove overly restrictive.
Regression trees address this limitation through recursive partitioning. Rather than fitting a single global surface, they divide predictor space into disjoint regions and assign a constant prediction to each region, producing a flexible, non-parametric, and interpretable model (James et al. 2021).
Here, \(x\) represents an input observation; \(R_h\) denotes region \(h\) in feature space; \(c_h\) is the prediction assigned to that region (typically the mean observed target response within \(R_h\)); and \(\mathbb{I}(x\in R_h)\) is an indicator function taking value one if \(x \in R_h\) and zero otherwise.
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
Definition. A regression tree is a model that partitions predictor feature space into disjoint regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_J\) and predicts a constant value \(c_h\) within each region: \[
\hat f(x)=\sum_{h=1}^{J} c_h\,\mathbb{I}(x\in R_h).
\tag{1}\]










Definition. The indicator function for region \(R_h\) is defined as: \[
\mathbb{I}(x\in R_h)=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } x\in R_h,\\
0, & \text{if } x\notin R_h.
\end{cases}
\tag{2}\]
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
2 Non-Linear Classifiers and Piecewise Models
In classification problems, linear classifiers separate classes using decision hyperplanes. When data are linearly separable, this approach is sufficient. However, in real-world applications, class boundaries are often curved, disjoint, or driven by non-linear feature interactions. In these scenarios, two main strategies exist: retaining a linear classifier while tolerating classification errors, or employing non-linear classifiers capable of learning flexible decision boundaries.
A intuitive way to construct non-linearity is combining linear pieces. The core concept involves partitioning a class into sub-classes or local sub-regions and assigning a local linear discriminant to each sub-region. The resulting global boundary transitions from a single hyperplane into a composite union of linear segments or faces. This logic directly foreshadows two key frameworks: decision trees (which split feature space via recursive orthogonal cuts) and nearest neighbors (which carry local decision making to its logical extreme by treating every training sample as a local reference point) (Duda et al. 2001; Hastie et al. 2009).






Definition. A piecewise linear classifier assigns to each class \(\omega_i\) a set of sub-classes \(\omega_i^1,\dots,\omega_i^{\ell_i}\), each possessing a linear discriminant \(g_i^\ell(x)\), defining the class discriminant function as a local maximum: \[
g_i(x)=\max_{\ell=1,\dots,\ell_i} g_i^\ell(x),\qquad
\hat y(x)=\arg\max_{i=1,\dots,c} g_i(x).
\tag{3}\]



Writing \(g_i^\ell(x)=w_{i\ell}^{\top}x+w_{i\ell,0}\), each sub-class contributes a linear boundary. The maximum operator selects the sub-region that best explains query point \(x\). As the number of sub-classes increases, the decision boundary can approximate complex non-linear shapes. However, this flexibility requires deciding how many sub-classes to instantiate, how to initialize them, and how to avoid overfitting noise.
From this perspective, decision trees construct piecewise constant approximations with axis-aligned boundaries. KNN, on the other hand, can be viewed as an extreme local classifier: rather than learning explicit sub-classes, it stores training examples directly and makes decisions based on local distances.
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
3 Step Functions
A regression tree produces a piecewise step function. For a single predictor \(x\), a simple model can be expressed as:
\[
\hat f(x)=
\begin{cases}
100, & x<10,\\
200, & 10\le x<20,\\
300, & x\ge 20.
\end{cases}
\]
Rather than fitting a continuous line, this model partitions the \(x\)-axis into intervals and assigns a constant target prediction to each interval. In two dimensions, regions form rectangular boxes; in \(p\) dimensions, they form hyper-rectangles. For instance, with age, income, and experience, a decision rule might read:
\[
\text{age}<30 \quad \text{and} \quad \text{income}>5000.
\]
Such explicit rules are easily human-readable, explaining the popularity of decision trees in domain-sensitive applications. However, axis-aligned splits impose a geometric constraint: linear diagonal or smooth oblique relationships require many step splits to approximate effectively (Hastie et al. 2009).
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
4 Prediction Within a Region
Once a tree defines region \(R_h\), the optimal prediction under squared-error loss is the arithmetic mean of target values residing in that region. Given observations within region \(R_h\) with target responses \(y_1, \ldots, y_{n_h}\), constant prediction \(c_h\) is chosen to minimize Sum of Squared Errors:
\[
\sum_{i:x_i\in R_h}(y_i-c_h)^2.
\]
Setting the derivative with respect to \(c_h\) to zero yields the sample mean.






Definition. Under squared-error loss, the optimal leaf prediction \(\hat c_h\) for region \(R_h\) in a regression tree is the mean of target responses falling into that leaf: \[
\hat c_h = \frac{1}{|R_h|}\sum_{i:x_i\in R_h} y_i.
\tag{4}\]



For example, if a region contains actual values \(\{20, 40, 100, 120\}\), its un-split prediction is:
\[
\hat c=\frac{20+40+100+120}{4}=70.
\]
If this region is partitioned into two sub-regions, \(R_1=\{20,40\}\) and \(R_2=\{100,120\}\), the new regional predictions become:
\[
\hat c_1=30,\qquad \hat c_2=110.
\]
Partitioning improves accuracy because each sub-region is represented by a mean that far better reflects its localized values.
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
5 Total Error and Split Criteria
A decision tree evaluates candidate splits by quantifying the reduction in error achieved when partitioning a region. In regression, the standard split criterion is the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) within leaf nodes (Breiman et al. 1984; James et al. 2021).






Definition. The total squared error of a regression tree with regions \(R_1,\dots,R_J\) is: \[
D(T)=\sum_{h=1}^{J}\sum_{i:x_i\in R_h}(y_i-\hat c_h)^2.
\tag{5}\]



When evaluating a candidate split of region \(R\) into left (\(R_L\)) and right (\(R_R\)) sub-regions, the algorithm compares total error before and after splitting:
\[
D_{\text{split}} = \sum_{i:x_i\in R_L}(y_i-\hat c_L)^2+
\sum_{i:x_i\in R_R}(y_i-\hat c_R)^2.
\]






Definition. The gain of a split is defined as the absolute error reduction achieved by the partition: \[
\text{Gain}=D_{\text{before}}-D_{\text{after}}.
\tag{6}\]



A candidate split is selected if it yields a large reduction in RSS. During training, the algorithm evaluates all candidate split points across all features (e.g., evaluating threshold cuts across age, income, experience) and selects the split maximizing gain.

  
    RSS Split Criterion — Interactive Explorer
    Drag the split threshold slider to observe how RSS changes before and after partitioning
  
  
    RAM Threshold = 6.0 GB
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
6 Recursive Binary Splitting
Decision tree training employs greedy top-down recursive binary splitting. The algorithm finds the optimal single split for the full training set. It then recursively applies the same splitting procedure to each child region until a stopping criterion is met (e.g., maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf, or minimum error gain).
Workflow steps:

Start with all training instances in a single root region.
For each predictor feature and candidate threshold cut-point, evaluate the RSS error reduction.
Select the single split maximizing RSS error reduction.
Recursively repeat steps 2–3 on each child sub-region.
Stop growing when stopping constraints or pruning criteria trigger.

Top-down greedy splitting is computationally efficient and generates interpretable rules. However, because it makes greedy local choices at each step without backtracking, it does not guarantee finding globally optimal tree structures (Breiman et al. 1984).

Consider a toy dataset predicting laptop prices based solely on RAM capacity.

Without splitting, the prediction for all laptops is the global sample mean:
\[
\bar y=\frac{6500+7200+10500+12000+21000+24000}{6}=13,533.33.
\]
Unsplit total RSS error is:
\[
D_{\text{unsplit}}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2=266{,}433{,}333.33.
\]
Evaluating candidate split: \(\text{RAM} < 12 \text{ GB}\).
This creates two sub-regions:
\[
R_1=\{6500,7200,10500,12000\},\qquad R_2=\{21000,24000\}.
\]
Leaf predictions are regional averages:
\[
\hat c_1=\frac{6500+7200+10500+12000}{4}=9050,
\]
\[
\hat c_2=\frac{21000+24000}{2}=22500.
\]
Post-split RSS error:
\[
D_{\text{split}}=
(6500-9050)^2+(7200-9050)^2+(10500-9050)^2+(12000-9050)^2
+(21000-22500)^2+(24000-22500)^2 = 25{,}230{,}000.
\]
Relative error reduction:
\[
\frac{D_{\text{unsplit}}-D_{\text{split}}}{D_{\text{unsplit}}}
=\frac{266{,}433{,}333.33-25{,}230{,}000}{266{,}433{,}333.33}
\approx 90.53\%.
\]
A single split reduces squared prediction error by 90.53%.

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
9 Overfitting and Pruning
Unconstrained trees split recursively until every training sample is isolated into its own leaf node, achieving zero training error. However, this memorizes noise and ruins out-of-sample generalization.
Cost-complexity pruning penalizes tree size during structure selection (Breiman et al. 1984; scikit-learn developers 2025).






Definition. The cost-complexity objective penalizes total empirical error with a complexity term scaled by leaf count \(J\): \[
C_{\alpha}(T)=\sum_{h=1}^{J}D_h+\alpha J.
\tag{7}\]



Here \(D_h\) is RSS error in leaf \(h\), \(J\) is the total leaf count, and \(\alpha \ge 0\) controls the penalty weight. Small \(\alpha\) allows deeper trees; large \(\alpha\) forces compact trees.
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_california_housing
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

housing = fetch_california_housing(as_frame=True)
X_h, y_h = housing.data, housing.target

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X_h, y_h, test_size=0.25, random_state=42
)

for alpha in [0.0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05]:
    model = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42, ccp_alpha=alpha)
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    y_pred_h = model.predict(X_te)
    print({
        "ccp_alpha": alpha,
        "n_leaves": model.get_n_leaves(),
        "MAE": round(mean_absolute_error(y_te, y_pred_h), 4),
        "R2": round(r2_score(y_te, y_pred_h), 4)
    })

text:
10 Regression Tree Evaluation Metrics






Definition. The coefficient of determination \(R^2\) is defined as: \[
R^2=1-\frac{SSE}{SS_{TOT}},
\qquad
SSE=\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2,
\qquad
SS_{TOT}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2.
\tag{8}\]



An \(R^2 = 0.90\) means the model explains 90% of target response variance relative to a baseline mean predictor. In addition to \(R^2\), Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) provide absolute error bounds in target units.
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
11 Bagging: Bootstrap Aggregating
Bagging reduces variance by training decision trees independently on multiple bootstrap samples of the training set and averaging their predictions (Breiman 1996).






Definition. A size-\(n\) bootstrap sample \(\mathcal{D}^{*(b)}\) is generated by sampling \(n\) instances uniformly at random with replacement from original training set \(\mathcal{D}\): \[
\mathcal{D}^{*(b)}=\{(x_1^{*(b)},y_1^{*(b)}),\dots,(x_n^{*(b)},y_n^{*(b)})\}.
\tag{9}\]









Definition. The bagging ensemble prediction for regression is the arithmetic mean across \(B\) bootstrap-trained trees: \[
\hat f_{bag}(x)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat f^{*(b)}(x).
\tag{10}\]



from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingRegressor

bag = BaggingRegressor(
    estimator=DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42),
    n_estimators=100,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

bag.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
y_pred_bag = bag.predict(X_te)

print("Bagging MAE :", round(mean_absolute_error(y_te, y_pred_bag), 4))
print("Bagging R2  :", round(r2_score(y_te, y_pred_bag), 4))
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
12 Random Forests
Random Forests extend bagging by injecting feature randomization into node split evaluation (Breiman 2001). At each split candidate, only a random subset of \(m \le p\) features is considered (typically \(m = \sqrt{p}\) for classification and \(m = p/3\) for regression), decorrelating trees and maximizing variance reduction.






Definition. A Random Forest is an ensemble of decorrelated decision trees built on bootstrap samples, where each node split considers only a random feature subset: \[
\hat f_{RF}(x)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat f_b(x).
\tag{11}\]



from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

rf = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=300,
    max_features="sqrt",
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

rf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
y_pred_rf = rf.predict(X_te)

print("Random Forest MAE :", round(mean_absolute_error(y_te, y_pred_rf), 4))
print("Random Forest R2  :", round(r2_score(y_te, y_pred_rf), 4))
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
13 Boosting
Unlike bagging, boosting builds models sequentially. Each new weak learner is trained to predict residual errors made by preceding trees (Freund and Schapire 1997; Schapire 1990; Friedman 2001).






Definition. Gradient Boosting for regression fits additive models sequentially: \[
F_M(x)=F_0(x)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\nu h_m(x),
\] where each tree \(h_m\) fits pseudo-residuals of \(F_{m-1}\) and \(\nu \in (0, 1]\) is the learning rate shrinking parameter. $$ {#eq-gradient-boosting}



from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor

gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(
    n_estimators=300,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=3,
    random_state=42
)

gb.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
y_pred_gb = gb.predict(X_te)

print("Gradient Boosting MAE :", round(mean_absolute_error(y_te, y_pred_gb), 4))
print("Gradient Boosting R2  :", round(r2_score(y_te, y_pred_gb), 4))

13.1 Comparison: Bagging vs. Boosting








Feature
Bagging (Random Forest)

Model Fitting

Reduce variance

Sample Focus
Uniform bootstrap
Focuses on high-error instances


Parallelization

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
14 Nearest Neighbor Classification (k-NN)
Nearest neighbor classification is a memory-based (lazy learning) method (Cover and Hart 1967; Duda et al. 2001). It stores training data directly without fitting explicit parametric parameters.






Definition. The 1-NN rule assigns query point \(x\) the label of its single nearest training instance under distance metric \(d\): \[
\hat y(x)=\theta_{i^*},\qquad i^*=\arg\min_{i=1,\dots,N} d(x,x_i).
\tag{12}\]









Definition. Minimum distance discriminant function for class \(\omega_j\): \[
g_j(x)=\min_{i:\theta_i=j} d(x,x_i),\qquad
\hat y(x)=\arg\min_{j=1,\dots,c} g_j(x).
\tag{13}\]




14.1 Distance Metrics






Definition. Minkowski distance of order \(s \ge 1\) between \(x, z \in \mathbb{R}^p\): \[
d_s(x,z)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{p}|x_j-z_j|^s\right)^{1/s}.
\tag{14}\]




Manhattan (\(s=1\)): \(d_1(x,z)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}|x_j-z_j|\) {#eq-manhattan-distance}
Euclidean (\(s=2\)): \(d_2(x,z)=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p}(x_j-z_j)^2}\) {#eq-euclidean-distance}
Chebyshev (\(s=\infty\)): \(d_{\infty}(x,z)=\max_{j=1,\dots,p}|x_j-z_j|\) {#eq-chebyshev-distance}
Mahalanobis: \(d_Q(x,z)=(x-z)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-z)\) {#eq-quadratic-distance}

    Drag p to observe unit ball shape changes: diamond (p=1), circle (p=2), square (p→∞)

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
15 k-NN Classifier






Definition. In \(k\)-NN classification, given \(N_k(x)\) containing the set of indices for the \(k\) nearest training points to \(x\): \[
g_j(x)=\sum_{i\in N_k(x)}\mathbb{I}(\theta_i=j),\qquad
\hat y(x)=\arg\max_{j=1,\dots,c}g_j(x).
\tag{15}\]









Definition. In \(k\)-NN regression, predictions average the responses of the \(k\) nearest neighbors: \[
\hat f(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in N_k(x)}y_i.
\tag{16}\]




  
    k-NN Classifier — Interactive Explorer
    Click anywhere on the canvas to place a query point; adjust k to observe decision boundary changes
  
  
    k = 3
    
  
  Click on canvas to query point
  



15.1 Cover-Hart Asymptotic Error Bound
Cover and Hart (1967) established that for \(N \to \infty\) i.i.d. samples, the asymptotic 1-NN error rate \(P_1\) is upper-bounded by Bayes error rate \(P^*\):






Definition. For \(c\) classes, Cover-Hart bound states: \[
P^*\le P_1\le P^*\left(2-\frac{c}{c-1}P^*\right) \le 2 P^*.
\tag{17}\]





15.2 Consistency Condition






Definition. \(k\)-NN consistency requires: \[
N\to\infty,\qquad k\to\infty,\qquad \frac{k}{N}\to 0.
\tag{18}\]





15.3 Curse of Dimensionality






Definition. In a \(p\)-dimensional unit hypercube, a local neighborhood with linear edge length \(r\) occupies relative volume: \[
V(r,p)=r^p.
\tag{19}\]



For \(p=10\) and \(r=0.1\), volume fraction is \(10^{-10}\), demonstrating why density estimation decays exponentially in high dimensions (Bellman 1961).


15.4 Computational Optimization and Pruning Rules

Branch-and-Bound Node Pruning: \(d(x, M_p) - r_p > B\) {#eq-branch-bound-prune}
Edited Nearest Neighbors: Remove \((x_i, y_i)\) if \(\hat y_{-i}(x_i) \neq y_i\) {#eq-edited-nn-rule}
Condensed Nearest Neighbors: Find small subset \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq S_N\) preserving decisions {#eq-condensed-nn}
crumbs: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors

title: 43  Regression Trees, Ensembles, and Nearest Neighbors
text:
16 Conclusions
Regression trees replace global linear equations with structured hierarchies of localized decision rules. They offer high interpretability but suffer from high variance, instability, and axis-aligned step constraints. Ensembles like Random Forests (bagging + feature randomization) and Gradient Boosted Trees (sequential residual fitting) dramatically improve accuracy and stability. Finally, Nearest Neighbors offers a memory-based distance-driven alternative, completing the spectrum of non-linear decision modeling.

title: 44  Gradient Boosting and XGBoost
text:
1 From Decision Trees to Boosting
XGBoost (eXtreme Gradient Boosting) was introduced by Chen and Guestrin in 2016 (Chen and Guestrin 2016) and has since dominated machine learning competitions on Kaggle and benchmark platforms. It is a regularized, second-order optimized implementation of the gradient boosting algorithm (Friedman 2001), incorporating key innovations in approximate split finding, efficient sparse data handling, and system-level scalability. This chapter covers the mathematical foundations of the algorithm, its primary hyperparameters, variable importance interpretation using SHAP, and practical implementation in Python.

title: 44  Gradient Boosting and XGBoost
text:
1.1 The Bias–Variance Trade-off and Individual Trees
A deep decision tree has the capacity to memorize training data: as depth increases, the model fits observed data ever more closely and its variance increases. Conversely, a shallow tree (or single-level decision stump) exhibits high bias due to limited expressive capacity. This bias–variance trade-off is central to machine learning and motivates ensemble learning.
Ensemble methods combine multiple weak learners to form a strong predictor. In bagging (e.g., Random Forest (Breiman 2001)), decision trees are trained independently on bootstrap samples, and predictions are averaged to reduce variance. In boosting, the strategy differs: models are constructed sequentially, where each new tree learns from the residual errors of the preceding ensemble, progressively reducing bias.


Show code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 80
X_raw = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n))
y_raw = np.sin(X_raw) + rng.normal(0, 0.35, n)
X_fit = X_raw.reshape(-1, 1)

X_plot = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 300).reshape(-1, 1)

profundidades = [1, 3, 10]
titulos = [
    "Depth 1 Tree (High Bias)",
    "Depth 3 Tree (Balanced)",
    "Depth 10 Tree (High Variance)"
]

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, subplot_titles=titulos)

for idx, (depth, titulo) in enumerate(zip(profundidades, titulos), start=1):
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=0)
    tree.fit(X_fit, y_raw)
    y_pred = tree.predict(X_plot)

    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=X_raw, y=y_raw,
            mode="markers",
            marker=dict(color="#94a3b8", size=5),
            name="Data",
            showlegend=(idx == 1)
        ),
        row=1, col=idx
    )
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=X_plot.flatten(), y=y_pred,
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color="#2563eb", width=2.5),
            name="Prediction",
            showlegend=(idx == 1)
        ),
        row=1, col=idx
    )
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=X_plot.flatten(), y=np.sin(X_plot.flatten()),
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color="black", dash="dash", width=1.5),
            name="True Function",
            showlegend=(idx == 1)
        ),
        row=1, col=idx
    )

fig.update_layout(
    height=380,
    template="plotly_white",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.25, xanchor="center", x=0.5)
)
fig.update_xaxes(title_text="x")
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="y", col=1)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Illustration of the bias-variance trade-off for decision trees of varying depth. A shallow tree (depth 1) exhibits high bias, while a very deep tree (depth 10) exhibits high variance.




Figure 44.1 demonstrates how tree depth controls the balance between bias and variance. A depth-3 tree achieves a reasonable fit without overfitting noise.


1.2 Boosting: Sequential Residual Learning
Boosting builds an additive model sequentially. Starting from a constant initial prediction:
\[F_0(\mathbf{x}) = \underset{\gamma}{\mathrm{argmin}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} L(y_i, \gamma) \tag{1}\]
At each iteration \(m = 1, \ldots, M\), negative gradients (pseudo-residuals) of the loss function evaluated at the current ensemble prediction are computed:
\[r_i^{(m)} = -\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i, F(\mathbf{x}_i))}{\partial F(\mathbf{x}_i)}\right]_{F = F_{m-1}} \tag{2}\]
A weak base learner \(h_m\) is fitted to these pseudo-residuals, and the ensemble is updated:
\[F_m(\mathbf{x}) = F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}) + \eta \cdot h_m(\mathbf{x}) \tag{3}\]
where \(\eta \in (0, 1]\) is the learning rate or shrinkage parameter. For squared error loss \(L(y, F) = \tfrac{1}{2}(y - F)^2\), the negative gradient simplifies to ordinary residuals \(r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}_i)\). Thus, the algorithm iteratively fits ensemble errors: each new tree targets what previous trees failed to explain.






Gradient Boosting (Simplified Overview)

Initialize constant prediction \(F_0(\mathbf{x}) = \bar{y}\) (target mean).
For \(m = 1, \ldots, M\):

Compute residuals \(r_i^{(m)} = y_i - F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}_i)\).
Fit weak base learner \(h_m\) to \(\{(\mathbf{x}_i, r_i^{(m)})\}_{i=1}^n\).
Update ensemble \(F_m(\mathbf{x}) = F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}) + \eta \cdot h_m(\mathbf{x})\).

Return final model \(F_M(\mathbf{x})\).




The following interactive plot illustrates the iterative convergence of gradient boosting implemented from scratch:


Show code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng2 = np.random.default_rng(7)
n2 = 60
X2 = np.sort(rng2.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n2)).reshape(-1, 1)
y2 = np.sin(X2.flatten()) + rng2.normal(0, 0.3, n2)
X_line = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
y_true_line = np.sin(X_line.flatten())


class Stump:
    def fit(self, X, r):
        best_feat, best_thr, best_loss = 0, 0, float("inf")
        for feat in range(X.shape[1]):
            thresholds = np.unique(X[:, feat])
            for thr in thresholds:
                left = r[X[:, feat] <= thr]
                right = r[X[:, feat] > thr]
                if len(left) == 0 or len(right) == 0:
                    continue
                loss = np.sum((left - left.mean()) ** 2) + np.sum((right - right.mean()) ** 2)
                if loss < best_loss:
                    best_loss = loss
                    best_feat, best_thr = feat, thr
                    self.val_left, self.val_right = left.mean(), right.mean()
        self.feat, self.thr = best_feat, best_thr

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.where(X[:, self.feat] <= self.thr, self.val_left, self.val_right)


eta = 0.5
M_max = 20
stumps = []
F_current = np.full(n2, y2.mean())

snapshots = {}
rondas = [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20]

for m in range(1, M_max + 1):
    residuos = y2 - F_current
    stump = Stump()
    stump.fit(X2, residuos)
    stumps.append(stump)
    F_current = F_current + eta * stump.predict(X2)
    if m in rondas:
        F_line = np.full(300, y2.mean())
        for s in stumps:
            F_line = F_line + eta * s.predict(X_line)
        snapshots[m] = {
            "F_line": F_line.copy(),
            "residuos": (y2 - F_current).copy()
        }

frames = []
for m in rondas:
    snap = snapshots[m]
    frame = go.Frame(
        data=[
            go.Scatter(
                x=X2.flatten(), y=y2,
                mode="markers",
                marker=dict(color="#94a3b8", size=6),
                name="Data"
            ),
            go.Scatter(
                x=X_line.flatten(), y=y_true_line,
                mode="lines",
                line=dict(color="black", dash="dash", width=1.5),
                name="True Function"
            ),
            go.Scatter(
                x=X_line.flatten(), y=snap["F_line"],
                mode="lines",
                line=dict(color="#2563eb", width=2.5),
                name="Prediction F_m"
            ),
            go.Scatter(
                x=X2.flatten(), y=snap["residuos"],
                mode="markers",
                marker=dict(color="#f97316", size=6, symbol="diamond"),
                name="Residuals"
            )
        ],
        name=str(m)
    )
    frames.append(frame)

snap0 = snapshots[1]
fig2 = go.Figure(
    data=[
        go.Scatter(x=X2.flatten(), y=y2, mode="markers",
                   marker=dict(color="#94a3b8", size=6), name="Data"),
        go.Scatter(x=X_line.flatten(), y=y_true_line, mode="lines",
                   line=dict(color="black", dash="dash", width=1.5), name="True Function"),
        go.Scatter(x=X_line.flatten(), y=snap0["F_line"], mode="lines",
                   line=dict(color="#2563eb", width=2.5), name="Prediction F_m"),
        go.Scatter(x=X2.flatten(), y=snap0["residuos"], mode="markers",
                   marker=dict(color="#f97316", size=6, symbol="diamond"), name="Residuals")
    ],
    frames=frames
)

steps = []
for m in rondas:
    step = dict(
        method="animate",
        args=[[str(m)], {"frame": {"duration": 600, "redraw": True}, "mode": "immediate"}],
        label=str(m)
    )
    steps.append(step)

fig2.update_layout(
    template="plotly_white",
    height=440,
    xaxis_title="x",
    yaxis_title="y",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.3, xanchor="center", x=0.5),
    sliders=[dict(
        active=0,
        currentvalue=dict(prefix="M = ", font=dict(size=14)),
        pad=dict(t=50),
        steps=steps
    )],
    updatemenus=[dict(
        type="buttons",
        showactive=False,
        y=1.1, x=0.5, xanchor="center",
        buttons=[
            dict(label="Play", method="animate",
                 args=[None, {"frame": {"duration": 800, "redraw": True}, "fromcurrent": True}]),
            dict(label="Pause", method="animate",
                 args=[[None], {"frame": {"duration": 0, "redraw": False}, "mode": "immediate"}])
        ]
    )]
)
fig2.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Iterative convergence of gradient boosting on a 1D regression problem. Each frame shows the accumulated ensemble prediction (blue) and current residuals (orange) after adding M trees.




As seen in Figure 44.2, residual errors (orange diamonds) progressively shrink as trees are added, and prediction curves (blue) converge toward the underlying true function (dashed black).
Learning rate \(\eta\) in Eq. 44.3 acts as a convergence rate controller. Setting \(\eta=1\) aggressively corrects errors at each step, accelerating overfitting risks. Smaller \(\eta\) values require more boosting rounds but yield superior generalization (shrinkage, Friedman (2002)).
Gradient boosting (Eq. 44.2) represents functional gradient descent: updating target functions directly in function space rather than updating parametric weights in Euclidean space (Friedman 2001).

title: 44  Gradient Boosting and XGBoost
text:
2 XGBoost Optimization Objective

2.1 Additive Model and Regularized Objective
XGBoost builds additive tree models:
\[\hat{y}_i^{(t)} = \sum_{k=1}^{t} f_k(\mathbf{x}_i), \quad f_k \in \mathcal{F} \tag{4}\]
where \(\mathcal{F}\) is the space of regression trees. At round \(t\), tree \(f_t\) is chosen to minimize the regularized objective:
\[\text{Obj}^{(t)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l\!\left(y_i,\, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(\mathbf{x}_i)\right) + \Omega(f_t) + \text{constant} \tag{5}\]
Regularization penalty \(\Omega\) penalizes leaf counts and weight magnitudes:
\[\Omega(f) = \gamma T + \frac{1}{2}\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \tag{6}\]
where \(T\) is the number of terminal leaves in \(f_t\) and \(\mathbf{w}\) denotes leaf weights. Parameter \(\gamma\) controls pruning thresholding while \(\lambda\) imposes L2 weight regularization.






Key Innovation in XGBoost: Unlike classic gradient boosting (Friedman 2001), XGBoost incorporates explicit structural regularization directly into its optimization objective and uses second-order Taylor expansions (hessians) to derive optimal leaf weights analytically.





2.2 Second-Order Taylor Approximation
Applying a second-order Taylor expansion around \(\hat{y}_i^{(t-1)}\):
\[l\!\left(y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)} + f_t\right) \approx l\!\left(y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)}\right) + g_i f_t(\mathbf{x}_i) + \frac{1}{2} h_i f_t^2(\mathbf{x}_i) \tag{7}\]
where:
\[g_i = \frac{\partial\, l(y_i, \hat{y}^{(t-1)})}{\partial\, \hat{y}^{(t-1)}} \quad \text{(first-order gradient)} \tag{8}\]
\[h_i = \frac{\partial^2\, l(y_i, \hat{y}^{(t-1)})}{\partial\, (\hat{y}^{(t-1)})^2} \quad \text{(second-order hessian / local curvature)} \tag{9}\]
Removing constant terms yields the simplified objective at step \(t\):
\[\tilde{\text{Obj}}^{(t)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[g_i f_t(\mathbf{x}_i) + \frac{1}{2}h_i f_t^2(\mathbf{x}_i)\right] + \gamma T + \frac{1}{2}\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{T}w_j^2 \tag{10}\]
This quadratic formulation is exact for squared error loss and provides an effective local quadratic approximation for any twice-differentiable loss function.


Show code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

y_obs = 1.0
F0 = -0.3

F_vals = np.linspace(-2.0, 2.5, 400)
loss_true = 0.5 * (y_obs - F_vals) ** 2

g_i = -(y_obs - F0)
h_i = 1.0

loss_linear = 0.5 * (y_obs - F0) ** 2 + g_i * (F_vals - F0)
loss_quadratic = 0.5 * (y_obs - F0) ** 2 + g_i * (F_vals - F0) + 0.5 * h_i * (F_vals - F0) ** 2

lam = 1.0
delta_vals = np.linspace(-3.0, 3.0, 400)
obj_delta = g_i * delta_vals + 0.5 * (h_i + lam) * delta_vals ** 2
delta_opt = -g_i / (h_i + lam)
obj_opt = g_i * delta_opt + 0.5 * (h_i + lam) * delta_opt ** 2

fig3 = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=[
        "Loss Curve & Taylor Approximation",
        "Quadratic Objective Contribution (with lambda)"
    ]
)

fig3.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=F_vals, y=loss_true, mode="lines",
               line=dict(color="black", width=2.5),
               name="True Loss L(y, F)"),
    row=1, col=1
)
fig3.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=F_vals, y=loss_linear, mode="lines",
               line=dict(color="#f97316", width=1.8, dash="dot"),
               name="Linear Approx (1st Order)"),
    row=1, col=1
)
fig3.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=F_vals, y=loss_quadratic, mode="lines",
               line=dict(color="#2563eb", width=2.0, dash="dash"),
               name="Quadratic Approx (2nd Order)"),
    row=1, col=1
)
fig3.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=[F0], y=[0.5 * (y_obs - F0) ** 2],
               mode="markers",
               marker=dict(color="red", size=10, symbol="circle"),
               name="Expansion Point F_0"),
    row=1, col=1
)

fig3.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=delta_vals, y=obj_delta, mode="lines",
               line=dict(color="#2563eb", width=2.5),
               name="g*Delta + (1/2)(h+lambda)*Delta^2",
               showlegend=True),
    row=1, col=2
)
fig3.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=[delta_opt, delta_opt],
        y=[obj_delta.min() - 0.3, obj_delta.max()],
        mode="lines",
        line=dict(color="red", dash="dash", width=1.8),
        name="Optimal Delta* = -g/(h+lambda)"
    ),
    row=1, col=2
)
fig3.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=[delta_opt], y=[obj_opt],
               mode="markers",
               marker=dict(color="red", size=10),
               name="Analytical Minimum",
               showlegend=False),
    row=1, col=2
)
fig3.add_annotation(
    x=delta_opt, y=obj_opt - 0.5,
    text=f"Delta* = {delta_opt:.2f}",
    showarrow=True, arrowhead=2,
    font=dict(size=12, color="red"),
    row=1, col=2
)

fig3.update_xaxes(title_text="F (Prediction)", row=1, col=1)
fig3.update_yaxes(title_text="Loss L(y, F)", row=1, col=1)
fig3.update_xaxes(title_text="Delta (Prediction Change)", row=1, col=2)
fig3.update_yaxes(title_text="Objective Contribution", row=1, col=2)
fig3.update_layout(
    height=420,
    template="plotly_white",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.35, xanchor="center", x=0.5)
)
fig3.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Second-order Taylor expansion of loss function. Left: true loss curve (black), linear approximation (orange), and quadratic approximation (blue) around expansion point F=-0.3. Right: quadratic objective contribution vs. Delta step, with analytical optimum highlighted.






2.3 Optimal Leaf Weights
Grouping sample indices by terminal leaf node \(j\) (\(I_j = \{i : q(\mathbf{x}_i) = j\}\)):
\[\tilde{\text{Obj}}^{(t)} = \sum_{j=1}^{T}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in I_j}g_i\right)w_j + \frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i\in I_j}h_i + \lambda\right)w_j^2\right] + \gamma T \tag{11}\]
Defining \(G_j = \sum_{i\in I_j} g_i\) and \(H_j = \sum_{i\in I_j} h_i\), solving \(\frac{\partial \tilde{\text{Obj}}}{\partial w_j} = 0\) yields optimal leaf weight \(w_j^*\):
\[w_j^* = -\frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda} \tag{12}\]
Substituting optimal weights back into the objective yields the structure score:
\[\text{Obj}^* = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{T}\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda} + \gamma T \tag{13}\]


2.4 Split Gain Metric
For a node split dividing parent node \(P\) into left (\(L\)) and right (\(R\)) children:
\[\text{Gain} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda} - \frac{G_P^2}{H_P+\lambda}\right] - \gamma \tag{14}\]
If \(\text{Gain} \le 0\), the candidate split is pruned.


Show code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng3 = np.random.default_rng(21)
n3 = 150
X3 = np.sort(rng3.uniform(0, 10, n3))
y3 = 2.0 * np.sin(X3 * 0.8) + rng3.normal(0, 0.5, n3)

F_prev = np.full(n3, y3.mean())
g_vals = -(y3 - F_prev)
h_vals = np.ones(n3)

lam3 = 1.0
G_total = g_vals.sum()
H_total = h_vals.sum()
score_parent = G_total ** 2 / (H_total + lam3)

thresholds = np.unique(X3)[1:-1]
gains = []

for thr in thresholds:
    left_mask = X3 <= thr
    right_mask = ~left_mask
    G_L = g_vals[left_mask].sum()
    H_L = h_vals[left_mask].sum()
    G_R = g_vals[right_mask].sum()
    H_R = h_vals[right_mask].sum()
    if H_L + lam3 <= 0 or H_R + lam3 <= 0:
        gains.append(float("nan"))
        continue
    gain = 0.5 * (G_L ** 2 / (H_L + lam3) + G_R ** 2 / (H_R + lam3) - score_parent)
    gains.append(gain)

gains = np.array(gains)
best_idx = np.nanargmax(gains)
best_thr = thresholds[best_idx]
best_gain = gains[best_idx]

fig4 = go.Figure()

fig4.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=thresholds, y=gains,
    mode="lines",
    fill="tozeroy",
    fillcolor="rgba(37, 99, 235, 0.15)",
    line=dict(color="#2563eb", width=2.0),
    name="Gain"
))
fig4.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[best_thr, best_thr],
    y=[gains.min() - 0.5, best_gain],
    mode="lines",
    line=dict(color="red", dash="dash", width=2.0),
    name=f"Optimal Threshold = {best_thr:.2f}"
))
fig4.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[thresholds.min(), thresholds.max()],
    y=[0, 0],
    mode="lines",
    line=dict(color="gray", dash="dash", width=1.5),
    name="Gain = 0 (Pruning)"
))
fig4.add_annotation(
    x=best_thr, y=best_gain + 0.3,
    text=f"Optimal: thr={best_thr:.2f}, Gain={best_gain:.2f}",
    showarrow=True, arrowhead=2,
    font=dict(size=12, color="red")
)
fig4.update_layout(
    template="plotly_white",
    height=400,
    xaxis_title="Split Threshold",
    yaxis_title="Gain",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.3, xanchor="center", x=0.5)
)
fig4.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Split gain as a function of cut threshold for a synthetic 1D dataset. Dashed red line indicates optimal split threshold (maximum gain). Dashed gray line indicates Gain=0 pruning threshold when gamma=0.






2.5 Approximate Split Finding and Sparsity Awareness
For massive datasets, exact greedy split search is computationally prohibitive. XGBoost employs a weighted quantile sketch strategy to propose candidate split points \(\mathcal{S}_k = \{s_{k1}, s_{k2}, \ldots, s_{kl}\}\) based on feature distributions weighted by hessians \(h_i\) (Chen and Guestrin 2016):
\[\text{rank}_k(z) = \frac{\sum_{(x,h): x_k < z} h}{\sum_{(x,h)} h} \tag{15}\]
XGBoost also features native sparsity awareness: it learns default split directions for missing or zero values at each node, bypassing pre-imputation requirements.
