title: 51  Neural Networks for Classification
text:
1 The Perceptron
Artificial neural networks are computational models inspired by biological neural structures. From Rosenblatt’s 1958 Perceptron (Rosenblatt 1958) to state-of-the-art deep architectures (LeCun et al. 2015), the foundational mathematical skeleton remains invariant: compositions of linear transformations followed by non-linearities, applied hierarchically to input data. The universal approximation theorem (Hornik et al. 1989) establishes that a single-hidden-layer feedforward network with sufficient hidden units can approximate any continuous function on compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) to arbitrary accuracy.

title: 51  Neural Networks for Classification
text:
1.1 Mathematical Model
The Perceptron accepts inputs \(x_1, \ldots, x_d\), computing a linear combination followed by a step activation:
\[z = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = \sum_{i=1}^d w_i x_i + b \tag{1}\]
\[\hat{y} = \text{sign}(z) \in \{-1, +1\} \tag{2}\]
The decision boundary \(\{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = 0\}\) forms a separating hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).


1.2 Learning Rule
For a misclassified instance \((\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\), weights and bias update via:
\[\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta \, y^{(i)} \mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \quad b \leftarrow b + \eta \, y^{(i)} \tag{3}\]
The Perceptron Convergence Theorem guarantees convergence in finite steps \(R^2/\gamma^2\) if the data is linearly separable with geometric margin \(\gamma > 0\) (Rosenblatt 1958).


Show code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

n_per_class = 20
X_neg = rng.multivariate_normal([-2.0, -1.5], [[0.6, 0.1], [0.1, 0.6]], n_per_class)
X_pos = rng.multivariate_normal([2.0, 1.5], [[0.6, 0.1], [0.1, 0.6]], n_per_class)
X = np.vstack([X_neg, X_pos])
y = np.array([-1] * n_per_class + [1] * n_per_class)

w = np.zeros(2)
b = 0.0
eta = 0.3
max_iters = 200
history = [(w.copy(), b, 0)]

converged = False
iteration = 0
while not converged and iteration < max_iters:
    errors = 0
    for i in range(len(y)):
        z = np.dot(w, X[i]) + b
        y_hat = 1 if z >= 0 else -1
        if y_hat != y[i]:
            w = w + eta * y[i] * X[i]
            b = b + eta * y[i]
            errors += 1
    iteration += 1
    history.append((w.copy(), b, errors))
    if errors == 0:
        converged = True

x_range = np.array([-5.0, 5.0])

frames = []
for t, (wt, bt, errs) in enumerate(history):
    scatter_neg = go.Scatter(
        x=X_neg[:, 0], y=X_neg[:, 1],
        mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color="#1f77b4", size=8, symbol="circle"),
        name="Class -1",
        showlegend=(t == 0)
    )
    scatter_pos = go.Scatter(
        x=X_pos[:, 0], y=X_pos[:, 1],
        mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color="#ff7f0e", size=8, symbol="diamond"),
        name="Class +1",
        showlegend=(t == 0)
    )
    if abs(wt[1]) > 1e-10:
        y_line = -(wt[0] * x_range + bt) / wt[1]
        line_trace = go.Scatter(
            x=x_range, y=y_line,
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color="#2ca02c", width=2.5),
            name="Boundary",
            showlegend=(t == 0)
        )
    else:
        line_trace = go.Scatter(x=[], y=[], mode="lines", showlegend=False)

    frames.append(go.Frame(
        data=[scatter_neg, scatter_pos, line_trace],
        name=str(t),
        layout=go.Layout(title_text=f"Iteration {t} | Errors: {errs}")
    ))

init_neg = go.Scatter(x=X_neg[:, 0], y=X_neg[:, 1], mode="markers",
                      marker=dict(color="#1f77b4", size=8, symbol="circle"), name="Class -1")
init_pos = go.Scatter(x=X_pos[:, 0], y=X_pos[:, 1], mode="markers",
                      marker=dict(color="#ff7f0e", size=8, symbol="diamond"), name="Class +1")
init_line = go.Scatter(x=[], y=[], mode="lines",
                       line=dict(color="#2ca02c", width=2.5), name="Boundary")

steps = []
for t in range(len(history)):
    steps.append(dict(
        method="animate",
        args=[[str(t)], dict(mode="immediate", frame=dict(duration=300, redraw=True),
                             transition=dict(duration=0))],
        label=str(t)
    ))

sliders = [dict(
    active=0, steps=steps, x=0.0, y=0.0, len=1.0,
    currentvalue=dict(prefix="Iteration: ", font=dict(size=13)), pad=dict(t=50)
)]

fig = go.Figure(
    data=[init_neg, init_pos, init_line],
    frames=frames,
    layout=go.Layout(
        title="Perceptron Learning Rule Convergence",
        xaxis=dict(range=[-5, 5], title="x1"),
        yaxis=dict(range=[-5, 5], title="x2"),
        sliders=sliders,
        width=680, height=520,
        legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99)
    )
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Perceptron learning convergence on linearly separable data.

title: 51  Neural Networks for Classification
51  Neural Networks for Classification
text:
3 Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) and Backpropagation
Forward propagation at layer \(\ell\):
\[\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)} = \mathbf{A}^{(\ell-1)} \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)} + \mathbf{b}^{(\ell)} \tag{4}\]
\[\mathbf{A}^{(\ell)} = g^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}) \tag{5}\]
Binary Cross-Entropy Loss:
\[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \left[ y^{(i)} \log \hat{y}^{(i)} + (1-y^{(i)}) \log(1-\hat{y}^{(i)}) \right] \tag{6}\]
Output error delta:
\[\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(L)} = \hat{\mathbf{Y}} - \mathbf{Y} \tag{7}\]
Hidden layer error recursion:
\[\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell)} = \left(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell+1)} \mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)\top}\right) \odot g'^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}) \tag{8}\]
Gradients:
\[\nabla_{\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{m} \mathbf{A}^{(\ell-1)\top} \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell)}, \quad \nabla_{\mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell)}_i \tag{9}\]

title: 51  Neural Networks for Classification
51  Neural Networks for Classification
text:
5 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
2D Convolution / Cross-correlation:
\[(I \star K)[i,j] = \sum_{u=0}^{k-1} \sum_{v=0}^{k-1} I[i+u, j+v] \cdot K[u,v] \tag{10}\]
CNN architectures leverage local receptive fields, weight sharing, and translation equivariance (LeCun et al. 1998).

title: 51  Neural Networks for Classification
text:
6 Regularization Techniques

L2 Regularization (Weight Decay): \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}} + \frac{\lambda}{2} \|\mathbf{W}\|_F^2\) {#eq-l2-reg}
Dropout: Randomly zeroes activations with probability \(1-p\) during training (Srivastava et al. 2014).
Batch Normalization: Normalizes activations per mini-batch ?eq-batchnorm.

title: 51  Neural Networks for Classification
text:
7 Summary
Multilayer neural networks combined with non-linear activations and backpropagation provide universal function approximation capabilities. Convolutional layers extend neural models to spatial image grids, while regularization and adaptive optimizers like Adam ensure robust optimization (Goodfellow et al. 2016).

2 PyTorch Fundamentals

2.1 Tensors and Autograd
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} \quad \forall \theta \text{ with } \texttt{requires\_grad=True}
\tag{1}\]
loss.backward() computes gradients automatically via chain rule backpropagation across dynamic computation graphs.

  
    ① train()
    ② zero_grad()
    ③ forward
    ④ backward()
    ⑤ step()
  
  
    
      model.train() — Activates training mode for Dropout/BatchNorm.
    
    
      optimizer.zero_grad() — Clears accumulated gradients before backward pass.
    
    
      logits = model(X_train) — Executes forward pass computation graph.
    
    
      loss.backward() — Computes gradients via autograd reverse graph traversal.
    
    
      optimizer.step() — Applies weight updates using computed gradients.
    
  
  
    ← Previous
    Step 1 / 5
    Next →
  



Numerically stable Binary Cross Entropy with Logits Loss:
\[
\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ \max(z_i, 0) - z_i y_i + \log\left(1 + e^{-|z_i|}\right) \right]
\tag{2}\]

title: 52  Practical Implementation: PyTorch and JAX
text:
3 JAX Fundamentals
JAX relies on pure functions and stateless pytrees.

  
    PyTorch — Imperative
    JAX — Functional
  
  
    Mutable object-oriented model encapsulation holding parameters internally.
  
  
    Stateless pure functions receiving parameters externally as explicit pytree dictionaries.
  


Single-instance scalar Binary Cross Entropy in JAX:
\[
\mathcal{L}(w) = -\left[ y \log \sigma(wx) + (1-y) \log(1 - \sigma(wx)) \right]
\tag{3}\]
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import optax

def loss_fn(params, x, y):
    logits = forward(params, x)
    return optax.sigmoid_binary_cross_entropy(logits, y).mean()

@jax.jit
def train_step(params, opt_state, x, y):
    loss, grads = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn)(params, x, y)
    updates, new_opt_state = optimizer.update(grads, opt_state, params)
    new_params = optax.apply_updates(params, updates)
    return new_params, new_opt_state, loss

title: 53  Introduction to Clustering and Evaluation Metrics
text:
1 The Clustering Problem
Supervised learning derives mappings from labeled instances to generalize predictions onto unseen data. Unsupervised learning operates on unlabeled data to discover underlying structure: grouping similar instances, uncovering latent factors, or constructing low-dimensional representations (Hastie et al. 2009; Bishop 2006).
Clustering is the primary unsupervised learning task. Given observations \(\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n\in\mathbb{R}^p\), the objective is partitioning them into clusters \(C_1,\dots,C_k\) such that within-cluster similarity is maximized relative to between-cluster separation (Aggarwal and Reddy 2013).
Let \(\mathcal{D}=\{\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n\}\) denote \(n\) instances in \(\mathbb{R}^p\). A \(k\)-cluster assignment is defined by mapping:
\[
\ell:\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,k\},
\]
where cluster \(C_j\) contains instances assigned to label \(j\):
\[
C_j=\{\mathbf{x}_i\mid \ell(i)=j\}.
\]
crumbs: 53  Introduction to Clustering and Evaluation Metrics

title: 53  Introduction to Clustering and Evaluation Metrics
text:
2 Distance and Similarity Measures






Definition. Metric Function Properties: 1. \(d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\geq 0\) and \(d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=0\Leftrightarrow\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}\) (positive definiteness), 2. \(d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=d(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})\) (symmetry), 3. \(d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})\leq d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})+d(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})\) (triangle inequality).




2.1 Minkowski Distance Family






Definition. Minkowski Distance of order \(p\ge 1\): \[
d_p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}|x_j-y_j|^p\right)^{1/p}.
\tag{1}\]




\(p=1\): Manhattan (\(L^1\)) distance.
\(p=2\): Euclidean (\(L^2\)) distance.
\(p\to\infty\): Chebyshev (\(L^\infty\)) distance.



Show code
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import euclidean_distances

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=[1, 100], size=(50, 2))

X_std = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

print("Unscaled mean Euclidean distance:", euclidean_distances(X).mean().round(2))
print("Scaled mean Euclidean distance:", euclidean_distances(X_std).mean().round(2))


Unscaled mean Euclidean distance: 81.02
Scaled mean Euclidean distance: 1.76

title: 53  Introduction to Clustering and Evaluation Metrics
text:
3 Internal Evaluation Metrics

3.1 Silhouette Coefficient






Definition. Silhouette Coefficient \(s(i)\): \[
s(i) = \frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}.
\tag{2}\]



where \(a(i)\) is mean intra-cluster distance, and \(b(i)\) is mean nearest-cluster distance (Rousseeuw 1987).


3.2 Davies-Bouldin Index






Definition. Davies-Bouldin Index: \[
\text{DB} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\max_{l\neq k}\frac{\bar{d}_k+\bar{d}_l}{d(k,l)}.
\tag{3}\]



Lower DB values indicate superior cluster compactness and separation (Davies and Bouldin 1979).


3.3 Calinski-Harabasz Index






Definition. Calinski-Harabasz Index: \[
\text{CH} = \frac{\text{SS}_B/(K-1)}{\text{SS}_W/(n-K)}.
\tag{4}\]



Higher CH values denote distinct, dense cluster separations (Caliński and Harabasz 1974).


Show code
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, davies_bouldin_score, calinski_harabasz_score

X, y_true = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=4, cluster_std=0.8, random_state=42)

for k in range(2, 6):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X)
    s = silhouette_score(X, labels)
    db = davies_bouldin_score(X, labels)
    ch = calinski_harabasz_score(X, labels)
    print(f"k={k} | Silhouette: {s:.3f} | Davies-Bouldin: {db:.3f} | Calinski-Harabasz: {ch:.1f}")

title: 53  Introduction to Clustering and Evaluation Metrics
text:
4 External Evaluation Metrics

4.1 Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)






Definition. Adjusted Rand Index: \[
\text{ARI} = \frac{\text{RI} - \mathbb{E}[\text{RI}]}{\max(\text{RI}) - \mathbb{E}[\text{RI}]}.
\tag{5}\]



ARI measures pair agreement against ground-truth partition, adjusted for chance (Hubert and Arabie 1985).
crumbs: 53  Introduction to Clustering and Evaluation Metrics

title: 53  Introduction to Clustering and Evaluation Metrics
text:
5 Summary
Unsupervised clustering organizes unlabeled data using geometric or probabilistic distance metrics. Internal evaluation metrics (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz) validate cluster quality without ground-truth labels, while external metrics (ARI, NMI) measure agreement against reference partitions.

title: 54  K-Means and K-Medoids
text:
1 K-Means Objective Function
K-Means is the most widely deployed clustering algorithm due to its conceptual simplicity, linear computational scaling per iteration, and interpretable mean-centroid cluster representations (MacQueen 1967; Lloyd 1982).
K-Means partitions \(n\) instances into \(k\) clusters \(C_1,\dots,C_k\) minimizing within-cluster sum-of-squares (WCSS):

title: 54  K-Means and K-Medoids
text:
Definition. K-Means WCSS Objective: \[
J(C_1,\dots,C_k) = \sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in C_j}\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2,
\tag{1}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_j = \frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in C_j}\mathbf{x}\) denotes the centroid vector of cluster \(j\).

title: 54  K-Means and K-Medoids
text:
2 Lloyd’s Algorithm






Lloyd’s K-Means Algorithm: 1. Initialize: Select \(k\) initial centroids \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\). 2. Assignment Step: Assign each instance \(\mathbf{x}_i\) to nearest centroid: \[\ell(i) = \arg\min_{j} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2\] 3. Update Step: Recompute centroids as mean of assigned points: \[\boldsymbol{\mu}_j = \frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{\ell(i)=j}\mathbf{x}_i\] 4. Convergence: Repeat steps 2-3 until cluster assignments stabilize.

title: 54  K-Means and K-Medoids
text:
3 K-Means++ Initialization
Standard random initialization is vulnerable to suboptimal local minima. K-Means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007) selects initial centroids using distance-proportional sampling \(P(\mathbf{x}_i) \propto D(\mathbf{x}_i)^2\), bounding expected WCSS within \(O(\log k)\) of global optimum.

title: 54  K-Means and K-Medoids
text:
4 K-Medoids (PAM)
K-Medoids represents clusters using actual exemplar data points (medoids) rather than spatial means, offering robustness against outliers (Kaufman and Rousseeuw 1990).






Definition. Medoid Selection: \[
\mathbf{m}_j = \arg\min_{\mathbf{x}\in C_j}\sum_{\mathbf{x}'\in C_j}d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}').
\tag{2}\]





Show code
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=4, cluster_std=0.7, random_state=7)

wcss = []
for k in range(1, 7):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
    km.fit(X)
    wcss.append(km.inertia_)
    print(f"k={k} | WCSS: {km.inertia_:.2f}")

title: 54  K-Means and K-Medoids
text:
5 Summary
K-Means partitions vector spaces by minimizing squared Euclidean distance from centroids. K-Means++ mitigates initialization sensitivity, while K-Medoids replaces cluster means with actual medoid observations to improve outlier robustness (MacQueen 1967; Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007; Kaufman and Rousseeuw 1990).

title: 55  Hierarchical Clustering
text:
1 Agglomerative Linkage Criteria
Hierarchical clustering constructs a tree-like nested decomposition (dendrogram) of instances rather than a flat partition. Users cut the dendrogram at height thresholds to extract arbitrary \(k\)-cluster partitions (Hastie et al. 2009; Aggarwal and Reddy 2013).

title: 55  Hierarchical Clustering
text:
Single Linkage: \(d_{\text{single}}(C_i,C_j) = \min_{\mathbf{x}\in C_i,\mathbf{y}\in C_j} d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\) {#eq-single-linkage}
Complete Linkage: \(d_{\text{complete}}(C_i,C_j) = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in C_i,\mathbf{y}\in C_j} d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\) {#eq-complete-linkage}
Average Linkage (UPGMA): \(d_{\text{avg}}(C_i,C_j) = \frac{1}{|C_i||C_j|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in C_i}\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in C_j}d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\) {#eq-average-linkage}
Ward Linkage: Minimizes increase in intra-cluster variance upon merge (Ward 1963): \[d_{\text{Ward}}(C_i,C_j) = \frac{|C_i||C_j|}{|C_i|+|C_j|}\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2 \tag{1}\]

    Select linkage criterion and adjust cutoff threshold
  
  
    Linkage:
    
      Ward

title: 55  Hierarchical Clustering
text:
2 Cophenetic Correlation






Definition. Cophenetic Correlation Coefficient \(r_c\): \[
r_c = \text{corr}(d_{ij}, c_{ij}),
\tag{2}\] where \(d_{ij}\) is original pairwise distance and \(c_{ij}\) is dendrogram cophenetic merge distance.





Show code
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, cophenet
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=80, centers=3, cluster_std=0.8, random_state=42)

for method in ["single", "complete", "average", "ward"]:
    Z = linkage(X, method=method)
    c, _ = cophenet(Z, pdist(X))
    print(f"Method: {method:10s} | Cophenetic r: {c:.4f}")

Hierarchical clustering builds binary dendrograms without requiring prior cluster count specification (\(k\)). Linkage criteria (Single, Complete, Average, Ward) control merge dynamics (Hastie et al. 2009; Ward 1963).

title: 56  DBSCAN and HDBSCAN
text:
1 Fundamental Definitions
Unlike K-Means or hierarchical methods which assume convex or compact clusters, density-based algorithms partition data by discovering contiguous regions of high point density separated by low-density noise (Ester et al. 1996).
DBSCAN requires two parameters: neighborhood radius \(\varepsilon\) and minimum points threshold \(\text{minPts}\).
Point Categorization: - Core Point: \(|N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x})|\geq\text{minPts}\). - Border Point: \(|N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x})|<\text{minPts}\) but \(\mathbf{x} \in N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{y})\) where \(\mathbf{y}\) is a core point. - Noise Point: Neither core nor border point.

title: 56  DBSCAN and HDBSCAN
text:
Definition. \(\varepsilon\)-Neighborhood: \[
N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}) = \{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{D} \mid d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\leq\varepsilon\}.
\tag{1}\]





  
    DBSCAN — ε-Neighborhood Explorer
    Adjust ε and minPts parameters to visualize core, border, and noise designations
  
  
    ε = 0.9
      
    minPts = 3

title: 56  DBSCAN and HDBSCAN
text:
2 HDBSCAN
Hierarchical DBSCAN (HDBSCAN) builds a hierarchical tree of density-based clusters, extracting persistent clusters across varying densities (Campello et al. 2013).






Definition. Mutual Reachability Distance: \[
d_{\text{mreach},k}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \max\{d_k(\mathbf{x}),\; d_k(\mathbf{y}),\; d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\},
\tag{2}\] where \(d_k(\mathbf{x})\) is the distance to the \(k\)-nearest neighbor of \(\mathbf{x}\).





Show code
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
import numpy as np

X, y_true = make_moons(n_samples=300, noise=0.05, random_state=42)

db = DBSCAN(eps=0.15, min_samples=5)
labels = db.fit_predict(X)

n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_noise = np.sum(labels == -1)

print(f"Clusters discovered: {n_clusters}")
print(f"Noise instances: {n_noise} ({100*n_noise/len(X):.1f}%)")


Clusters discovered: 2
Noise instances: 0 (0.0%)

text:
3 Summary
DBSCAN and HDBSCAN identify non-spherical clusters of arbitrary geometric shapes without requiring a prior specified cluster count \(k\), automatically isolating noise instances (Ester et al. 1996; Campello et al. 2013).

title: 57  t-SNE, UMAP, and Non-Linear Dimensionality Reduction
text:
1 t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding)
High-dimensional spaces pose visualization and computational challenges. Linear techniques like PCA project data onto variance-maximizing orthogonal axes (Jolliffe 2002). However, non-linear manifolds require methods preserving local topological relationships (Maaten and Hinton 2008; McInnes et al. 2018).
t-SNE models high-dimensional pairwise conditional similarities via Gaussian distributions and low-dimensional similarities via heavy-tailed Student-\(t\) distributions (Maaten and Hinton 2008).
High-dimensional conditional similarity:
\[
p_{j|i} = \frac{\exp\left(-\|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j\|^2/(2\sigma_i^2)\right)}{\sum_{k\neq i}\exp\left(-\|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_k\|^2/(2\sigma_i^2)\right)}
\tag{1}\]
Symmetric joint probability: \(p_{ij} = (p_{j|i}+p_{i|j})/(2n)\).
Low-dimensional Student-\(t\) Cauchy similarity:
\[
q_{ij} = \frac{(1+\|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j\|^2)^{-1}}{\sum_{k\neq l}(1+\|\mathbf{y}_k-\mathbf{y}_l\|^2)^{-1}}
\tag{2}\]
Kullback-Leibler divergence objective:
\[
C = \text{KL}(P\|Q) = \sum_{i\neq j} p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}
\tag{3}\]

2 UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection)
UMAP preserves local and global manifold structure via fuzzy simplicial sets (McInnes et al. 2018):
\[
v_{j|i} = \exp\left(-\frac{d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)-\rho_i}{\sigma_i}\right)
\tag{4}\]

t-SNE and UMAP compress high-dimensional feature spaces for low-dimensional non-linear visualization. UMAP preserves global topological relationships better and scales computationally to large datasets (Maaten and Hinton 2008; McInnes et al. 2018).

title: Appendix B — Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms
text:
B.1 A
This glossary consolidates the core terms and definitions covered throughout the theoretical and technical modules of the course, including cloud infrastructure, data storage, processing, and governance.

title: Appendix B — Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms
text:
Advanced Provisioning: A cloud delivery model in which the user enters into a formal agreement with the cloud service provider and pays a fixed price or is billed monthly.
Apache Hadoop: An open-source framework that enables distributed storage and processing of large datasets across clusters of computers using simple programming models.
Archival Policy: A guideline defining where, how, and for how long data should be stored after an analytics project has concluded.
Audit (Data Audit): A formal and systematic examination of how users access and utilize data, designed to ensure compliance with security policies and identify vulnerabilities.
Autoscaling: A cloud service that monitors applications and automatically adjusts compute capacity (scaling up or down) based on real-time demand.
crumbs: B  Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms

title: Appendix B — Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms
text:
B.2 B

Backend Platform: The collection of physical and logical components within a cloud architecture that support system execution (servers, networks, storage).
Batch Processing: A data processing method consisting of collecting a large volume of transactions or operations over a period of time and processing them together in a single execution.
Business Data Request: A formal question or requirement submitted by a business area that can be answered or resolved through data extraction and analysis.
crumbs: B  Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms

title: Appendix B — Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms
text:
B.3 C

Cloud Data Storage: A technology solution that enables organizations to store, access, and maintain digital data on remote servers managed by a service provider (e.g., Google Cloud Storage).
Complex Data Types: Non-primitive data structures (such as Arrays and Structs) used in modern databases like BigQuery to store nested records and optimize query performance on denormalized data.
crumbs: B  Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms

title: Appendix B — Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms
text:
B.4 D

Data Catalog: A centralized inventory of an organization’s data assets providing detailed metadata to help analysts discover, understand, and evaluate the quality of available sources.
Data Governance: The set of processes, policies, roles, and standards that ensure the secure, reliable, and efficient use of data within an organization.
Data Lake: A storage repository that holds large volumes of raw data in its native format (structured, semi-structured, or unstructured) until needed for analysis.
Data Warehouse: A relational database system optimized for data analytics (OLAP) that consolidates cleansed information from multiple transactional systems (OLTP).
crumbs: B  Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms

title: Appendix B — Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms
text:

Normalization: A database design technique that organizes relational tables to minimize data redundancy and enforce referential integrity.
crumbs: B  Unified Glossary of Data and Cloud Computing Terms

Streaming Processing: A data processing method that continuously analyzes and transforms records in real time as they are generated by source systems.

title: Appendix C — Preparation for Analytics Interviews
text:
C.1 1. The Importance of the Thought Process
In technical recruitment for analytics, data mining, and data engineering roles, interviews and coding assessments no longer focus solely on whether you memorize exact SQL syntax or Scikit-Learn function signatures. Interviewers primarily evaluate how you reason through and solve complex problems.
Structuring your thought process clearly demonstrates to employers that: * You navigate ambiguity (ill-defined business problems) effectively. * You test hypotheses systematically rather than jumping to conclusions. * You prioritize business impact over algorithmic complexity. * You communicate technical findings clearly to non-technical stakeholders.

title: Appendix C — Preparation for Analytics Interviews
text:
C.2 2. The 4-Step Problem-Solving Framework
When presented with an open-ended business case or technical interview problem, avoid blurting out an immediate solution. Instead, use this 4-step framework to guide your interviewer through your solution:
graph TD
    P1["Step 1: Understand & Scope<br>(Ask business questions)"]
    --> P2["Step 2: Data & Hypotheses<br>(Identify sources and metrics)"]
    --> P3["Step 3: Analytical Methodology<br>(ETL, EDA, Modeling)"]
    --> P4["Step 4: Impact & Communication<br>(Stakeholder Results)"]

C.2.1 Step 1: Understand and Scope the Problem

What to do: Ask clarifying questions to define the problem’s scope. Never make assumptions.
Useful phrasing:

“Before designing the schema, what is the primary business goal for this analysis?”
“Are we measuring customer retention on a monthly or annual basis?”




C.2.2 Step 2: Formulate Hypotheses and Identify Data Sources

What to do: Propose required variables and data sources. Explain which assumptions you intend to validate.
Useful phrasing:

“My hypothesis is that churning customers exhibit low login frequency over the last 15 days. To test this, I need user activity logs and subscription tables.”




C.2.3 Step 3: Define Analytical Methodology

What to do: Walk through your data pipeline step by step (from ingestion and EDA to model training and evaluation).
Useful phrasing:

“First, I’ll clean and impute missing historical fields, then conduct exploratory data analysis (EDA) to evaluate feature correlations. If the goal is predictive, I’d train an XGBoost model evaluated primarily on Recall, as false negatives are costly here.”




C.2.4 Step 4: Translate to Business Impact

What to do: Conclude by articulating how you would present actionable recommendations to executive stakeholders.
Useful phrasing:

“Finally, I would deliver an interactive dashboard highlighting estimated cost savings achieved by retaining 10% of high-risk customers identified by the model.”

title: Appendix C — Preparation for Analytics Interviews
text:
C.3 3. Common Practice Interview Cases

C.3.1 Case 1: Designing an Ingestion Pipeline

Interviewer Question: “Our mobile app generates millions of clickstream events per second, and we need daily analytics to optimize product recommendations. How would you design this architecture?”


Recommended approach:

Classify processing requirements: Identify the hybrid nature (continuous streaming ingestion, batch analytical aggregation).
Propose cloud ecosystem tools: Recommend low-cost object storage (e.g., Google Cloud Storage) for raw streams and a distributed computing framework (e.g., PySpark) for nightly batch processing.
Incorporate governance: Highlight the need for a data catalog to index semi-structured JSON schemas.




C.3.2 Case 2: Selecting Evaluation Metrics

Interviewer Question: “We built an e-commerce fraud detection model achieving 99% overall Accuracy. Should we deploy it to production?”


Recommended approach:

Challenge the metric: Explain that on severely imbalanced datasets (e.g., fraud where only 0.1% of transactions are fraudulent), accuracy is misleading (a naive model predicting ‘No Fraud’ for everything yields 99.9% accuracy).
Propose appropriate metrics: Recommend F1-Score, Precision, or Recall depending on the relative business costs of False Positives (blocking legitimate customers) versus False Negatives (allowing fraudulent transactions).
